					<description><![CDATA[Taiwan&#8217;s National Taxation Bureau of Taipei, Ministry of Finance, on 29 July 2026 issued guidance reminding profit-seeking enterprises that only realised foreign exchange gains and losses may be recognised for profit-seeking enterprise income tax purposes. The guidance states that book differences arising solely from exchange rate adjustments do not constitute actual gains or losses and...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Taiwan&#8217;s National Taxation Bureau of Taipei, Ministry of Finance, on 29 July 2026 issued <a href="https://www.mof.gov.tw/Eng/singlehtml/f48d641f159a4866b1d31c0916fbcc71?cntId=3ace5701c8004a3ea782529f59409f07" target="_blank" rel="noopener">guidance </a>reminding profit-seeking enterprises that only realised foreign exchange gains and losses may be recognised for profit-seeking enterprise income tax purposes.</p>
<p>The guidance states that book differences arising solely from exchange rate adjustments do not constitute actual gains or losses and therefore may not be recognised when determining taxable income.</p>
<p>The Bureau said the clarification is based on Articles 29 and 98 of the Regulations Governing Assessment of Profit-seeking Enterprise Income Tax, which provide that foreign exchange gains and losses are recognised as income or deductible losses only when they have been realised.</p>
<p><strong>Unrealised exchange differences not recognised</strong></p>
<p>According to the Bureau, book differences created solely by exchange rate adjustments are not regarded as current-year income and cannot be claimed as deductible losses for tax purposes.</p>
<p>Although financial accounting rules require foreign currency deposits to be translated using the year-end exchange rate, with the resulting adjustments recorded as foreign exchange gains or losses in the financial statements, these amounts remain unrealised. Consequently, they must not be reported as foreign exchange gains or losses when filing a profit-seeking enterprise income tax return.</p>
<p><strong>Bureau reminds businesses to comply</strong></p>
<p>The Bureau urged profit-seeking enterprises to pay close attention to the applicable tax regulations when reporting foreign exchange gains and losses. It warned that incorrectly reporting unrealised exchange differences could result in adjustments to tax filings and additional tax assessments following a review by the tax authorities.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Bahrain&#8217;s National Bureau for Revenue (NBR) has published an updated <a href="https://www.nbr.gov.bh/publications/view/Excise_Registration_Manual" target="_blank" rel="noopener">excise registration manual</a> on 28 July 2026, setting out revised guidance for excise payers on using the online excise portal and the procedures for submitting key excise-related applications.</p>
<p>The updated manual outlines the processes for excise registration and deregistration, managing products on the excise goods list, and applying for and administering excise warehouse licences. It also explains the steps required for different application types submitted through the NBR&#8217;s online system.</p>
<p><strong>Excise registration requirements</strong></p>
<p>The manual states that all entities involved in the commercial production, importing or storage of excise goods in Bahrain must register with the National Bureau for Revenue (NBR).</p>
<p>Applicants are required to create a profile through the NBR website, provide entity information including identification, address and business activity, and submit supporting documents such as Commercial Registration Certificates and bank IBAN documents.</p>
<p>The guidance also states that amendments to registration details must be submitted at least 30 days before the changes take effect.</p>
<p>For deregistration, excise payers must settle all outstanding liabilities and cancel any active excise warehouse licences before an application can be completed.</p>
<p><strong>Excise goods list management</strong></p>
<p>The manual explains that the NBR maintains the official list of excisable products permitted in Bahrain. Businesses may not import, produce or store products that are not included on the excise goods list.</p>
<p>Excise payers may apply to add new products to the list, with up to 100 products permitted in a single application, either individually or through a bulk upload template.</p>
<p>Applications may also be submitted to update existing product information, including brand, producer, item name or base price. The NBR generally processes these product update requests within seven working days.</p>
<p><strong>Excise warehouse procedures</strong></p>
<p>The guidance outlines the operation of excise warehouses under an excise suspension arrangement, allowing excise goods to be produced or stored without immediate payment of Excise. Liability arises when the goods are released from the warehouse.</p>
<p>To obtain an excise warehouse licence, an applicant must be registered for Excise and operate a facility located in Bahrain but outside Customs jurisdictions.</p>
<p>The manual states that renewal applications must be submitted within the 90-day period before a licence expires. If a licence is not renewed, all goods held in the warehouse immediately become liable for Excise.</p>
<p>Warehouse licences must also be cancelled if the warehouse remains unused for more than 90 days or if the company&#8217;s Commercial Registration (CR) expires.</p>
<p><strong>Online application process</strong></p>
<p>According to the manual, all applications must be submitted through the NBR&#8217;s online portal, with Google Chrome identified as the preferred browser.</p>
<p>The NBR generally processes excise registration and warehouse-related applications within 30 days, while product update requests are typically processed within seven working days.</p>
<p>Where an application is rejected because of missing information, applicants generally have 30 calendar days to provide the required amendments and resubmit the application before the request is automatically cancelled by the system.</p>

		<link>https://regfollower.com/australia-updates-globe-minimum-tax-provisions-on-cfc-interaction-deferred-tax-assets-flow-through-entities/?utm_source=rss&#038;utm_medium=rss&#038;utm_campaign=australia-updates-globe-minimum-tax-provisions-on-cfc-interaction-deferred-tax-assets-flow-through-entities</link>

					<description><![CDATA[Australia has issued the Taxation (Multinational—Global and Domestic Minimum Tax) Amendment (2026 Measures No. 2) Rules 2026 (the Amending Rules), introducing minor amendments to the Taxation (Multinational—Global and Domestic Minimum Tax) Rules 2024 to maintain consistency with the OECD&#8217;s Global Anti-Base Erosion (GloBE) Model Rules. This legal instrument also updates technical procedures for calculating effective...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Australia has issued the <a href="https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2026L00908/asmade/text" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Taxation (Multinational—Global and Domestic Minimum Tax) Amendment (2026 Measures No. 2) Rules 2026 (the Amending Rules)</a>, introducing minor amendments to the Taxation (Multinational—Global and Domestic Minimum Tax) Rules 2024 to maintain consistency with the OECD&#8217;s Global Anti-Base Erosion (GloBE) Model Rules.</p>
<p>This legal instrument also updates technical procedures for calculating effective tax rates and managing foreign tax credits. Key revisions focus on the allocation of taxes under controlled foreign company regimes and the treatment of deferred tax assets arising from domestic losses. Furthermore, the rules clarify the status of flow-through entities and adjust timelines for specific safe harbour provisions. These amendments ensure that local tax administration remains aligned with international standards for multinational taxation.</p>
<p>The instrument commences on the day after registration and applies retrospectively in relation to fiscal years starting on and after 1 January 2024.</p>
<p><strong>Key areas covered in Schedule 1</strong></p>
<p><strong>New GloBE rule fixes how Blended CFC regimes interact with jurisdictional ETR (Part 1) </strong></p>
<p>A new section 4-56 defines the GloBE Jurisdictional ETR for tested entities and permanent establishments, setting out three calculation paths depending on whether an MNE Group uses standard ETR rules, qualifies for a safe harbour (Transitional CbCR or QDMTT), or relies on Qualified Financial Statements.</p>
<p>The substantive change sits in the adjustments. CFC taxes get stripped out of the standard ETR calculation entirely, since they&#8217;re not supposed to count toward a jurisdiction&#8217;s own tax take. But where a Blended CFC Tax Regime allows the parent to claim foreign tax credits, the rule adds back the QDMTT payable into the mix. That&#8217;s the piece worth flagging for clients running blended CFC structures: It stops top-up tax from being effectively cancelled out by a domestic minimum tax credit claimed at the CFC regime level.</p>
<p><strong>Substitute loss carry-forward DTA (Part 2)</strong></p>
<p>The amending rules replaces section 4-95 to define when a Constituent Entity has a Substitute Loss Carry-forward Deferred Tax Asset (DTA). It arises when local tax laws require foreign source income (from CFCs, hybrid entities, or permanent establishments) to offset domestic tax losses before applying foreign tax credits. The amending rules also establish precise valuation formulas based on the applicable jurisdictional tax rate and credit carry-forwards or income recharacterisation rules, while updating rules on taking account of DTA reversals in deferred tax expenses.</p>
<p><strong>Flow-through &amp; tax transparent entities (Part 3)</strong></p>
<p>The amending rules introduce the concept of a reference entity for flow-through entities, refine the definition of a tax transparent entity by linking fiscal transparency to the jurisdiction of the reference entity, and clarify that an entity located in a jurisdiction with no corporate income tax system is treated as a Hybrid Entity if it is fiscally transparent in its owner&#8217;s jurisdiction.</p>
<p><strong>Administration &amp; safe harbours (Part 4)</strong></p>
<p>The amending rules insert section 8-95 providing detailed rules for allocating profit/loss, total revenue, and simplified covered taxes between Investment Entities and their Constituent Entity-owners under the Transitional CbCR Safe Harbour.</p>
<p>It also adds section 8-201, enabling an MNE Group to deem its Jurisdictional Top-up Tax to be zero for a stateless jurisdiction if the actual jurisdiction of creation or business location applies to an eligible QDMTT and an annual election is made.</p>
<p>Furthermore, the rules extend specific transitional relief years in Chapter 8 (e.g., updating year references from 2026/2028 to 2027/2029).</p>
]]></content:encoded>

					<description><![CDATA[The South African Revenue Service (SARS) has outlined the requirements and procedures for registered importers making qualifying advance import payments under South African Reserve Bank (SARB) regulations. Importers applying for advance foreign exchange payments of ZAR 100,000.00 and above must submit an Advance Payment Notification (APN) through SARS eFiling before requesting payment from an authorised...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The South African Revenue Service (SARS) has outlined the requirements and procedures for registered importers making qualifying advance import payments under South African Reserve Bank (SARB) regulations. Importers applying for advance foreign exchange payments of ZAR 100,000.00 and above must submit an Advance Payment Notification (APN) through SARS eFiling before requesting payment from an authorised dealer.</p>
<p>The APN requirement forms part of the regulatory framework governing Advance Import Payments (AIP) and applies only to importers registered with Customs.</p>
<p><strong>Scope and eligibility</strong></p>
<p>The APN requirement applies to advance foreign exchange payments of ZAR 100,000.00 and above. Importers must be registered with Customs before submitting an APN, and the general Customs client number (70707070) cannot be used for this purpose.</p>
<p>SARS said APNs can only be submitted through an Organisation Tax Practitioner’s eFiling profile, as the functionality is not available through individual portfolios.</p>
<p>The notification must be completed and submitted via eFiling before the importer applies to an authorised dealer to process the advance payment.</p>
<p><strong>APN submission process</strong></p>
<p>Importers must access the Submit New Advance Payment Notification option under the Customs menu in SARS eFiling.</p>
<p>The submission requires details including the Customs code, importer name and physical address, authorised dealer, foreign currency amount and currency code, estimated ZAR amount, country of export, supplier name, and the description or reason for the payment.</p>
<p>At least one supporting document must accompany the notification, such as a Purchase Order, Contract, Pro-forma Invoice or Commercial Invoice.</p>
<p>Once all mandatory information has been validated, SARS issues a unique APN reference number, which must be provided to the authorised dealer.</p>
<p><strong>Amendments and validity</strong></p>
<p>An APN may be amended or cancelled through eFiling if the information is incorrect or no longer current, provided the authorised dealer has not yet transferred the payment to the foreign supplier.</p>
<p>If the authorised dealer does not make the payment within 30 days of the APN being submitted to SARS, the notification is automatically cancelled.</p>
<p><strong>Bank generated APNs</strong></p>
<p>In limited circumstances, authorised dealers may issue a Bank Generated APN (BGA). This may occur where pre-payment notification was impractical, a SARS system failure prevented submission, or exchange rate movements caused a payment initially below ZAR 100,000 to exceed the threshold.</p>
<p>Where a BGA has been issued, the importer must still notify SARS by submitting a new APN or amending an existing notification to include the BGA reference before lodging a goods declaration.</p>
<p><strong>Goods declaration requirements</strong></p>
<p>Following an advance payment, importers must submit a valid goods declaration to customs within four months of the payment date. The declaration must include the APN reference number in the additional information field. After the declaration has been released, a copy must be provided to the authorised dealer as proof of release.</p>
<p><strong>Correspondence and supporting documents</strong></p>
<p>Where a goods declaration is not submitted within the required four-month period, SARS may open a case and request supporting documentation.</p>
<p>Correspondence relating to such requests is available through the SARS Correspondence section under the Returns menu in eFiling. Supporting documents must be uploaded in PDF format, be clearly named, and not exceed 5MB per file.</p>
<p>Importers are required to ensure all requested documents have been successfully attached before selecting Confirm to submit them to SARS for processing.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

					<description><![CDATA[Azerbaijan’s tax authority has published a new administrative guidance clarifying the tax treatment of employees&#8217; meal expenses, including their deductibility, income tax withholding obligations, and the calculation of social insurance contributions. The AZN 5 threshold Employers can deduct meal expenses up to AZN 5 per employee per day, regardless of how the expense is structured—direct...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Azerbaijan’s tax authority has published a new administrative guidance clarifying the tax treatment of employees&#8217; meal expenses, including their deductibility, income tax withholding obligations, and the calculation of social insurance contributions.</p>
<p><strong>The AZN 5 threshold</strong></p>
<p>Employers can deduct meal expenses up to AZN 5 per employee per day, regardless of how the expense is structured—direct cash payments, employer-provided catering, or invoices from external caterers. This limit comes from Article 119.2 of the Tax Code and the Cabinet of Ministers&#8217; Resolution on deductible food, housing, and representation expenses.</p>
<p>The key rule is that meal expenses that remain within the daily limit of AZN 5 are not treated as taxable income for employees. Consequently, they are exempt from both personal income tax and mandatory state social insurance contributions.</p>
<p>Three conditions apply for employers paying employees directly. First, non-cash payments must clearly state they&#8217;re for meal expenses. Second, if purchasing from external caterers, the electronic invoice must specifically reference employee meals. Third, if supplying food directly, all purchase contracts, invoices, and customs documents must follow Tax Code requirements.</p>
<p><strong>Excess payments and catering exceptions</strong></p>
<p>Once meal expenses exceed AZN 5 per day, the overage becomes taxable income subject to income tax and social contributions. But there&#8217;s a carve-out: when an employer purchases catering services from a registered caterer via electronic invoice, or provides meals directly to staff, those amounts escape taxation entirely, regardless of how much is spent. The distinction matters—the delivery method, not the amount, determines the tax outcome.</p>
<p>Food expenses at any level never count toward unemployment insurance or compulsory health insurance premiums, since they&#8217;re classified as social benefits rather than salary.</p>
<p><strong>VAT recovery on meal expenses</strong></p>
<p>VAT treatment depends on the employer&#8217;s setup. VAT-registered businesses that buy catering services externally can offset VAT on the portion of meals within the AZN 5 norm (AZN 0.76 per employee, leaving AZN 4.24 as the VAT-free base).</p>
<p>Direct employee payments or employer-supplied meals incur no VAT.</p>
<p>However, VAT compensation is blocked for social expenses generally. The exception applies only to representation, housing, and meal costs when delivered through the specific channels outlined above—and only for businesses whose operations are classified as entertainment or social in nature.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Belarusian Council of Ministers has issued <a href="https://pravo.by/document/?guid=12551&amp;p0=C22600369" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Resolution No. 369</a> on 23 July 2026, expanding VAT relief for businesses importing goods. <p>Resolution No. 369 reaffirms and extends that measure through 30 June 2027, giving importers continued breathing room on cash flow while goods move through the supply chain.</p>
<p>The resolution was published on 24 July 2026 and entered into force on 25 July 2026.</p>
<p>Businesses already using VAT deferrals under the 2022 decree can continue without interruption under these terms.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The OECD’s Global Forum on Transparency and Exchange of Information for Tax Purposes (Global Forum) has <a href="https://www.oecd.org/en/networks/global-forum-tax-transparency/news-events/2026/cook-islands-namibia-and-tanzania-receive-positive-ratings-on-transparency-and-exchange-of-information-on-request-for-tax-purposes.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">published</a> three new peer review reports on transparency and exchange of information on request (EOIR) for tax purposes for the Cook Islands, Namibia and Tanzania on 29 July 2026.</p>
<p>The reports were approved by the Global Forum’s Peer Review and Monitoring Group in June 2026 and subsequently adopted by the Global Forum members. All three jurisdictions were rated overall as “Largely Compliant” with the EOIR standard.</p>
<p>Since 2016, 135 jurisdictions have been fully reviewed by the Global Forum and the <a href="https://www.oecd.org/en/networks/global-forum-tax-transparency/resources/exchange-of-information-on-request-ratings.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">ratings assigned</a> are positive: 91% of the jurisdictions are rated “Compliant” or “Largely Compliant” with the standard, 6% are assessed as “Partially Compliant”, and 3% as “Non-Compliant”.</p>
<p>A summary of the jurisdiction-specific findings and recommendations are as follows:</p>
<p><strong>The Cook Islands</strong> joined the Global Forum in 2009. In this second review of its EOIR practice, it maintains its Largely Compliant rating. The Cook Islands has made a number of improvements to its transparency framework, designed to strengthen the availability of legal and beneficial ownership information under both its anti-money laundering framework and company law. The coverage of these frameworks and a robust supervision of the international financial sector have ensured the Cooks Islands is equipped to satisfy requests for information related to that sector. While exchange of information on the domestic sector has rarely been necessary, some areas for improvement were identified to ensure the availability of information in all cases. The Cook Islands is also recommended to further strengthen its supervision and enforcement of laws relied upon to ensure the availability of ownership and identity information, as well as accounting information. The Cook Islands has shown improvements since its previous review in the quality and timeliness of responses to requests from exchange partners.  <a href="https://doi.org/10.1787/6eb14e18-en" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Access the report</a></p>
<p><strong>Namibia</strong> joined the Global Forum in 2019. In this first full assessment, Namibia is rated as overall Largely Compliant with the EOIR standard. Namibia’s legal and regulatory framework contains requirements relating to the availability of legal and beneficial ownership, accounting and banking information. The peer review report points to areas for improvement, including the availability of information where nominee arrangements are used, the retention of records when a bank ceases its operations in Namibia, as well as ensuring the confidentiality of the exchanged information. Since commencing exchanges in 2022, Namibia has strengthened its practices, demonstrating notable improvements in the timeliness of exchanges. Continued efforts in this direction are encouraged to ensure further progress. The supervision of entities with respect to their tax and beneficial ownership reporting requirements are also noted as important areas of improvement.  <a href="https://doi.org/10.1787/60b2024d-en" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Access the report</a></p>
<p><strong>Tanzania</strong> joined the Global Forum in 2015. In this first full assessment, Tanzania is rated as overall Largely Compliant with the EOIR standard. Tanzania’s legal and regulatory framework generally provides for the availability of legal and beneficial ownership information, accounting information and banking information in mainland Tanzania and Zanzibar. Some gaps are noted in respect of nominee arrangements, bearer share warrants in Zanzibar and in the definition of beneficial ownership and ensuring such information is kept up-to-date. Tanzania also needs to further implement its supervisory and oversight mechanisms to check non-compliance in ensuring the availability of legal and beneficial ownership and accounting information. Due to its small treaty network, Tanzania’s EOIR experience has been limited, but this may change, especially as it works towards broadening its exchange relationships. The report also notes that Tanzania needs to monitor its organisational resources and processes to ensure effective exchange of information.  <a href="https://doi.org/10.1787/55831c5b-en" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Access the report </a></p>

The agreement confirms that, under the Repetro-Sped regime, the same legal entity may simultaneously act as both a consortium...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Brazilian Federal Revenue Service (RFB) has <a href="https://www.gov.br/receitafederal/pt-br/assuntos/noticias/2026/julho/receita-federal-e-petrobras-firmam-termo-de-consensualidade-antes-de-uma-fiscalizacao" target="_blank" rel="noopener">published </a>the Executive Declaratory <a href="https://normasinternet2.receita.fazenda.gov.br/#/consulta/externa/152470" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Act Sutri No. 4/2026</a>, dated 21 July 2026, formally binding both the tax authority and Petrobras to Consensual Agreement No. 3/2026 on 24 July 2026.</p>
<p>The agreement confirms that, under the Repetro-Sped regime, the same legal entity may simultaneously act as both a consortium operator and a service provider, provided it complies with the applicable accounting, tax, and customs control requirements.</p>
<p><strong>What the agreement covers</strong></p>
<p>The core issue: whether a single entity can simultaneously operate as both a consortium operator and service provider under Repetro-Sped. The agreement says yes, provided that accounting, tax, and customs controls applicable to the regime are properly maintained.</p>
<p>This outcome emerged from Brazil&#8217;s Consensus Revenue program, established under RFB Ordinance No. 467 of 2024. The program exists to resolve tax and customs disputes before they escalate into formal audits. Participation is currently open to taxpayers enrolled in Federal Revenue Service compliance initiatives: companies certified through the Confia Program, operators designated as Authorised Economic Operators (AEOs), and businesses ranked A+ in the Sintonia program.</p>
<p><strong>How the procedure works</strong></p>
<p>Taxpayers can initiate the consensual route to examine how specific business operations interact with Brazilian tax and customs law—even before the revenue service begins an audit. If both sides reach agreement, the Federal Revenue Service issues an Executive Declaratory Act that binds the agency and the taxpayer within the scope of what was analysed. The entire process runs for up to 90 days, with one extension of equal length permitted.</p>
<p>Any tax payment that flows from a Consensual Agreement avoids accrual of late-payment penalties, as long as statutory requirements are met. All submissions remain confidential under applicable law. Importantly, the Consensus Revenue program does not grant tax benefits, renegotiate taxes, or relax existing legislation—it simply creates space to agree on how the law applies to a particular situation.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Taiwan&#8217;s Ministry of Finance has issued a <a href="https://www.mof.gov.tw/eng/singlehtml/f48d641f159a4866b1d31c0916fbcc71?cntId=e8405aacef294b96889226b7e810538c" target="_blank" rel="noopener">notice</a> on 20 July 2026  reminding foreign taxpayers of their obligation to file a separate income tax return for qualifying house and land transactions, rather than including such income in gross consolidated income under the Income Tax Act.</p>
<p>The Beigang Office of the National Taxation Bureau of the Central Area said the requirement has applied since 1 January 2016, and covers income derived from transactions involving houses, land, house utilisation rights, presale houses, and certain share or capital transfers that satisfy the prescribed conditions.</p>
<p>Foreign taxpayers must file an individual house and land transactions income tax return if the transaction falls under any of the following circumstances:</p>
<ul>
<li>The transferred house, the associated share of land, or land on which a construction permit may lawfully be issued was acquired on or after 1 January 2016.</li>
<li>The transferred right of using a house by creation of superficies was acquired on or after 1 January, 2016.</li>
<li>The transferred right or the presale house together with its building location was acquired on or after 1 January 2016.</li>
<li>The transaction involves shares or capital of an individual or profit-seeking enterprise that directly or indirectly holds more than half of the total shares or capital of an enterprise inside or outside the Republic of China (R.O.C.), where at least 50% of the value of those shares or capital is derived from house and land located within the R.O.C. This provision does not apply to shares traded on the Taiwan Stock Exchange, Taipei Exchange, or the Emerging Board.</li>
</ul>
<p>The Ministry said taxable income from house and land transactions is calculated by subtracting the amount of land value increment calculated in accordance with the Land Tax Act from the amount of house and land transaction income.</p>
<p>For non-residents of the R.O.C., the applicable tax rate depends on the holding period. Income from property held for less than two years is subject to a 45% tax rate, while a 35% rate applies where the holding period exceeds two years.</p>
<p>Foreign taxpayers are required to file the house and land transaction income tax return with the tax collection authority within 30 days from the day following the completion of the ownership transfer registration of the house and land, or from the transaction date for the right to use a house by creation of superficies.</p>
<p>The Ministry also warned that failure to submit the required return may result in a fine ranging from more thanTWD 3,000 to TWD 30,000.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Argentina&#8217;s tax authority (ARCA) <a href="https://servicioscf.afip.gob.ar/publico/sitio/contenido/novedad/ver.aspx?id=5826" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced</a> it has issued <a href="http://biblioteca.arca.gob.ar/search/query/norma.aspx?p=t:RAG%7Cn:5882%7Co:9%7Ca:2026%7Cf:27/07/2026" target="_blank" rel="noopener">General Resolution 5882/2026</a>, which establishes procedures for settling criminal tax liabilities. The resolution was published and entered into force on 28 July 2026.</p>
<p>This resolution outlines the procedural requirements for taxpayers seeking to terminate criminal proceedings related to tax evasion in Argentina. Under the Tax Penal Regime, individuals must fully settle their original debts and interest while also paying a mandatory 50% surcharge on the total amount.</p>
<p>To facilitate this, the Customs Control and Revenue Agency (ARCA) has established a specific method for generating Electronic Payment Volantes (VEP) using designated tax codes. Once payment is processed, the taxpayer is responsible for submitting proof of settlement to the judicial system to validate the extinction of legal action.</p>
<p><strong>Additional 50% payment procedure under Article 16, Law 27.430</strong></p>
<p>Taxpayers must submit payments through AFIP&#8217;s online portal at<a href="https://auth.afip.gob.ar/contribuyente_/login.xhtml?action=SYSTEM&amp;system=setidj" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> auth.afip.gob.ar</a>. Each payment requires a separate VEP (electronic payment voucher) labelled &#8220;Additional Payment of 50% &#8211; Art. 16 Law 27.430&#8221; for each tax type and period involved.</p>
<p>When generating the VEP, enter the following information:</p>
<ul>
<li>Tax: Use the specific code corresponding to the original tax obligation.</li>
<li>Concept: Enter 762 (Additional article 16 RPT).</li>
<li>Subconcept: Enter 762 (Additional article 16 RPT).</li>
<li>Period: Specify the imputation period to which the payment applies.</li>
<li>Calculation: Input the principal and interest amounts in the fields labelled &#8220;Amount of Principal Paid Subject to Criminal Complaint&#8221; and &#8220;Amount of Interest Paid Subject to Criminal Complaint.&#8221; The system will automatically calculate the additional 50% based on these figures. An editable field is available if the calculated amount differs from any court settlement.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Accreditation in legal proceedings</strong></p>
<p>The Electronic Payment Voucher (VEP) and its corresponding proof of payment serve as sufficient evidence in court. Taxpayers must include the following documents in their court file:</p>
<ul>
<li>The VEP payment receipt for the additional 50% charge</li>
<li>Documentation proving payment of the principal amount and interest used to calculate the additional charge</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Reallocating prior payments</strong></p>
<p>Those who paid the additional amount before this resolution took effect using a different payment code must request correction through the <a href="https://auth.afip.gob.ar/contribuyente_/login.xhtml?action=SYSTEM&amp;system=pres_dig_ext" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Digital Submissions </a>service. Select the procedure &#8220;<a href="http://arca.gob.ar/presentaciones-digitales/documentos/req-reimputacion-de-pagos-form-399.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Re-allocation of payments—Form 399</a>&#8221; and attach payment receipts.</p>
<p><strong>Judicial rejection and recovery</strong></p>
<p>If the court denies the extinction of criminal action, the additional amount paid will not be automatically refunded. Recovery is available only through a separate recovery lawsuit, as provided under <a href="https://biblioteca.arca.gob.ar/search/query/dcp/TOR_C_011683_1998_07_13#articulo0109____img" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Article 81 of Law 11.683</a>.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Ireland&#8217;s Department of Finance has <a href="https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-finance/press-releases/t%C3%A1naiste-and-minister-odonovan-confirm-eu-approval-for-expanded-digital-games-tax-credit/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced</a> on 28 July 2026 that the European Commission has approved the expansion of the Digital Games Tax Credit.</p>
<p>As announced in Budget 2026, the 32% tax credit has been extended until 31 December 2031 and expanded to cover eligible post-release content development, subject to specified conditions.</p>
<p>The approval marks another significant step in strengthening Ireland’s digital games sector.</p>
<p>Announced in Budget 2026, the extension recognises that our games products continue to evolve long after their launch, with new levels, features, updates and downloadable content forming an essential part of modern game development.</p>
<p>By supporting eligible post-release development for up to three years, the expanded tax credit will help studios invest for longer, create more high-quality content and support increased expression of Irish and European culture in the world of digital games.</p>
<p>The extended credit covers eligible expenditure for up to three years post-release and is granted at a rate of 32%  of the lowest of: eligible expenditure, 80% of qualifying expenditure, or EUR 25 million (for the game as a whole, including both pre- and post-release expenditure). The minimum amount that must be spent on the development of a game remains EUR 100,000.</p>
<p>Regulations to support the measure are in development with input from industry stakeholders and, once completed, the extension of the credit to Post-Release Content will be commenced.</p>
<p>Access to the credit for post-release content will be available to digital games development companies that have obtained an interim cultural certificate from the Department of Culture, Communications and Sport following commencement of the section. Only digital games companies that qualify for and claim the credit in respect of pre-release costs may apply for a post-release extension.</p>
<p>Work has commenced on drafting the regulations necessary to underpin the new post-release provisions, a process which will involve engagement with the industry to ensure the regulations are clear and operate as intended. The provision will then be commenced.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Egypt&#8217;s Ministry of Finance, the Egyptian Tax Authority (ETA) and the Financial Regulatory Authority (FRA) have approved a package of tax incentives for securities activities as part of the second tax facilitation package, according to the head of the Egyptian Tax Authority, Rasha Abdel Aal.</p>
<p>In a press <a href="https://sis.gov.eg/en/media-center/news/tax-authority-chief-outlines-new-tax-incentives/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">release </a>issued on Sunday,  26 July 2026, Abdel Aal said the measures were approved through full coordination between the Ministry of Finance, the Egyptian Tax Authority and the Financial Regulatory Authority, in line with Minister of Finance Ahmed Kouchouk&#8217;s directives to encourage investment, stimulate the stock market and support the economy.</p>
<p>She said amendments to Income Tax Law No. 91 of 2005 and Stamp Duty Law No. 111 of 1980 were designed to eliminate double taxation on dividend distributions, provide cash incentives for companies listing shares on the stock exchange and exempt capital gains from listed securities from income tax, while subjecting them only to proportional stamp duty.</p>
<p>Abdel Aal said the amendments also excluded the sale of unlisted securities from stamp duty, making such transactions subject only to income tax and thereby eliminating double taxation.</p>
<p>She added that market maker activities had been exempted from stamp duty to support the Egyptian Exchange and increase trading volumes.</p>
<p>The Egyptian Tax Authority chief also said a clear mechanism had been established to calculate the acquisition cost of unlisted securities, with the aim of simplifying tax accounting for capital gains arising from their disposal.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>India’s  Ministry of Finance has updated its <a href="https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/documents/d/guest/e-book-crs-and-fatca-guidance-note-faqs-pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Guidance Note</a> on FATCA and CRS, providing detailed guidance for crypto exchanges and other intermediaries on their reporting obligations as Reporting Financial Institutions (RFIs) under section 508 of the Income Tax Act, 2025, and Rules 238 to 240 and Form 166 of the Income Tax Rules, 2026.</p>
<p>The updated Guidance Note, issued on 24 July 2026, aligns India&#8217;s reporting framework with internationally accepted Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) standards and expands guidance on reporting, due diligence and compliance requirements.</p>
<p><strong>Reporting entities</strong></p>
<p>The Guidance Note confirms that reporting obligations apply to entities classified as Reporting Financial Institutions (RFIs), including depository institutions, custodial institutions, investment entities and specified insurance companies. It also clarifies that crypto exchanges and other intermediaries falling within the definition of RFIs must comply with the reporting framework.</p>
<p><strong>Financial and reportable accounts</strong></p>
<p>The document explains the scope of financial accounts and reportable accounts, including depository accounts, custodial accounts, equity and debt interests, and specified insurance contracts. It also provides guidance on identifying Reportable Accounts, including those held by Reportable Persons and Passive NFEs with Reportable Controlling Persons.</p>
<p>The Guidance Note also identifies certain low-risk accounts that are excluded from review and reporting requirements.</p>
<p><strong>Due diligence requirements</strong></p>
<p>RFIs are required to apply due diligence procedures to distinguish between pre-existing and new accounts. The guidance requires self-certifications to establish tax residency and enhanced review procedures for certain high-value accounts. It also addresses situations where foreign indicia are identified and the documentation required to validate or cure such cases.</p>
<p>The Guidance Note includes detailed guidance on crypto assets covered and issues relating to fiscally transparent entities such as trusts and partnerships.</p>
<p><strong>Reporting obligations</strong></p>
<p>RFIs must maintain and report information through Form 166, which replaced Form 61B from April 2026. The required information includes the account holder&#8217;s name, address, Tax Identification Number (TIN), date of birth, account number and year-end balance.</p>
<p>The updated guidance also reflects recent CRS reporting changes requiring additional data, including joint account indicators, the number of joint account holders and the roles of Controlling Persons.</p>
<p><strong>Compliance and enforcement</strong></p>
<p>Annual reporting through Form 166 is due by 31 May following the relevant calendar year. The Directorate of Intelligence and Criminal Investigation (I&amp;CI), together with sectoral regulators such as the RBI and SEBI, will continue to oversee compliance.</p>
<p>The Guidance Note states that penalties apply for furnishing inaccurate information, failing to furnish correct information or failing to comply with due diligence requirements. Under FATCA, significant non-compliance may result in an RFI being treated as a Non-Participating Financial Institution (NPFI), leading to a 30% withholding tax on certain US-source payments.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>China&#8217;s Ministry of Finance and the State Taxation Administration have jointly issued <a href="https://fgk.chinatax.gov.cn/zcfgk/c102416/c5251406/content.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Announcement No. 22 of 2026</a> revising the urban land use tax policy on 27 July 2026, phasing out longstanding tax exemptions previously available to energy generation, mining, and oil and gas enterprises under regulations issued between 1989 and 2015.</p>
<p><strong>Transition period locks in 50% discount</strong></p>
<p>Previously exempt land under document (89) Guoshui Di Zi No. 013 (covering power and related sectors) shifts to a graduated schedule. From 1 September 2026 through 31 August 2027, companies pay half the standard urban land use tax. Starting 1 September 2027, the full rate applies, and the original exemption documents are repealed.</p>
<p><strong>Targeted exemptions for infrastructure and safety assets</strong></p>
<p>The announcement creates permanent exemptions for land used in specific functions across energy and extraction industries. Oil and natural gas producers—including those working with shale gas and coalbed methane—can skip tax on fire protection, flood control, wind protection and sand prevention facilities within industrial zones, plus dedicated rail lines and highways serving the operation outside the main production, office, and residential areas. Long-distance pipelines for oil and gas also qualify, including temporary construction land for these projects.</p>
<p>Hydroelectric facilities get broad coverage: reservoir inundation areas, dams (excluding power plant buildings themselves), dikes, slope protection, waterways and waterway infrastructure, fish stocking stations, fish passage facilities, irrigation systems, and flood discharge structures all sit outside the tax.</p>
<p>Nuclear plants qualify for exemptions on dike and slope protection land. Thermal power facilities and power supply companies escape tax on land supporting transmission lines and tower foundations, plus dedicated transportation corridors.</p>
<p>Coal mines receive exemptions for explosives depot safety zones, railway special lines, highways, and public parks and green belts outside the production area. Mining companies extracting metal or non-metal minerals, along with building materials producers, get similar treatment for explosives warehouse safety zones.</p>
<p><strong>Documentation and next steps</strong></p>
<p>Eligible companies must apply for the reductions and exemptions according to existing regulations, then maintain ownership certificates, land use permits, project documents, and related records.</p>
<p>The rules take effect immediately for new qualifying land, including any used during the construction phase of approved projects.</p>

<p>India ranks second globally in Russian crude purchases, alongside China, the Slovak Republic, Hungary, and Azerbaijan as primary targets under the legislation.</p>
<p>The bill, introduced in April 2025 and named after Senator Lindsey Graham, includes sanctions on Russian officials, oligarchs, financial institutions, and the &#8220;shadow fleet&#8221; that Moscow uses to circumvent oil export restrictions. The measure faced broad backing from both parties, though some Democrats expressed concern that Trump&#8217;s tariff authority could inflate consumer prices and damage European relationships.</p>

<p><strong>How India got squeezed into Russia&#8217;s energy orbit</strong></p>
<p>India turned to Russian crude when the Iran-US war erupted in February 2026, blockading the Strait of Hormuz and cutting off Gulf supplies that previously provided roughly 40% of India&#8217;s oil imports. The disruption forced Indian refiners to substitute Russian oil as their primary alternative source.</p>
<p>The US initially penalised India over this trade relationship in August 2025, slapping an additional 25% tariff on Indian goods for &#8220;fueling Putin&#8217;s war.&#8221; That pushed total tariffs against India to 50%, matching China and Brazil as the highest rates applied. Trade negotiations between Washington and New Delhi stalled afterwards.</p>
<p>When energy crisis conditions worsened, the US provided India a waiver in February 2026 allowing resumed Russian oil purchases, with the American argument that no profits would reach Russia through the deal. That exemption proved illusory. Indian imports of Russian crude climbed 34% in June 2026 to record levels, valued at EUR 4.5 billion and accounting for roughly 36% of Russia&#8217;s crude oil export revenues.</p>
<p><strong>What the bill actually permits</strong></p>
<p>The legislation includes an exemption for countries importing less than 15% of their natural gas from Russia and actively working to reduce that share. India currently far exceeds that threshold, making it vulnerable to the full tariff threat. Trump already signalled support for this revised version after negotiations with the White House.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[The Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) has revised its guidance on Applying for a Certificate of Residence/ Tax Reclaim Form. The update provides clearer guidance on the conditions that foreign-owned investment holding companies must satisfy to demonstrate that they have valid reasons for establishing operations in Singapore. The updated section of the guidance states...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) has revised its <a href="https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/corporate-income-tax/income-deductions-for-companies/companies-receiving-foreign-income/applying-for-a-certificate-of-residence-tax-reclaim-form" target="_blank" rel="noopener">guidance</a> on Applying for a Certificate of Residence/ Tax Reclaim Form. The update provides clearer guidance on the conditions that foreign-owned investment holding companies must satisfy to demonstrate that they have valid reasons for establishing operations in Singapore. The updated section of the guidance states the following:</p>
<p><strong>What is certificate of residence </strong></p>
<p>The Certificate of Residence (COR) is a letter issued by IRAS to certify that the company is a tax resident of Singapore (i.e. the <a href="https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/corporate-income-tax/basics-of-corporate-income-tax/tax-residency-of-a-company" target="_blank" rel="noopener">control and management</a> of its business is exercised in Singapore) for the purpose of claiming tax benefits under the DTAs or Limited Treaties.</p>
<p>Generally, income derived by a Singapore tax resident company from foreign persons or companies may be subject to tax in that foreign jurisdiction.</p>
<p>Under the <a href="https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/international-tax/list-of-dtas-limited-dtas-and-eoi-arrangements" target="_blank" rel="noopener">DTAs or Limited Treaties</a> that Singapore has concluded with foreign jurisdictions (i.e. DTA partners), Singapore tax residents may enjoy tax benefits (e.g. tax exemptions or lower withholding tax rates) on income derived from the foreign jurisdictions. Non-residents do not enjoy these benefits.</p>
<p>To enjoy such tax benefits, the COR is required by and must be submitted to the tax authority of the DTA partners to prove that the company is a Singapore tax resident generally when claiming such tax benefits. In this regard, Singapore tax resident companies should submit their COR application to IRAS prior to claiming treaty benefits or at the latest, within 2 calendar years from the actual or expected date of receipt of income if they wish to avail themselves of treaty benefits.</p>
<p><strong>Who is eligible for a certificate of residence</strong></p>
<p>To obtain a Certificate of Residence (COR), a company must be a <a href="https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/corporate-income-tax/basics-of-corporate-income-tax/tax-residency-of-a-company" target="_blank" rel="noopener">tax resident of Singapore</a>. Generally, foreign-owned investment holding companies, nominee companies and non-Singapore incorporated companies are not eligible for a COR.</p>
<p><strong>Foreign-owned investment holding companies</strong></p>
<p>Foreign-owned investment holding companies with purely passive sources of income and/or receiving only foreign-sourced income, are generally not considered tax residents of Singapore because these companies usually act on the instructions of its foreign companies/shareholders, and therefore are not eligible for a COR. A foreign-owned company is a company where 50% or more of its shares are held by:</p>
<ul>
<li>Foreign companies that are incorporated outside Singapore; or</li>
<li>Individual shareholders who are not citizens of Singapore.</li>
</ul>
<p>The ownership is applied at the ultimate holding company level.</p>
<p>However, IRAS may still issue a COR if these companies can show that:</p>
<ul>
<li>The control and management of the company&#8217;s business is exercised in Singapore; and</li>
<li>The company has valid reasons for setting up an office in Singapore.</li>
</ul>
<p>This includes demonstrating that decisions on strategic matters are made in Singapore (e.g. by showing IRAS that their Board of Directors&#8217; meetings are held in Singapore). In addition, to substantiate that the company has a genuine commercial reason for setting up operations in Singapore, the company must also:</p>
<ul>
<li>Have at least 1 director based in Singapore who holds an executive position and is not a nominee director;</li>
<li>Have at least 1 key employee (e.g. CEO, CFO, COO) based in Singapore; or</li>
<li>Be managed by a related company based in Singapore (e.g. the related company makes the decisions relating to the operations of the foreign-owned investment holding company or reviews the performance of the investments of the company).</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Nominee companies</strong></p>
<p>Nominee companies are not eligible for a COR as they are not the beneficial owner of the income derived from the DTA partner. A nominee company is a company that acts as a custodian of shares on behalf of the beneficial owners.</p>
<p><strong>Non-Singapore incorporated companies</strong></p>
<p>Non-Singapore incorporated companies are generally not eligible for a COR as these companies are not controlled or managed in Singapore. This also applies to Singapore branches of foreign companies, as they are controlled and managed by their overseas parent company.</p>
<p>However, in exceptional situations, IRAS may still issue a COR if these companies can show that:</p>
<ul>
<li>The control and management of the company&#8217;s business is exercised in Singapore (i.e. the Singapore branch is exercising the full control and management of the company); and</li>
<li>The company has valid reasons for not incorporating in Singapore.</li>
</ul>
<p>IRAS may request for additional information on the company.</p>
<p><strong>Variable Capital Companies (VCC)</strong></p>
<p>For tax purposes, a VCC incorporated under the Variable Capital Companies Act 2018 is treated as a company.</p>
<p>To obtain a COR, a VCC must be a tax resident of Singapore. The tax residence of a VCC&#8217;s sub-funds is determined at the umbrella level of the VCC. To obtain a COR for its sub-fund, the VCC, and not the sub-fund, has to apply for the COR. The COR will show the details (tax reference number and name) of the VCC and sub-fund.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Uruguay&#8217;s General Tax Directorate (DGI) has issued <a href="https://www.impo.com.uy/bases/resoluciones-dgi-originales/1517-2026" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Resolution No. 1.517/2026</a>, establishing detailed rules for the collection of tax on foreign income earned by individuals from 1 January 2026 under changes introduced by Law No. 20.446.</p>
<p>The resolution published on 30 June 2026, implements provisions contained in Articles 653 and following of Law No. 20.446 of 16 December 2025 and Decree No. 95/2026 of 6 May 2026. The legislation amended the Personal Income Tax (IRPF) treatment of income derived from non-resident entities, while the decree authorised the implementation of withholding regimes and rules governing tax credits for taxes paid abroad.</p>
<p><strong>Withholding and reporting requirements</strong></p>
<p>The DGI has amended several provisions of Resolution No. 662/2007. The revised rules update reporting obligations for designated withholding agents, requiring declarations to include the total amounts subject to withholding, broken down by applicable rate, together with the corresponding withheld tax. The resolution also repeals numeral 22 bis of Resolution No. 662/2007.</p>
<p><strong>Dividend allocation rules</strong></p>
<p>The new framework revises the rules governing the allocation of provisional profits and dividends for withholding purposes. Where distributions exceed specified thresholds and originate from both taxable and non-taxable IRAE income, the excess will generally be treated as taxable under IRAE unless non-taxable income exceeds 90% of total income for the fiscal year, in which case only 5% of the excess will be regarded as taxable under IRAE.</p>
<p>The resolution also establishes a detailed order for allocating dividends or profits distributed by non-resident entities. Distributions must first be allocated to income imputed or assigned up to 31 December 2025, followed by Uruguayan-source income subject to the Non-Resident Income Tax earned before that date. After those amounts are exhausted, allocations will apply to income imputed from 1 January 2026, pure Uruguayan-source capital income subject to the Non-Resident Income Tax, and finally to income generated from that date that is not subject to the applicable imputation and allocation regimes.</p>
<p><strong>Foreign tax credits and valuation</strong></p>
<p>The resolution introduces operational guidance on verification of foreign taxes paid through imputing entities, tax credits for indirect transfers, and proof requirements for fiscal cost and foreign taxes.</p>
<p>It also sets out rules for determining the fiscal cost of investments acquired before 31 December 2025, permits the use of Bloomberg financial data for valuation purposes, and provides guidance on the compensation of negative results and the application of exchange rate rules.</p>
<p><strong>Additional compliance measures</strong></p>
<p>Further provisions address the allocation of dividends distributed by IRAE taxpayers, exclusion from imputation regimes where income has already been taxed under IRAE, withholding rules for ownership chains involving resident and non-resident entities, and exclusions for qualifying collective investment funds operating under conditions of free competition.</p>
<p>The resolution also clarifies custody definitions for resident entities acting through non-resident custodians, introduces options for definitive withholding and simplified regimes, and establishes payment schedules for capital income from abroad.</p>
<p><strong>Transitional provisions</strong></p>
<p>Resolution No. 1.517/2026 includes transitional measures extending deadlines for certain withholding and payment obligations until October 2026 to facilitate implementation of the new rules.</p>
<p>The resolution was signed by Director General of Taxes Gustavo González Amilivia.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) has <a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/media-centre/ato-reveals-tax-time-dos-and-donts-as-lodgments-get-underway" target="_blank" rel="noopener">issued</a> a set of recommendations from Assistant Commissioner Anita Challen to assist individuals during the 2026 tax lodgment season on 27 July 2026.</p>
<p>The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) now has over 100 million pieces of information ready to be pre-filled into individual tax returns and is giving taxpayers the go-ahead to lodge.</p>
<p>The data has been provided to the ATO from a range of third parties including employers, banks, private health insurers, share registries, and government agencies, and is designed to help taxpayers and tax professionals lodge more accurately and with less effort.</p>
<p>ATO Assistant Commissioner Anita Challen said taxpayers with straightforward tax affairs can now review their information and start lodging, either by using myTax or through a registered tax professional.</p>
<p><em>&#8220;For those who have been patiently waiting to lodge, most income statements and pre-fill information is now available,&#8221; Ms Challen said. &#8220;Before hitting submit, taxpayers should take a few extra minutes to check details to avoid delays and mistakes. Pre-fill data should be verified as correct, all income declared, and only entitled deductions claimed. Lodging a tax return is a legal declaration that the information provided is true and correct.&#8221;</em></p>
<p>This year, the ATO is expanding pre-fill services to include income reported through the<a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/preparing-lodging-and-paying/reports-and-returns/taxable-payments-annual-report/taxable-payments-reporting-and-contractors" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> Taxable Payment Annual Report,</a> to help more contractors get their tax returns right the first time. Taxpayers in industries including building and construction, cleaning, courier services, information technology, road freight, and security services may see this income automatically added to their return from late August.</p>
<p><strong>What taxpayers should avoid</strong></p>
<p>Overclaiming deductions or inflating expenses is discouraged. The ATO has sophisticated data-matching and analytics that can quickly identify claims that don&#8217;t stack up, and refunds may be held for further investigation if they appear suspicious.</p>
<p>All income must be reported — including income from side hustles, cash jobs, rental properties, and online activities and content creation. Excluding income may result in the ATO amending a tax return, with interest and penalties potentially applied.</p>
<p>Copying and pasting from previous years&#8217; returns is also flagged as a risk. If a taxpayer&#8217;s job or circumstances have changed, that needs to be reflected in claims and the return.</p>
<p>Acting on information from third-party sources such as artificial intelligence platforms, &#8220;finfluencers,&#8221; or advice from family or friends without verifying with a registered tax professional or the ATO is not recommended.</p>
<p>Taxpayers should also not claim the newly announced AUD 1,000 standard work-related deduction — this does not apply until Tax Time 2027.</p>
<p><strong>What taxpayers should do</strong></p>
<p>The ATO advises taxpayers to take time to check personal information and ensure bank and super details are up to date. Reviewing the ATO&#8217;s <a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/income-deductions-offsets-and-records/guides-for-occupations-and-industries/occupation-and-industry-specific-guides" target="_blank" rel="noopener">industry and occupation-specific guides</a> will help clarify what can be claimed and what records are required to prove it.</p>
<p>Those planning to use a registered tax agent should engage one before 31 October and verify the agent is <a href="https://www.tpb.gov.au/public-register" target="_blank" rel="noopener">registered</a> with the Tax Practitioners Board. Downloading the ATO app allows taxpayers to manage their tax and super, and track the progress of their return. The myDeductions feature within the app can be used to keep and organise records for expenses and deductions.</p>
<p>Taxpayers are also reminded to stay alert to scams. The ATO will never project a number when calling or send an unsolicited message with a link asking for personal information or login to ATO online services. Information should only be taken from verified sources such as the ATO website, the ATO app, or a registered tax professional.</p>
<p>Those who lodged in early July and have since identified a mistake — such as omitting income — <a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/your-tax-return/amend-your-tax-return" target="_blank" rel="noopener">can lodge an amendment</a>.</p>
<p>The ATO is also reminding taxpayers that calling the ATO will not speed up the processing of returns. &#8220;Most returns are processed within 12 business days, and the fastest way to check the progress of a return is through the ATO app or ATO online services,&#8221; Ms Challen said.</p>
<p>The lodgment deadline for self-preparers is 31 October. Those engaging a tax agent may have a later deadline but should be on the agent&#8217;s books by 31 October.</p>

As an example, the Bureau noted that residents of Germany must continue to submit applications no later than the end of the fourth calendar year following the year in which withholding tax was levied, meaning the domestic 10-year extension does not apply.</p>

Eligible taxpayers should submit an application form, contracts with Chinese translations, a certificate of residence and income-related supporting documents issued by the tax authority of the other Contracting State. Where an application is submitted through an agent, the original power of attorney must also be provided.</p>

<p>It also clarified that the amendment applies to taxpayers, including establishments, enterprises, Omani companies and permanent establishments, that incur additional costs while complying with decisions issued by units of the State&#8217;s Administrative Apparatus and other public legal entities in the course of their business activities. Such expenses may be deductible provided they do not result from a breach of any obligation by the taxpayer, regardless of its source.</p>
<p>According to the Tax Authority, the amendment is intended to prevent taxpayers from bearing additional tax burdens arising from compliance with applicable laws and regulations, while supporting the national economy and upholding the principle of tax fairness.</p>
<p>The new rules will apply to tax years beginning on or after 1 January 2027.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Taiwan’s Central Area National Taxation Bureau of the Ministry of Finance stated that, under the House and Land Integrated Income Tax 2.0 regime, effective from 1 July 2021, a profit-seeking enterprise that disposes of shares or equity interests in a domestic or foreign profit-seeking enterprise in which it has held more than 50% ownership (directly or indirectly on any day during the one-year period preceding the transaction date) must determine whether the transaction falls within the House and Land Integrated Income Tax rules.</p>
<p>If more than 50% of the value of the invested enterprise&#8217;s shares or equity interests is derived from real property located in Taiwan, house use rights, pre-sale properties, and the land associated with those pre-sale properties (collectively referred to as &#8220;real property&#8221;), the transaction is treated as a real property transaction and is subject to the House and Land Integrated Income Tax. <p>The Bureau further explained that the Ministry of Finance amended and reissued the &#8220;Guidelines for Filing House and Land Integrated Income Tax Returns&#8221; on 21 April 2026. The amendments provide that, where the invested enterprise can reasonably and objectively measure the value of all its assets (for example, based on certified audit reports prepared by a certified public accountant using actual market values), the total fair market value of those assets may be used to determine the value of the enterprise&#8217;s shares or equity interests. This allows the proportion of real property value within the invested enterprise&#8217;s equity value to more accurately reflect the actual situation.</p>
<p>In addition, for transactions involving shares acquired before 30 June 2021, the portion of the gain attributable to the invested enterprise&#8217;s ownership of real property acquired on or before 31 December 2015 (i.e. real property subject to the previous tax regime) is exempt from the House and Land Integrated Income Tax. This treatment applies to all cases that have not yet been finally assessed.</p>
<p>The Bureau reminded businesses that, when disposing of shares or equity interests, they should carefully assess whether the transaction falls within the scope of the House and Land Integrated Income Tax.</p>

In June this year, the Government published the Action Plan to Promote the Development of CTCs in Hong Kong...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Hong Kong’s Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau (FSTB) and the Inland Revenue Department (IRD) <a href="https://www.ird.gov.hk/eng/ppr/archives/26072701.htm" target="_blank" rel="noopener">launched</a> a <a href="https://www.fstb.gov.hk/fsb/en/publication/consult/doc/ctcConsultEn.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">public consultation</a> on 27 July 2026, on proposed enhancements to the tax concession regime for corporate treasury centres (CTCs).</p>
<p>In June this year, the Government published the Action Plan to Promote the Development of CTCs in Hong Kong (Action Plan), which sets out a &#8220;4T&#8221; framework covering (i) tax revamp, (ii) tax agreements, (iii) targeted promotions, and (iv) talent and dialogue, with a view to attracting more multinational corporations to establish CTCs in Hong Kong, and enabling existing CTCs operating in Hong Kong to scale up their operations and fully leverage the city&#8217;s comprehensive financial ecosystem.</p>
<p>Following the direction of tax revamp under the Action Plan, the consultation paper proposes the introduction of a tiered regime for CTC tax concessions, with key features as follows:</p>
<p><strong>Tier 1: Refine and broaden existing regime</strong></p>
<p>Tier 1 of the proposed tiered regime comprises refinements to the existing tax concessionary measures applicable to qualifying corporate treasury centres (QCTCs) and corporations conducting intra-group financing business in Hong Kong.</p>
<p>The key proposals include:</p>
<ul>
<li>Allowing a CTC to defer tax deduction of interest expenses paid to a non-Hong Kong associated corporation to a year in which that corporation becomes subject to tax, if that corporation is not required to pay tax on the interest income in a particular year of assessment</li>
<li>Expanding the scope of tax deduction of interest expenses to cover a broader range of corporations, including those carrying on a business of carrying out corporate treasury activities</li>
<li>Making legal and administrative clarifications (such as the substantial activity requirement, the benchmark for intra-group financing business, and the definition of corporate treasury transactions, etc) to enhance tax certainty.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Tier 2: Introduce a pre-approval mechanism</strong></p>
<p>Under Tier 2 of the proposed tiered regime, CTCs and their associated corporations that meet a set of specified conditions may, upon pre-approval by the IRD, enjoy additional tax benefits or flexibilities within a validity period of five years, including:</p>
<ul>
<li>Exemption for a pre-approved QCTC from complying with the &#8220;dedicated CTC condition&#8221; and the &#8220;safe harbour rule&#8221;</li>
<li>A 50% tax exemption for interest income derived by pre-approved Hong Kong associated corporations from the pre-approved QCTC</li>
<li>Exemption for a pre-approved QCTC from complying with the &#8220;subject to tax condition&#8221; on interest paid to its pre-approved non-Hong Kong associated corporations; and</li>
<li>Removal of the &#8220;anti-tax arbitrage rule&#8221; for pre-approved Hong Kong associated corporations. Such corporations may claim full tax deduction for expenses paid or payable to the pre-approved QCTC, subject to a cap set at 30 per cent of its earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (i.e. EBITDA) for interest expense deduction.</li>
</ul>
<p>Comments can be sent by post (24/F, Central Government Offices, 2 Tim Mei Avenue, Tamar, Hong Kong) or by email (ctc-consult@fstb.gov.hk) on or before 4 September 2026.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Bulgaria’s National Assembly gave final approval to the State Social Security Budget Bill and the National Health Insurance Fund Budget Bill, followed by the State Budget Bill on 22 July 2026.</p>
<p>All three bills were tabled on 1 July, and adopted on 24 July, introducing personal social insurance contributions for civil servants along with higher social insurance income thresholds, both taking effect on 1 August 2026. Until adoption, an interim act had kept public revenue and spending running, so the new budgets apply only for the rest of 2026.</p>
<p><strong>Phased reform of civil servant insurance contributions</strong></p>
<p>According to this <a href="https://www.parliament.bg/bg/bills/ID/167157" target="_blank" rel="noopener">legislation</a>, starting 1 August 2026, Bulgaria will reform the social security and health insurance contributions for civil servants and judiciary employees by requiring them to pay a portion of their own contributions under a transitional 80:20 employer-employee ratio.</p>
<p>To protect these workers from a reduction in take-home pay, their basic salaries will be recalculated so that their net income remains equal to or higher than what they earned on 31 July 2026. This phased approach will culminate on 1 January 2027, when their contribution ratio will fully align with the standard rates (such as the generally applicable 60:40 ratio) paid by all other insured individuals.</p>
<p>Furthermore, the government plans to develop and apply a similar personal contribution mechanism for other specialised public sector workers, such as defence and internal affairs employees, beginning in 2027.</p>
<p><strong>Social insurance thresholds increase</strong></p>
<p>A central feature of this <a href="https://www.parliament.bg/bg/bills/ID/167156" target="_blank" rel="noopener">legislation</a> is the adjustment of social insurance income thresholds starting 1 August 2026. From this date, the minimum monthly social insurance income for self-insured persons will increase to EUR 620.20, directly aligning with the new statutory minimum wage, while the maximum monthly social insurance income for all insured persons will rise to EUR 2,300.00.</p>
<p>Alongside these general adjustments, the minimum monthly insurance income thresholds based on specific economic activities and occupational groups will also be updated in the second half of the year, with managerial categories experiencing the most substantial absolute increases.</p>
<p>Furthermore, a significant policy shift will require civil servants and judiciary employees to begin a phased transition toward paying personal social insurance contributions starting 1 August 2026.</p>
<p><strong>Mandatory health insurance contribution rates and ratios</strong></p>
<p>As per this <a href="https://www.parliament.bg/bg/bills/ID/167155" target="_blank" rel="noopener">legislation</a>, the 2026 Budget Act of the Bulgarian National Health Insurance Fund (NHIF), which totals approximately EUR 5.25 billion, confirms the mandatory health insurance contribution rate at 8%. This contribution maintains the standard 60:40 payment ratio between employers and insured employees.</p>
<p>Starting 1 August 2026, the contribution ratio for civil servants and certain groups under the Social Insurance Code will shift to 80:20, with a planned adjustment to their overall compensation to prevent any reduction in their net income.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[Taiwan’s National Taxation Bureau of the Northern Area (NTBNA) has reiterated, on 28 July 2026, the key exemption criteria under the country’s Controlled Foreign Company (CFC) regime, urging businesses to ensure compliance with the rules when preparing their annual income tax filings. Taiwan introduced its CFC regime from the 2023 fiscal year to prevent profit-seeking...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Taiwan’s National Taxation Bureau of the Northern Area (NTBNA) has <a href="https://www.mof.gov.tw/Eng/singlehtml/f48d641f159a4866b1d31c0916fbcc71?cntId=aff32d48919d4ae0a0eec0959ccedfb4" target="_blank" rel="noopener">reiterated</a>, on 28 July 2026, the key exemption criteria under the country’s Controlled Foreign Company (CFC) regime, urging businesses to ensure compliance with the rules when preparing their annual income tax filings.</p>
<p>Taiwan introduced its CFC regime from the 2023 fiscal year to prevent profit-seeking enterprises from using subsidiaries established in low-tax jurisdictions with little or no substantive business activity to defer or avoid domestic tax liabilities. Under the rules, unless a CFC qualifies for a statutory exemption under Article 43-3 of the Income Tax Act, Taiwanese enterprises must calculate and recognise their share of the CFC’s investment income based on their ownership interest and holding period, and include that amount in their taxable income for the relevant year.</p>
<p>The NTBNA noted that the CFC framework includes exemptions intended to avoid placing an unnecessary burden on multinational groups conducting genuine commercial activities. A CFC may qualify for exemption if it has substantial operating activities or if its annual earnings do not exceed TWD 7 million.</p>
<p>However, the tax authority cautioned that the “substantial operating activities” exemption is frequently misunderstood or misapplied. Under the Regulations Governing Application of Recognizing Income from Controlled Foreign Company for Profit-Seeking Enterprise, a CFC is regarded as having substantial operating activities only if it maintains a fixed place of business in its jurisdiction of incorporation, employs staff to conduct actual business operations locally, and derives less than 10% of its combined operating and non-operating income from passive sources such as investment income, dividends, interest, royalties, rental income, and gains from asset disposals.</p>
<p>The NTBNA emphasised that the CFC rules are designed to strengthen Taiwan’s anti-tax avoidance framework while accommodating the legitimate operational needs of multinational enterprises. Businesses should carefully assess the activities of their foreign subsidiaries and disclose the required CFC information in the prescribed format when filing their annual income tax returns.</p>
<p>Where an exemption is claimed, taxpayers must submit the necessary supporting documentation and complete the filing within the statutory deadline. The tax authority also encouraged businesses to consult the relevant legislation and guidance or seek assistance where necessary.</p>

		<title>Vietnam issues comprehensive guidance on the implementation of DTA, MAP, APA</title>
		<link>https://regfollower.com/vietnam-issues-comprehensive-guidance-on-the-implementation-of-dta-map-apa/?utm_source=rss&#038;utm_medium=rss&#038;utm_campaign=vietnam-issues-comprehensive-guidance-on-the-implementation-of-dta-map-apa</link>

				<category><![CDATA[General rules]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[MAP]]></category>

		<category><![CDATA[Vietnam]]></category>
