					<description><![CDATA[The Vietnamese Ministry of Finance has issued Circular No. 95/2026/TT-BTC, effective from 1 July 2026, setting out comprehensive guidance on the implementation of Double Taxation Agreements (DTAs), Mutual Agreement Procedures (MAP), and Advance Pricing Arrangements (APA). The Circular replaces Circular No. 205/2013/TT-BTC and Circular No. 45/2021/TT-BTC and establishes updated rules on treaty application, dispute resolution,...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Vietnamese Ministry of Finance has issued <a href="https://gdt.gov.vn/wps/wcm/connect/1b51d6c3-e9f5-4ddf-88b9-a3e1c3ceba67/95_07072026_171508.pdf?MOD=AJPERES&amp;CACHEID=ROOTWORKSPACE1b51d6c3-e9f5-4ddf-88b9-a3e1c3ceba67" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Circular No. 95/2026/TT-BTC</a>, effective from 1 July 2026, setting out comprehensive guidance on the implementation of Double Taxation Agreements (DTAs), Mutual Agreement Procedures (MAP), and Advance Pricing Arrangements (APA).</p>
<p>The Circular replaces Circular No. 205/2013/TT-BTC and <a href="https://regfollower.com/vietnam-mof-implements-new-rules-on-advance-pricing-agreements/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Circular No. 45/2021/TT-BTC</a> and establishes updated rules on treaty application, dispute resolution, transfer pricing arrangements, and taxpayer obligations.</p>
<p><strong>Scope and general principles</strong></p>
<p>The Circular confirms that where a tax treaty conflicts with domestic tax legislation, the provisions of the applicable treaty take precedence. However, applying a treaty cannot create a tax liability that does not exist under domestic law or increase a taxpayer&#8217;s tax burden beyond what Vietnamese legislation prescribes.</p>
<p>Terms that are not defined in a treaty are to be interpreted under Vietnamese tax law. If neither the treaty nor domestic legislation defines a term, the competent authorities of the contracting states are required to negotiate a common interpretation.</p>
<p>For Vietnam, the Minister of Finance or an authorised representative, typically the General Department of Taxation, serves as the country&#8217;s &#8220;Competent Authority&#8221; for treaty administration.</p>
<p><strong>Double taxation agreements</strong></p>
<p>The Circular sets out detailed conditions for claiming treaty benefits and determining tax residency for both individuals and organisations.</p>
<p>For individuals, residency is assessed based on factors including permanent home, centre of vital interests, habitual abode and nationality. For organisations, residency is determined by the place of establishment, head office or place of effective management.</p>
<p>The guidance also strengthens the application of the beneficial ownership requirement. Tax authorities may deny treaty benefits where an applicant is not considered the beneficial owner of the income, including cases where the recipient acts as an agent or nominee or transfers more than 50% of the income to a third-country resident within 12 months.</p>
<p>The Circular also updates the definition of a Permanent Establishment (PE), covering fixed places of business such as branches, offices and factories, construction sites or projects exceeding the applicable treaty threshold, and dependent agents that habitually conclude contracts on behalf of foreign enterprises.</p>
<p><strong>Tax treatment of specific income</strong></p>
<p>The guidance provides detailed rules for several categories of income covered by tax treaties:</p>
<table>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center;"><strong>Income category</strong></td>
<td style="text-align: center;"><strong>General treaty treatment</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center;">Immovable property</td>
<td style="text-align: center;">Taxed in the country where the property is located</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center;">Business profits</td>
<td style="text-align: center;">Taxable in Vietnam only where the foreign enterprise has a PE in Vietnam</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center;">International transport</td>
<td style="text-align: center;">Income from ships and aircraft in international traffic is generally exempt or subject to reduced taxation in the host country</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center;">Dividends, interest and royalties</td>
<td style="text-align: center;">Subject to treaty-specific maximum withholding tax rates</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center;">Capital gains</td>
<td style="text-align: center;">Rules apply to gains from immovable property, business assets and shares, particularly where company value is mainly derived from immovable property</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>To eliminate double taxation, Vietnam continues to apply the Tax Credit Method. Tax paid in a treaty partner jurisdiction may be credited against Vietnamese tax liability, provided the credit does not exceed the Vietnamese tax payable on the same income.</p>
<p><strong>Mutual Agreement Procedure</strong></p>
<p>The Circular provides updated guidance on the Mutual Agreement Procedure (MAP), which allows taxpayers to seek relief when they believe taxation is inconsistent with a tax treaty.</p>
<p>Applications may be refused if they are submitted more than three years after the first notification of the disputed tax action, or two years where specified by the applicable treaty. Requests may also be rejected where tax evasion is involved.</p>
<p>The MAP process includes receiving the application, reviewing the case, negotiating with the foreign competent authority and implementing any agreement reached.</p>
<p>The Circular also confirms Vietnam&#8217;s commitment to exchange tax information with treaty partners through exchanges on request, automatic exchanges and spontaneous exchanges, subject to confidentiality requirements.</p>
<p><strong>Advance Pricing Arrangements</strong></p>
<p>The Circular sets out updated procedures for Advance Pricing Arrangements (APA), allowing taxpayers engaged in related-party transactions to agree transfer pricing methods with tax authorities before filing tax returns.</p>
<p>Three types of APA are available:</p>
<ul>
<li>Unilateral APA between the Vietnamese tax authority and the taxpayer.</li>
<li>Bilateral APA involving Vietnam and one foreign tax authority.</li>
<li>Multilateral APA involving multiple tax authorities.</li>
</ul>
<p>Eligible transactions must be genuine, ongoing and transparent, and must not already be subject to tax disputes.</p>
<p>Taxpayers are required to submit Form 01/APA-ĐN together with supporting documentation. The tax authority will assess the proposed transfer pricing methodology, comparable data and critical assumptions before reaching an agreement.</p>
<p>An APA is generally valid for up to three tax years. The Circular also permits a rollback of up to five previous tax years where business activities and relevant facts remain substantially unchanged.</p>
<p>Taxpayers operating under an APA must submit annual compliance reports and promptly notify the tax authority of significant business changes that could affect the agreement.</p>
<p><strong>Taxpayer rights and obligations</strong></p>
<p>The Circular outlines both the rights and responsibilities of taxpayers participating in treaty procedures.</p>
<p>Taxpayers are entitled to receive guidance from tax authorities, withdraw MAP or APA applications before an agreement is signed, and engage independent experts for professional advice.</p>
<p>They are also required to provide complete, accurate and timely information, maintain supporting records and cooperate fully during reviews. Applications for both MAP and APA are generally expected to be submitted electronically.</p>
<p>The Circular took effect on 1 July 2026 and establishes the framework governing Vietnam&#8217;s implementation of tax treaties, dispute resolution mechanisms and advance transfer pricing agreements, replacing the country&#8217;s previous guidance in these areas.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

Following a review initiated in January 2026, the Commission has released updated technical documentation dated 24 July 2026 to assist report preparers, software developers, and IT teams. The taxonomy and the...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The European Commission has updated its <a href="https://finance.ec.europa.eu/publications/public-country-country-reporting-taxonomy-project_en" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Public Country-by-Country (CbC) Reporting Taxonomy project</a>, originally launched in 2025 to support the preparation of public CbC reports. Following a review initiated in January 2026, the Commission has released updated technical documentation dated 24 July 2026 to assist report preparers, software developers, and IT teams.</p>
<p>The taxonomy and the report generator are now available along with all related guidance on how to use them.</p>
<p><strong>Public country‑by‑country reporting taxonomy</strong></p>
<p>This <a href="https://finance.ec.europa.eu/document/download/ec1ef870-f94e-4395-8828-31480a086be3_en?filename=2025-pcbcr-taxonomy.zip" target="_blank" rel="noopener">document</a> is the core pCbCR taxonomy file in all EU languages. It is structured with all the elements that are needed to be tagged when creating an iXBRL report. Fully supports the creation of the iXBRL in xHTML format using the developed report generator.</p>
<p><strong>Public country‑by‑country reporting taxonomy documentation</strong></p>
<p>This <a href="https://finance.ec.europa.eu/document/download/2a5f7f94-5a94-44a5-9568-82a312a4f000_en?filename=2025-pcbcr-taxonomy-documentation_en.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">document</a> outlines the architecture and content of the pCBCR taxonomy and details the XBRL features implemented within it. It is intended primarily for reporting entities (preparers) and software developers or IT depts. providing solutions enabling the creation of iXBRL reports on income tax information.</p>
<p>The pCBCR Taxonomy and its accompanying documentation reflect Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2952, as published in the Official Journal of the European Union on 2 December 2024, and the corrigendum published on 5 May 2026. Any following amendments, corrections, or other modifications to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2952 may not be incorporated into the pCBCR Taxonomy and accompanying documentation or be incorporated with significant delay. Users/preparers should always consult the latest version of the regulation in the Official Journal and the related national laws, requirements or instructions for reporting purposes.</p>
<p><strong>Public country‑by‑country reporting iXBRL reporting manual</strong></p>
<p>This is the <a href="https://finance.ec.europa.eu/document/download/8d32dc14-1996-4535-a638-67b913479c54_en?filename=2025-pcbcr-ixbrl-reporting-manual_en.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">guidance</a> for preparers of the pCbC reports and IT departments/software firms on specific technical issues related with preparation of an iXBRL report on income tax information, with the use of the developed pCBCR taxonomy.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>This week was marked by a significant tightening of UK trade policy, headlined by a major expansion of the anti-dumping regime for bicycles. New 48.5% duties were applied to imports from Malaysia and Pakistan, and in a key anti-circumvention move, to a wide range of bicycle components from China. Alongside this major trade defence action, a notable tactical shift emerged as UK authorities implemented new specific, per-item duties for product groups in both the construction and live animal sectors, moving away from traditional percentage-based tariffs.</p>
<p><strong>The week in brief</strong></p>
<p>After a quiet start, UK tariff activity escalated mid-week into a significant tightening of trade policy, driven by a major trade defence action and a notable shift in tariff methodology. The week’s high volume of over 980 changes was dominated by the reinforcement and expansion of anti-dumping duties on bicycles and their parts, signaling a robust enforcement posture. Concurrently, a new tactical approach to setting duties emerged, with specific, per-item levies being applied to disparate sectors on consecutive days. The week concluded with two days of minor administrative updates, leaving the mid-week policy shifts as the period’s defining developments.</p>
<p><strong>What mattered most</strong></p>
<p>The week’s activity was concentrated in two key developments that took effect mid-week:</p>
<ol>
<li><strong> Major expansion of bicycle anti-dumping regime:</strong> The most consequential action was the comprehensive reinforcement of the UK’s trade defence framework for bicycles. Effective 23 July, a new 48.5% anti-dumping duty was applied to certain bicycles imported from Malaysia and Pakistan. In a strategically significant anti-circumvention move, the 48.5% duty was also extended to cover a wide range of key bicycle parts originating from China, including frames, forks, hubs, and brakes. This was accompanied by administrative updates extending the validity of existing duties on bicycles from China, Cambodia, Indonesia, the Philippines, and Sri Lanka until late 2029, confirming a long-term commitment to the measures.</li>
<li><strong> Tactical shift to specific duties:</strong> A clear trend in tariff methodology emerged as new duties were implemented based on a specific, per-item (&#8216;p/st&#8217;) levy rather than a percentage-based ad valorem rate. This shift occurred in two completely different sectors: first, on 21 July, for certain plastic and steel doors and windows (HS 3925200000, 7308300000); and second, on 22 July, for a wide range of live animals, including primates, reptiles, and birds of prey (Chapter 1). The application of this tactic across unrelated product groups suggests a deliberate change in approach by UK authorities.</li>
</ol>
<p><strong>Threads to watch</strong></p>
<p>The week’s developments point to two key trends for trade professionals to monitor. First is the UK’s robust trade defence enforcement, highlighted by the anti-circumvention action against Chinese bicycle parts. This signals a willingness to close perceived loopholes in existing regimes and could have implications for supply chains in other sectors subject to trade defence measures. Second is the potential expansion of specific, per-item duties. Importers should watch closely to see if this model is applied to other product categories, as it represents a fundamental change from the more common ad valorem tariff structure. In the background, the ongoing investigation into Chinese track-laying excavators, which prompted a new registration requirement last week, remains the most significant active trade defence file to watch.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>A week largely defined by the routine activation of hundreds of seasonal agricultural tariffs took a sharp turn in its final hours with the imposition of significant new anti-dumping duties on a wide range of industrial goods from China. While the bulk of the 2,730 measures that took effect during the week were pre-planned updates for farm goods, the week’s defining story became a major publication on Saturday that introduced new protective measures on Chinese steel fasteners, specialty plastics, and plywood, all with immediate effect.</p>
<p><strong>The week in brief</strong></p>
<p>The week’s regulatory activity followed a two-part narrative. The first four days were dominated by the implementation of large-scale, pre-planned adjustments to the EU’s agricultural tariff schedule. Hundreds of measures took effect, activating new tariff quotas for bovine animals and updating the seasonal entry price system for a wide array of fruits and vegetables. This routine but high-volume activity was abruptly overshadowed on Saturday by a massive publication of over 1,400 changes. This update marked a decisive pivot to industrial trade defence, with the EU enacting a suite of assertive new anti-dumping measures targeting imports from China, shifting the week’s posture from administrative maintenance to active protectionism.</p>
<p><strong>What mattered most</strong></p>
<p>The most consequential development was the suite of new trade defence measures targeting Chinese industrial goods, all loaded and made effective on 25 July.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>New anti-dumping duties on China:</strong> Three significant regulations introduced new duties. Regulation R1785/26 imposed definitive anti-dumping duties on iron and steel fasteners (including screws and bolts under HS codes in the 7318 range), with a residual duty of 86.5% and a lower 39.6% rate for certain cooperating companies. The action also includes anti-circumvention measures for goods consigned from Malaysia. Further duties were introduced on aliphatic-aromatic copolyesters (PBAT), a specialty plastic, under Regulation R1747/26, and on various types of plywood via Regulation R1840/26.</li>
<li><strong>Immediate implementation: </strong>In a critical move for importers, all new anti-dumping duties took effect on the day of publication, 25 July. This immediate application requires urgent supply chain review for businesses importing the affected fasteners, plastics, and plywood from China.</li>
<li><strong>Agricultural tariff activations: </strong>While eclipsed by the trade defence news, the week also saw major scheduled changes in the agricultural sector. On 20 July, 565 measures took effect, primarily establishing new tariff quotas for live bovine animals. This was followed on 23 July by the activation of 581 measures updating the entry price system for produce including tomatoes, lemons, and table grapes from numerous origins.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Threads to watch</strong></p>
<p>With the new anti-dumping duties on Chinese industrial goods now in force, the immediate focus for affected businesses will be assessing their impact and adjusting supply chains. The assertiveness of the action, particularly the high duty rate on fasteners and the immediate effective date, signals a hardening stance. Beyond this, publications during the week also loaded over 250 future-dated measures, many of which relate to industrial goods in the iron and steel (Chapter 72) and machinery (Chapter 84) sectors. This pipeline suggests that further adjustments for industrial products remain a key area of regulatory activity to monitor in the weeks ahead.</p>

		<title>Netherlands updates hybrid mismatch guidance with new rules on US tax regimes, permanent establishments</title>
		<link>https://regfollower.com/netherlands-updates-hybrid-mismatch-guidance-with-new-rules-on-us-tax-regimes-permanent-establishments/?utm_source=rss&#038;utm_medium=rss&#038;utm_campaign=netherlands-updates-hybrid-mismatch-guidance-with-new-rules-on-us-tax-regimes-permanent-establishments</link>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Mohammed Al Mamun]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Mon, 27 Jul 2026 13:37:18 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Anti-Avoidance/Anti-Evasion]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[CFC]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[PE rules]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Policy announcements by government]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Europe]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Netherlands]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://regfollower.com/?p=85446</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[The Netherlands published the Hybrid Mismatch Policy Decision 2026 (Decree No. 2026-12123), issued by the State Secretary of Finance on 24 July 2026, replacing the previous policy decision that was originally issued in 2021 and subsequently updated in 2022. The 2026 Policy Decree on Hybrid Mismatches provides official guidance from the Dutch State Secretary for...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Netherlands published the <a href="https://zoek.officielebekendmakingen.nl/stcrt-2026-26405.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Hybrid Mismatch Policy Decision 2026 (Decree No. 2026-12123)</a>, issued by the State Secretary of Finance on 24 July 2026, replacing the previous policy decision that was originally issued in <a href="https://zoek.officielebekendmakingen.nl/stcrt-2021-42915.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">2021</a> and subsequently updated in <a href="https://zoek.officielebekendmakingen.nl/stcrt-2022-29035.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">2022</a>.</p>
<p>The 2026 Policy Decree on Hybrid Mismatches provides official guidance from the Dutch State Secretary for Finance regarding measures to prevent tax avoidance through international legal discrepancies. These regulations target situations where differences between national tax systems lead to double deductions or payments that are deductible in one country but remain untaxed in another.  The policy updates previous guidelines by introducing specific rules for US tax regimes like GILTI and NCTI, as well as providing clarity on the treatment of fixed assets and inventory.</p>
<p>Aside from the specific additions outlined below and some minor editorial adjustments, no other substantive changes were made compared to the prior policy.</p>
<p>The key additions and changes introduced in the new decree:</p>
<p><strong>New Section 2.3: GILTI and NCTI regimes (US tax regimes) </strong></p>
<p>This section clarifies how the Dutch hybrid mismatch rules interact with US Controlled Foreign Company (CFC)-like regimes, specifically the Global Intangible Low-Taxed Income (GILTI) regime, which was in place until 2025, and its 2026 replacement, the Net CFC Tested Income (NCTI) regime.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>No inclusion in taxation:</strong> Under both regimes, a US shareholder faces an additional tax on the income of their foreign subsidiaries, but this is offset by a substantial base reduction (up to 50% for GILTI and up to 40% for NCTI). Because of this base reduction, the income is not fully taxed at the regular statutory rate. Consequently, this (additional) US taxation does not qualify as an &#8220;inclusion in taxation&#8221; for the hybrid mismatch rules.</li>
<li><strong>No double deduction:</strong> If a Dutch corporate taxpayer takes a cost deduction that is also factored in by its US shareholder when applying the GILTI or NCTI regimes, this overlap cannot lead to a &#8220;double deduction&#8221; under the hybrid mismatch rules.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>New Section 2.4: Business assets, inventory, or stock goods </strong></p>
<p>This section addresses the timing and capitalisation of expenditures.</p>
<p>Buying assets, inventory, or stock doesn&#8217;t trigger hybrid mismatch rules at purchase—those costs are capitalised on the balance sheet rather than immediately deducted. The risk emerges later: when the asset is depreciated or written down, a double deduction can occur if both jurisdictions claim the same depreciation expense.</p>
<p>Timing differences between when each jurisdiction recognises depreciation are disregarded in this check. If a company claims duplicate depreciation alongside dual-inclusion income (for example, from selling the asset), the Netherlands may deny its deduction to the extent it exceeds that dual-inclusion income.</p>
<p><strong>New Section 4.1: Disregarded permanent establishments (PE) </strong></p>
<p>A &#8220;disregarded permanent establishment&#8221; occurs when the head office state assumes that a permanent establishment exists in another state, but that other state&#8217;s national tax laws do not recognise it as such.</p>
<p>Example case: The decree highlights the Maquiladora regime in Mexico as a primary example. If a Dutch BV operates an enterprise in Mexico, the Netherlands may consider it a PE under Dutch corporate tax law. However, if Mexican national law (via the Maquiladora regime) dictates that the Dutch BV does not have a PE there, it qualifies as a disregarded permanent establishment under the mismatch rules.</p>
<p><strong>New Section 4.2: Permanent Establishment Cessation Losses </strong></p>
<p>This section provides clarity on the treatment of &#8220;cessation losses&#8221; when a taxpayer ceases to derive profits from a foreign PE.</p>
<p>The Dutch object exemption doesn&#8217;t cover cessation losses from a permanent establishment, so losses can be deducted in the Netherlands. Since these losses are permanent and unavailable for relief in the former PE&#8217;s home state, claiming them in the Netherlands doesn&#8217;t constitute double deduction. The only exception occurs if the identical loss is also claimed in a third jurisdiction.</p>
<p><strong>Updated Section 4.3: Dual-inclusion income and cost-plus situations </strong></p>
<p>This section focuses on scenarios where income is taken into account twice, providing relief from the ATAD2 deduction limitations to prevent double taxation.</p>
<p>Following consultations with the European Commission, the State Secretary determined that in certain cost-plus situations, there is room to conclude that &#8220;dual-inclusion income&#8221; exists. The decree adds complex new examples (e.g., cost-plus situations involving a US  &#8216;partnership&#8217; or a US parent company where the Dutch entity is disregarded for US tax purposes).</p>
<p>In these structures, even if a cost triggers a double deduction, the ATAD2 limitation may not apply in the Netherlands if the sales revenue tied to the Dutch entity&#8217;s cost-plus remuneration is taxed at the parent level, thereby qualifying as dual-inclusion income. The burden of proof remains on the taxpayer to demonstrate their situation matches these examples.</p>
<p>The decree also officially removes an outdated deviating arrangement that was previously listed under this section, as its relevance has completely lapsed.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

					<description><![CDATA[UK’s His Majesty&#8217;s Revenue and Customs (HMRC) has published two reports from the General Anti-Avoidance Rule (GAAR) Advisory Panel concluding that arrangements designed to reduce Inheritance Tax (IHT) through the use of employee benefit trusts (EBTs) were unreasonable and therefore fall within the scope of GAAR. 										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>UK’s His Majesty&#8217;s Revenue and Customs (HMRC) has published two reports from the General Anti-Avoidance Rule (GAAR) Advisory Panel concluding that arrangements designed to reduce Inheritance Tax (IHT) through the use of employee benefit trusts (EBTs) were unreasonable and therefore fall within the scope of GAAR.</p>
<p>The opinions, <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/gaar-advisory-panel-opinion-of-30-january-2026-reducing-the-value-of-an-estate-for-inheritance-tax-and-avoiding-inheritance-tax-on-a-lifetime-transfer--2" target="_blank" rel="noopener">published</a> on 22 July 2026, relate to two separate inheritance tax planning arrangements that sought to rely on the Inheritance Tax Act 1984 (IHTA 1984) exemptions for gifts of shares to employee trusts under sections 28 and 86. In both cases, the independent panel concluded that the arrangements did not represent reasonable courses of action under the relevant tax provisions.</p>
<p>A separate GAAR Advisory Panel opinion dated 30 January 2026, published on 22 July 2026, also addressed arrangements involving reducing the value of an estate for Inheritance Tax and avoiding Inheritance Tax on a lifetime transfer by acquiring shares in a company and gifting those shares to an employee trust. The panel concluded that both entering into and carrying out such tax arrangements were not reasonable courses of action.</p>
<p><strong>Family investment company arrangement</strong></p>
<p>In the<a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/gaar-advisory-panel-opinion-of-30-january-2026-reducing-the-value-of-an-estate-for-inheritance-tax-and-avoiding-inheritance-tax-on-a-lifetime-transfer--2" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> first case</a>, the deceased was the sole employee and director of a family investment company and owned almost all of its shares.</p>
<p>A few days before the individual&#8217;s death, advisers implemented a series of steps that included establishing an employee benefit trust, transferring the deceased&#8217;s shares to the trust, appointing family members as directors and employees, and placing the company&#8217;s shares under the trust. According to the GAAR Advisory Panel, the company had no employees other than the deceased when the trust was created, and its business primarily consisted of holding property investments, cash and financial assets.</p>
<p>Although the shares were formally transferred to an employee benefit trust, the panel concluded that the arrangement did not reflect the normal transfer of a business for the benefit of a broad workforce. It found there was no evidence that the deceased intended to expand the workforce or benefit future non-family employees, while family members retained influence over the company and the trust through directorships, shareholdings and provisions in the trust deed.</p>
<p>The panel said the arrangements were inconsistent with the principles and policy objectives of section 28 of the Inheritance Tax Act 1984, which was intended to encourage genuine employee trusts rather than structures allowing family wealth to remain under family influence while obtaining an Inheritance Tax exemption.</p>
<p>Property investment business arrangement</p>
<p>The <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/gaar-advisory-panel-opinion-of-30-january-2026-reducing-the-value-of-an-estate-for-inheritance-tax-and-avoiding-inheritance-tax-on-a-lifetime-transfer--3" target="_blank" rel="noopener">second opinion</a> concerned a property investment business that had been operated by the deceased as a sole trader.</p>
<p>Before the individual&#8217;s death, a partnership was formed with the deceased&#8217;s two sons, after which the business was incorporated and the deceased gifted company shares to an employee benefit trust.</p>
<p>The GAAR Advisory Panel concluded that the planning was &#8220;not consistent with the principles and objectives for exemption under section 28&#8221; of the Inheritance Tax Act 1984, and therefore did not amount to a reasonable course of action under the relevant tax provisions.</p>
<p><strong>Panel&#8217;s conclusions</strong></p>
<p>In its detailed opinion, the GAAR Advisory Panel said the arrangements involved contrived or abnormal steps designed to sidestep the restrictions on the section 28 exemption and reduce the intended Inheritance Tax charge on the deceased&#8217;s estate. It also noted that while future employees could theoretically benefit from the trust, there was no evidence of business expansion or any intention to benefit non-family employees. The panel therefore concluded that both entering into and carrying out the arrangements were not reasonable courses of action in relation to the relevant tax provisions.</p>
<p><strong>GAAR framework</strong></p>
<p>The <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/tax-avoidance-general-anti-abuse-rules" target="_blank" rel="noopener">General Anti-Avoidance Rule (GAAR)</a> is contained in the Finance Act 2013 for income tax and the National Insurance Contributions Act 2014 for national insurance liabilities. It is intended to counter abusive tax avoidance, while the independent GAAR Advisory Panel provides opinions on cases where HMRC considers that GAAR may apply.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

		<title>Australia: ATO updates guidance on monthly GST reporting, extends authority to mandate switch for non-compliant businesses</title>
		<link>https://regfollower.com/australia-ato-updates-guidance-on-monthly-gst-reporting-extends-authority-to-mandate-switch-for-non-compliant-businesses/?utm_source=rss&#038;utm_medium=rss&#038;utm_campaign=australia-ato-updates-guidance-on-monthly-gst-reporting-extends-authority-to-mandate-switch-for-non-compliant-businesses</link>

		<category><![CDATA[Asia-Pacific]]></category>

					<description><![CDATA[The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) has updated its guidance on changing to monthly GST reporting, including new guidance on voluntarily switching GST reporting. It has also revised its guidance on when it may change a business&#8217;s GST reporting cycle, including circumstances in which businesses may be moved from quarterly to monthly reporting. Why the ATO...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) has updated its <a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/preparing-lodging-and-paying/business-activity-statements-bas/changing-to-monthly-gst-reporting" target="_blank" rel="noopener">guidance</a> on changing to <a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/preparing-lodging-and-paying/business-activity-statements-bas/changing-to-monthly-gst-reporting/why-we-may-change-your-gst-reporting-cycle" target="_blank" rel="noopener">monthly GST reporting</a>, including new guidance on<a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/preparing-lodging-and-paying/business-activity-statements-bas/changing-to-monthly-gst-reporting/voluntarily-changing-your-gst-reporting" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> voluntarily switching GST reporting</a>. It has also revised its guidance on when it may change a business&#8217;s GST reporting cycle, including circumstances in which businesses may be moved from quarterly to monthly reporting.</p>
<p><span style="text-decoration: underline"><strong>Why the ATO may change a business&#8217;s GST reporting cycle</strong></span></p>
<p><strong>Why the ATO can change GST reporting</strong></p>
<p>The ATO will direct a business to move to monthly GST reporting if it has determined that any of the following apply:</p>
<ul>
<li>The business meets the<a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/gst-excise-and-indirect-taxes/gst/lodging-your-bas-or-annual-gst-return/options-for-reporting-and-paying-gst" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> tax period turnover threshold</a>.</li>
<li>The business will be operating in Australia for less than 3 months.</li>
<li>The business has a history of failing to comply with tax obligations.</li>
</ul>
<p>Examples of failing to comply with tax obligations include:</p>
<ul>
<li>lodging or paying late</li>
<li>failing to lodge or pay</li>
<li>reporting tax obligations incorrectly.</li>
</ul>
<p>The ATO will notify the business in writing if it moves the business to <a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/gst-excise-and-indirect-taxes/gst/lodging-your-bas-or-annual-gst-return/options-for-reporting-and-paying-gst/monthly-gst-reporting" target="_blank" rel="noopener">monthly GST reporting</a>. The business will then need to calculate, report and pay GST on a monthly basis on the BAS.</p>
<p><strong>Effect on other reporting obligations</strong></p>
<p>If a business has wine equalisation tax (WET), luxury car tax (LCT) or fuel tax credit obligations, these amounts will also need to be reported each month in the BAS. This change occurs automatically as part of changing the GST reporting cycle.</p>
<p>A business can choose to align other reporting and payment obligations, for example pay as you go (PAYG) withholding.</p>
<p>If there is a disagreement with the change</p>
<p>If a business disagrees with the change, an objection can be lodged within 60 days from the date of notification of the ATO&#8217;s decision.</p>
<p><strong>Lodge and pay on time</strong></p>
<p>Businesses must lodge and pay the BAS in full and on time to avoid a <a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/paying-the-ato/interest-and-penalties/penalties/failure-to-lodge-on-time-penalty" target="_blank" rel="noopener">failure to lodge on time penalty</a> and <a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/paying-the-ato/interest-and-penalties/interest-we-charge/general-interest-charge" target="_blank" rel="noopener">general interest charge</a>.</p>
<p>If there is concern about meeting the due date, before the due date the business should either:</p>
<ul>
<li>contact a registered tax professional</li>
<li>find out about the support options available.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Requesting a change to the GST reporting cycle</strong></p>
<p>If a determination is made, the business must report GST monthly for a minimum of 12 months. To revert to quarterly or annual reporting, a request must be made for the determination to be revoked.</p>
<p>A request for revocation can be made by contacting a registered tax agent or contacting the ATO directly. The ATO will only approve requests if satisfied that the grounds for the determination no longer apply. For more information, see Why the ATO can change a business&#8217;s GST reporting cycle.</p>
<p><strong>Example: Change to monthly reporting</strong></p>
<p>Jack has been running a small business for over 5 years and his turnover ranged from AUD 350,000 to AUD 550,000 per year. He uses a digital accounting software package for BAS preparation. His tax agent has set it up for quarterly GST reporting.</p>
<p>With the demands of running a busy business, Jack has developed a pattern of lodging and paying late. Over the past 18 months, Jack has fallen behind and stopped engaging with the ATO. At this point:</p>
<ul>
<li>he hasn&#8217;t lodged a number of past BAS</li>
<li>some of his previous BAS were lodged late</li>
<li>his last business income tax return has not been lodged</li>
<li>he has an overdue tax debt</li>
<li>he has defaulted on the payment plans he had set up to pay the overdue tax debt.</li>
</ul>
<p>Jack receives a letter from the ATO advising him that he will now have to report and pay his GST monthly. He understands from the letter that this decision is based on his history of failing to comply with his tax obligations.</p>
<p>Jack decides to bring his lodgments up to date and enters into a new payment plan for the overdue debt.</p>
<p>This marks a turning point in his business. Jack finds it easier to stay on track with accurate, up-to-date record-keeping, which helps him make better business decisions. After the 12-month period, Jack saw the benefits of monthly reporting and decided to keep his reporting cycle as monthly.</p>
<p><span style="text-decoration: underline"><strong>Voluntarily changing your GST reporting</strong></span></p>
<p><strong>Advantages of monthly GST reporting</strong></p>
<p>Moving to monthly reporting could help businesses manage their operations and cashflow.</p>
<p>Many businesses that have voluntarily moved to monthly GST reporting have found that it aligns better with other business obligations that occur monthly, and that smaller, more manageable payments help them understand their transaction history and how much GST to pay or put aside.</p>
<p><strong>Effect on related BAS reporting obligations</strong></p>
<p>This change will impact related obligations on the BAS, such as wine equalisation tax (WET), luxury car tax (LCT) and fuel tax credits. This will occur automatically as part of changing the GST reporting cycle.</p>
<p>Businesses can choose to align other reporting and payment obligations to monthly — for example, pay as you go (PAYG) withholding.</p>
<p><strong>How to change to monthly GST reporting</strong></p>
<p>Businesses can voluntarily change to monthly GST reporting in <a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/online-services/businesses-and-organisations-online-services" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Online services for business</a> by accessing the Profile menu and selecting Tax registration.</p>
<p>Tax and BAS agents can also make the change in <a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/tax-and-super-professionals/digital-services/online-services-for-agents/online-services-for-agents-user-guide" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Online services for agents</a>.</p>
<p>Sole traders will need to phone the ATO or apply in writing.</p>
<p>If a change to monthly reporting is made, it will take effect from the start of the next quarter.</p>
<p>For more information, see Changing your reporting and payment cycle.</p>
<p><strong>Lodge and pay on time</strong></p>
<p>Businesses must lodge and pay their BAS in full and on time to avoid a <a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/paying-the-ato/interest-and-penalties/penalties/failure-to-lodge-on-time-penalty" target="_blank" rel="noopener">failure to lodge on time penalty</a> and <a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/paying-the-ato/interest-and-penalties/interest-we-charge/general-interest-charge" target="_blank" rel="noopener">general interest charge</a>.</p>
<p>If there are concerns about being unable to lodge and pay by the due date, businesses should — before the due date — contact a registered tax professional or find out about the support options available.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[The Colombian Ministry of Finance submitted a new 2026 Tax Reform Bill to Congress on 20 July 2026, introducing a broad package of tax measures aimed at strengthening public finances. Although the legislation is titled the 2026 Tax Reform Bill, most of its provisions are proposed to take effect from 2027. The bill follows the...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Colombian Ministry of Finance submitted a <a href="https://www.camara.gov.co/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/proyectos-ley/documentos/proyecto-36102/P.L.004-2026SC-REFORMA-TRIBUTARIA.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">new 2026 Tax Reform Bill</a> to Congress on 20 July 2026, introducing a broad package of tax measures aimed at strengthening public finances. Although the legislation is titled the 2026 Tax Reform Bill, most of its provisions are proposed to take effect from 2027. The bill follows the rejection of an earlier 2026 tax reform proposal at the end of 2025.</p>
<p>The reform forms part of the government&#8217;s fiscal consolidation strategy, which seeks to address structural pressures on public finances while maintaining macroeconomic stability. The government targets additional revenue of COP 21.9 trillion, equivalent to about 1.0% of GDP, in 2027 and an average of 1.5% of GDP annually from 2028.</p>
<p><strong>Corporate and business taxation</strong></p>
<p>Among the key business measures, the bill proposes increasing the corporate income tax surtax on financial institutions from 5% to 15% above the standard corporate income tax rate, resulting in a total tax rate of 50%. The higher surtax will become permanent from the 2027 tax year.</p>
<p>The optional tax rate on gross income earned by non-resident entities providing digital services or selling in Colombia under the Significant Economic Presence (SEP) rules will increase from 3% to 5% from 1 January 2027.</p>
<p>The proposal also establishes a permanent 1% tax on the FOB export value or domestic sales invoice value for crude oil and coal for companies with net ordinary income of at least 50,000 UVT. In addition, surtax rules for coal extraction will be aligned with those already applied to crude oil.</p>
<p>Preferential corporate income tax regimes for hotels, theme parks, ecotourism, docks and mega-investment schemes will be reduced or removed from the 2027 tax year.</p>
<p><strong>Individual income and wealth taxes</strong></p>
<p>The bill will raise the maximum marginal individual income tax rate from 39% to 41% for net taxable income exceeding 31,000 UVT from the 2027 tax year. Other income tax brackets will also be revised, including increases in the 29%, 35%, 37% and 39% bands.</p>
<p>The additional deduction of 72 UVT per dependent, introduced in 2022, will be eliminated, while the existing deduction of 10% of gross income, capped at 32 UVT per month, will remain.</p>
<p>The wealth (equity) tax threshold will be reduced from 72,000 UVT to 40,000 UVT. The revised scale will introduce rates ranging from 0.5% to 5%, with the highest 5% rate applying to wealth exceeding 2,000,000 UVT.</p>
<p>Other proposed changes include repealing the dividend tax discount and the non-taxable inflationary component deduction on financial yields for individuals from 1 January 2027.</p>
<p>The tax rate on winnings from lotteries, raffles and gambling, together with related occasional gains, will increase from 20% to 30% from the date the law enters into force.</p>
<p><strong>VAT and consumption tax measures</strong></p>
<p>The reform includes several VAT changes affecting multiple sectors.</p>
<p>Online gambling and sports betting platforms will become permanently subject to the general 19% VAT rate from 1 January 2027, replacing the current preferential treatment and aligning them with physical betting establishments.</p>
<p>The VAT rate on hybrid vehicles will rise from the preferential 5% rate to the standard 19% rate from the date of enactment, while the reduced rate will remain available for zero-emission electric vehicles.</p>
<p>Producer-level VAT on motor gasoline and diesel willincrease from 5% to 10% on 1 January 2027 and to the general 19% rate from 1 January 2028. Biodiesel will become subject to the 19% VAT rate from 1 January 2027, followed by fuel ethanol from 1 July 2027. A multi-stage VAT system will also be introduced for the gasoline supply chain, applying 19% VAT to retail margins from 1 January 2027.</p>
<p>The government also proposes applying the general 19% VAT rate to alcoholic beverages from the first day of the month following enactment.</p>
<p>The bill will eliminate the VAT exemption for imported goods valued below USD 200, removing the de minimis relief for low-value online purchases. It willalso end the VAT exemption for hotel and accommodation services supplied to non-resident foreign tourists in Colombia while retaining the existing VAT refund mechanism at airports and border crossings.</p>
<p>For non-conventional renewable energy projects, the current VAT exemption for equipment, machinery and related services will be replaced with zero-rated treatment, allowing businesses to recover input VAT.</p>
<p>In addition, the national consumption tax rate will increase from 16% to 19% from 2027.</p>
<p><strong>Environmental measures</strong></p>
<p>The proposal willincrease the carbon tax base rate from COP 29,070.49 to COP 42,609 per ton of CO2 from 2027. Coal will be phased into the carbon tax regime, with taxation reaching 40% of the full rate in 2027, 60% in 2028, 80% in 2029 and 100% from 2030.</p>
<p>The fiscal strategy also includes the introduction of Energy Transition Bonds, allowing investors to deduct 50% of qualifying investments.</p>
<p><strong>Social security and fiscal impact</strong></p>
<p>The bill will reduce the salary threshold for employer exemptions from health and parafiscal contributions, including SENA and ICBF contributions, from employees earning up to 10 minimum wages (SMMLV) to those earning up to 3 SMMLV.</p>
<p>The government estimates the package will have a one-off inflationary effect of about 0.43% in 2027 from VAT measures and 0.74% from other consumption-related taxes. It also argues that increased public investment funded by the additional revenue will result in GDP growth being around 0.20% higher over the next decade than under a scenario based on spending cuts.</p>
<p>Several measures included in the bill had previously been introduced under Legislative Decree No. 1474 of 29 December 2025, which was later declared unconstitutional. The current tax value unit (Unidad de Valor Tributario &#8211; UVT) is COP 52,374 for 2026.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Canada&#8217;s Department of Finance has <a href="https://www.canada.ca/en/department-finance/news/2026/07/government-launches-consultation-on-draft-legislation-for-various-tax-measures.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">released </a>draft legislative proposals for public consultation on 23 July 2026 to implement a range of previously announced tax measures, along with other technical amendments to the country&#8217;s tax system.</p>
<p>Canada’s government is committed to maintaining a tax system that is fair, effective, and competitive. The proposed changes aim to clarify and improve tax rules, close gaps to prevent tax avoidance, and ensure existing measures work as intended. They would also promote investment, productivity, and clean growth, while making the tax system easier to administer and understand. Together, these measures support the government&#8217;s broader efforts to build a stronger, more competitive Canadian economy.</p>
<p>The government invites stakeholders to provide feedback on these draft legislative proposals to ensure they are effective, fair, and aligned with policy objectives.</p>
<p>The proposed tax measures include:</p>
<ul>
<li>Amendments to the Disability Tax Credit (DTC) to streamline the application process for individuals with certain long-lasting medical conditions and expand the list of medical practitioners who can certify eligibility for the DTC.</li>
<li>Amendments to confirm the taxable status of the Red Seal Completion Bonus, which would increase apprenticeship completion rates by providing a one-time CAD 5,000 bonus to apprentices obtaining certification in a Red Seal trade.</li>
<li>Amendments to the Investment Tax Credit for Carbon Capture, Utilisation, and Storage (CCUS) so that the storage of CO2 through enhanced oil recovery be made eligible for the purposes of the CCUS investment tax credit, at half the credit rates available for dedicated geological storage.</li>
<li>Amendments to reinstate the accelerated capital cost allowances for eligible liquefied natural gas (LNG) equipment and related buildings for low-carbon LNG facilities.</li>
<li>Amendments to ensure that the investment income of a foreign affiliate on assets backing Canadian insurance risk be considered foreign accrual property income and therefore subject to taxation in Canada.</li>
<li>Amendments to allow for simplified transfer pricing documentation in four scenarios involving: small taxpayers and partnerships, small transfers of tangible property, small intragroup services transactions, and small loans.</li>
<li>A second package of amendments to address hybrid mismatch arrangements, implementing recommendations of the report under Action 2 of the OECD/G20 Base Erosion and Profit Shifting project, titled Neutralising the Effects of Hybrid Mismatch Arrangements.</li>
<li>Amendments to establish a Goods and Services Tax/Harmonized Sales Tax (GST/HST) reverse charge mechanism for certain supplies in the telecommunications sector to help prevent carousel fraud and improve the overall fairness of the Canadian tax system.</li>
<li>Amendments to the Agriculture and Fishing Property (GST/HST) Regulations to add agricultural quotas supplied by lease, licence or similar arrangement as prescribed property that is zero-rated under the GST/HST.</li>
<li>Amendments to the Federal Book Rebate (GST/HST) Regulations to permit Wonderful World of Books, a registered charity operating in British Columbia, to claim the federal printed book rebate for GST paid on printed books and certain audio recordings in the course of promoting literacy.</li>
<li>Other technical amendments to tax statutes and related regulations such as the Income Tax Act, the Excise Tax Act, the Income Tax Regulations and the Global Minimum Tax Act to ensure Canada&#8217;s tax laws align with their underlying policy objectives.</li>
</ul>
<p>The government invites all interested Canadians and stakeholders to provide feedback on these draft legislative proposals by emailing their comments to consultation-legislation@fin.gc.ca by 4 September 2026.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Italian Revenue Agency <a href="https://www.fiscooggi.it/portale/-/global-minimum-tax-codici-tributo-per-regolarizzarsi-con-ravvedimento" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced</a>, on 23 July 2026, that it has introduced new tax codes for paying penalties through the F24 form for voluntary disclosure of violations relating to the Global Minimum Tax&#8217;s information and reporting obligations under Legislative Decree No. 209/2023.</p>
<p><a href="https://www.agenziaentrate.gov.it/portale/documents/20143/10196141/RIS_n_27_del_23_07_2026.pdf/210a18fd-c714-bb16-878b-c75d566ad98a?t=1784818998516" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Resolution No. 27</a> of 23 July 2026 implements this final piece of Legislative Decree No. 209/2023, letting multinational and large domestic groups correct non-compliance under the ravvedimento mechanism.</p>
<p>The announcement follows Resolution No. 63/E of 10 November 2025, which had established codes for the underlying Global Minimum Tax payments themselves—the Income Inclusion Rule (IIR), Undertaxed Profits Rule (UTPR), and Qualified Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax (QDMTT). The new codes now handle penalties for voluntary corrections of violations under Article 51 (information obligations) and Article 53 (reporting obligations) of the decree.</p>
<p><strong>Three codes for three violation types</strong></p>
<p>The new tax codes, used in the F24 payment form&#8217;s Treasury section, are:</p>
<ul>
<li>2735: penalties for missing relevant communications under Article 51</li>
<li>2736: penalties for missed notification obligations under Article 51</li>
<li>2737: late-filed annual minimum tax returns under Article 53</li>
</ul>
<p>Companies filing the F24 must enter the applicable code in the Treasury section, specify the payment amount in the &#8220;amounts paid&#8221; column, and note the relevant tax year in YYYY format. This allows operators to regularise failures without waiting for the Revenue Agency to assess them.</p>
<p><strong>The penalty structure and what triggers it</strong></p>
<p>Article 51 of Decree 209/2023 requires Italian-based companies and transparent entities to submit mandatory communications and notifications within statutory deadlines.</p>
<p>The penalties are graduated by severity: failing to submit entirely or delaying more than three months brings a EUR 100,000 fine; delays under three months or incomplete/incorrect information cost EUR 10,000 to EUR 50,000. A single annual ceiling of EUR 1 million applies across all group companies in Italy. Notification-only violations carry lower penalties of EUR 250 to EUR 2,000.</p>
<p>Article 53 covers the annual declaration of supplementary minimum tax, UTPR, and national minimum tax, filed alongside the relevant communications. Late filings of this declaration can also be corrected through the voluntary disclosure mechanism.</p>
<p><strong>Three-year grace period with reduced penalties</strong></p>
<p>The law includes a transitional regime for the first three financial years: information obligation penalties won&#8217;t be imposed except in cases of willful misconduct or gross negligence.</p>
<p>For information penalties that do apply, the amounts are reduced by 50%. This breathing room gives multinational and large national groups time to build compliance infrastructure around the new regime&#8217;s technical requirements.</p>
<p><a href="https://regfollower.com/italy-clarifies-gmt-penalties-90-day-return-cutoff-under-voluntary-disclosure-centralised-globe-filings/">Earlier</a>, the Italian Revenue Agency published a new FAQ on the Pillar Two GMT on 17 July 2026, expanding on the guidance first issued on 29 May 2026.</p>

The move marks the first major tariff action after the US Supreme Court dismantled his previous reciprocal duty scheme in...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Trump administration imposed new tariffs across 60 trading partners—the EU, China, Japan, Canada, and dozens more—alleging they&#8217;ve failed to prevent goods made by forced labour from entering their supply chains on 24 July 2026.</p>
<p>The move marks the first major tariff action after the US Supreme Court <a href="https://regfollower.com/us-supreme-court-invalidates-emergency-tariffs-trump-raises-global-tariffs-to-15-following-ruling/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">dismantled</a> his previous reciprocal duty scheme in February 2026. The new duties, issued under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, take effect immediately as a temporary 10% global tariff expires.</p>
<p>According to a Federal Register <a href="https://ustr.gov/sites/default/files/files/Press/Releases/2026/FLIP%20301%20Investigation%20Final%20Action%20FRN%207-23-26%20FINAL.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">notice</a>, the new tariffs apply to 99.4% of US imports, with exemptions for products such as oil and gas, fertiliser, and certain food items.</p>
<p>Countries face either a flat 10% or 12.5% rate—or combined rates reaching those thresholds where existing tariffs already apply.</p>
<p><strong>Why Section 301 matters</strong></p>
<p>The legal manoeuvre sidesteps the Supreme Court&#8217;s rejection of Trump&#8217;s national emergency powers. Section 301 has survived prior court challenges, giving the administration a more durable foundation. Trump officials signalled this was a deliberate strategy to rebuild the tariff wall while respecting previous trade commitments—particularly with the EU, which had negotiated tariff caps.</p>
<p><strong>Who pays what</strong></p>
<p>Eighteen countries including Bangladesh, Cambodia, Mexico, and the UK face a straight 10% rate for allegedly having forced labour bans but failing to enforce them. The EU, Taiwan, Japan, South Korea, and Switzerland hit either 10% or 12.5% when combined with existing rates.</p>
<p>Another 38 countries—Vietnam, China, India, Brazil, Australia, and others—absorb 12.5%. China&#8217;s rate is rising from the current 10% toward a planned 20%, the level agreed in November 2025 with President Xi Jinping but never reached.</p>
<p><strong>Reactions: mixed, sceptical, muted</strong></p>
<p>The EU acknowledged that tariff caps held firm—a small win. Britain highlighted preserved whisky exemptions and better steel treatment than competitors. But Australia, Brazil, and Norway rejected the forced labour justification outright. Canada barely responded, already reeling from Monday&#8217;s additional tariffs on USD 20 billion in goods. China called the move unilateral and pointless.</p>
<p>A separate Section 301 investigation into excess capacity remains pending, targeting the same 16 partners including the EU, China, and Japan. Bond markets barely stirred. The real test comes when those duties land.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>South Korea&#8217;s National Tax Service (NTS) has introduced a Fast-track procedure for Advance Pricing Agreement (APA) renewals and rolled out a broader package of tax support measures for foreign-invested enterprises (FIEs) aimed at strengthening the country&#8217;s investment climate.</p>
<p>The initiatives were <a href="https://www.nts.go.kr/nts/na/ntt/selectNttInfo.do?mi=2201&amp;bbsId=1028&amp;nttSn=1351244" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced </a>during the NTS&#8217;s first joint meeting on 14 May 2026 with representatives of eight major foreign chambers of commerce and the Foreign Investment Ombudsman.</p>
<p><strong>APA Fast-track procedure</strong></p>
<p>The new Fast-track procedure applies to bilateral and multilateral APA renewal applications that are substantially similar to previously approved agreements. Eligible applications will undergo an initial desk review within three months of submission, after which the NTS will consult with the relevant tax authority or authorities to designate the case as a priority.</p>
<p>To qualify, an application must be submitted within six months before the expiration of the existing APA, retain the same transaction structure, corporate functions and business risks, maintain a similar proportion of related-party transactions, and request an arm&#8217;s length price range comparable to the previously agreed range. The procedure applies to pre-filing consultation applications submitted on or after 14 May 2026.</p>
<p><strong>Tax audit relief and R&amp;D support</strong></p>
<p>The NTS said foreign-invested enterprises that increase domestic investment or youth employment by more than 10% compared with the previous year will receive a one-year exemption from corporate tax reporting verifications in the international tax field.</p>
<p>These companies will also receive priority processing of R&amp;D Tax Credit Pre-assessments, regardless of the order in which applications are submitted.</p>
<p><strong>Dedicated consultation desks</strong></p>
<p>The NTS has established dedicated consultation desks at the Seoul, Jungbu and Incheon Regional Tax Offices to assist foreign companies with Korean tax laws.</p>
<p>The desks provide guidance on the tax system, reporting requirements and payment procedures through dedicated hotlines, web-mail and scheduled in-person consultations.</p>
<p><strong>Global minimum tax assistance</strong></p>
<p>Ahead of the first Global Minimum Tax filing in June 2026, the NTS is providing English-language guidance videos and leaflets, along with one-to-one consultations for companies requiring assistance with the filing process.</p>
<p><strong>Corporate tax consulting for SMEs</strong></p>
<p>Small and medium-sized foreign enterprises will be able to receive Corporate Tax consulting on available tax credits and reductions. The NTS will verify eligibility and calculate potential benefits in advance to help businesses claim incentives for which they qualify.</p>
<p>NTS Commissioner Lim Kwang-hyun said foreign investment remains an important driver of future economic growth and reaffirmed the agency&#8217;s commitment to creating a predictable and attractive tax environment for global investors.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Bahrain&#8217;s National Bureau for Revenue (NBR) has released<a href="https://www.nbr.gov.bh/publications/view/VAT_Registration_" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> Version 1.10 of its VAT Registration Guide on 22 July 2026</a>, updating the processing timelines for VAT registration and amendment applications.</p>
<p>Under the revised guidance, the NBR will review and process change or amendment applications within five working days from the date of submission. The guide also states that new VAT registration applications and VAT registration amendment applications will generally be processed within 21 working days from the submission date.</p>
<p>The updated guide continues to provide step-by-step instructions for individuals and businesses registering for Value Added Tax (VAT) through the NBR&#8217;s electronic portal.</p>
<p><strong>Registration requirements remain unchanged</strong></p>
<p>The guidance confirms that VAT, introduced in Bahrain on 1 January 2019 at a 5% standard rate, has been applied at a 10% standard rate since 1 January 2022.</p>
<p>For resident businesses, mandatory registration applies where annual taxable supplies exceeded BHD 37,500 during the previous 12 months or are expected to exceed that amount in the coming 12 months. Voluntary registration remains available where annual taxable supplies or expenses exceed BHD 18,750.</p>
<p>For non-residents, there is no registration threshold. Registration is required from the first BHD 1 of taxable supplies made to non-registered persons in Bahrain. The guide also notes that non-residents may appoint a tax representative to meet their VAT obligations.</p>
<p><strong>Registration process</strong></p>
<p>Applicants must first create an account on the NBR electronic portal before completing the VAT registration application. Supporting documents include the Commercial Registration (CR) certificate, identification of the authorised person, proof of address, financial statements where available, and bank account details.</p>
<p>Following approval, the NBR issues a VAT registration certificate, which must be displayed at the taxpayer&#8217;s place of business.</p>
<p><strong>VAT Groups and compliance</strong></p>
<p>The guide reiterates that two or more legal persons may register as a VAT Group if they are Bahrain residents, conduct an economic activity, are individually registered for VAT, and qualify as related parties through common control.</p>
<p>It also restates the compliance rules for registration. Businesses that fail to register within 30 days of exceeding the mandatory registration threshold may face administrative fines of up to BHD 10,000. Delaying registration for more than 120 days may result in a conviction for tax evasion.</p>
<p><strong>De-registration rules</strong></p>
<p>The guidance also maintains the existing de-registration requirements. Taxable persons must apply to cancel their VAT registration if they cease carrying on an economic activity or if their taxable supplies remain below the voluntary registration threshold of BHD 18,750 for 12 consecutive months. Taxpayers that registered voluntarily must remain registered for at least 24 months before applying for de-registration.</p>

		<title>Belgium introduces tiered capital gains tax on financial assets with progressive rates, exemptions</title>
		<link>https://regfollower.com/belgium-introduces-tiered-capital-gains-tax-on-financial-assets-with-progressive-rates-exemptions/?utm_source=rss&#038;utm_medium=rss&#038;utm_campaign=belgium-introduces-tiered-capital-gains-tax-on-financial-assets-with-progressive-rates-exemptions</link>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Mohammed Al Mamun]]></dc:creator>

				<category><![CDATA[Taxation of capital gains]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Belgium]]></category>

					<description><![CDATA[The Belgian Ministry of Finance has published Circular 2026/C/74 on 22 July 2026. Circular 2026/C/74 outlines the Belgian tax framework for financial capital gains following legislation enacted on 6 April 2026. Circular 2026/C/74 provides comprehensive guidance on the new capital gains tax on financial assets specifically for personal income tax purposes, leaving the rules for...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Belgian Ministry of Finance has published<a href="https://www.minfin.fgov.be/myminfin-web/pages/public/fisconet/document/7f6b62c6-1baa-487a-8f59-c883dd5485c4" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> Circular 2026/C/74</a> on 22 July 2026.</p>
<p>Circular 2026/C/74 outlines the Belgian tax framework for financial capital gains following legislation enacted on 6 April 2026. Circular 2026/C/74 provides comprehensive guidance on the new capital gains tax on financial assets specifically for personal income tax purposes, leaving the rules for corporate entities and withholding tax to be covered in separate circulars.</p>
<p>The new tax applies to capital gains realised by individuals managing their private wealth (non-speculative) and categorises these gains into three main types, each with its own tax rates and exemption rules:</p>
<p><strong>Category A (Type A): Internal capital gains </strong></p>
<p>This category targets the transfer of shares or profit certificates to a company over which the transferor, either alone or together with their close family, exercises direct or indirect control.</p>
<p>These internal capital gains are taxed at a flat rate of 33% (excluding local communal surcharges).</p>
<p>Due to the internal nature of the transaction (where the taxpayer is essentially both the assignor and the assignee), no withholding tax is applied at the source, but it triggers strict reporting obligations.</p>
<p><strong>Category B (Type B): Substantial participations </strong></p>
<p>This specific regime applies to gains from the transfer of shares where the taxpayer holds a substantial interest of at least 20% in the company&#8217;s capital. Taxpayers benefit from a first instalment exemption of EUR 1 million, which is available over a consecutive five-year taxable period.</p>
<p>After the exemption is applied, the remaining gains are subject to progressive tax rates ranging from 1.25% to 10% (1.25% for gains up to EUR 2.5 million, up to 10% for gains exceeding EUR 10 million).</p>
<p>If the shares belong to a non-resident company whose principal establishment is located outside the European Economic Area (EEA), a distinct flat rate of 16.5% applies.</p>
<p><strong>Category C (Type C): General/residual financial assets</strong></p>
<p>Category C covers all other financial assets not included in Categories A or B, such as financial instruments, insurance contracts, crypto-assets, and certain investment funds. Capital gains are taxed at 10%, with an annual tax-free exemption of EUR 10,000 (indexed and applicable for the 2027 assessment year). Taxpayers may also accumulate an additional exemption, starting at EUR 1,000 from 2028, for years in which no capital gains are realised.</p>
<p><strong>Calculating the tax base and historical exemption </strong></p>
<p>The tax base is calculated as the positive difference between the sale price received and the acquisition value. A core principle of this new regime is the exemption of historical capital gains. For financial assets acquired before 1 January 2026, the acquisition value is determined by a &#8220;snapshot&#8221; (moment-photo) valuation of the asset&#8217;s worth on 31 December 2025.</p>
<p><strong>Exit tax and payment deferrals</strong></p>
<p>The Circular introduces an exit tax on unrealised capital gains when an individual ceases to be a Belgian tax resident by moving their domicile or wealth abroad. Taxpayers relocating to an EU/EEA country or a jurisdiction with a qualifying tax treaty may obtain a payment deferral, which is automatic for EU/EEA moves and available on request for certain non-EU/EEA countries subject to the provision of adequate security. Annex II lists the eligible non-EU/EEA treaty jurisdictions that qualify for the deferral regime.</p>
<p><strong>Additional exemptions </strong></p>
<p>Aside from the monetary thresholds, the tax does not apply in several specific scenarios:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Transfers without consideration:</strong> Inheritances, donations, and transfers due to death do not trigger the tax because no &#8220;realisation&#8221; of a gain has occurred.</li>
<li><strong>Division of co-ownership:</strong> Assets acquired during a division of co-ownership, such as following a divorce or the end of legal cohabitation, are exempt from being taxed at the time of the division.</li>
<li><strong>Corporate restructurings:</strong> Capital gains realised when exchanging shares during mergers, spin-offs, or contributions to holding companies are temporarily exempt.</li>
<li><strong>Pensions and double taxation:</strong> Second- and third-pillar pension savings are exempt. Furthermore, income that is already taxed under the &#8220;Cayman Tax&#8221; or the &#8220;Reynders Tax&#8221; is excluded to prevent double taxation.</li>
</ul>
]]></content:encoded>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Argentina&#8217;s tax authority (ARCA) has <a href="https://servicioscf.afip.gob.ar/publico/sitio/contenido/novedad/ver.aspx?id=5824" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced</a> that it has streamlined VAT credit recovery for mining exploration companies through <a href="https://biblioteca.arca.gob.ar/search/query/norma.aspx?p=t:RAG%7Cn:5879%7Co:9%7Ca:2026%7Cf:22/07/2026" target="_blank" rel="noopener">General Resolution No. 5879/2026</a>, published in the Official Gazette on 23 July 2026.</p>
<p>The new procedure consolidates fragmented rules and shifts VAT credit returns into the Comprehensive Recovery System (SIR), superseding the previous framework under General <a href="https://biblioteca.arca.gob.ar/search/query/norma.aspx?p=t:RAG%7Cn:1761%7Co:3%7Ca:2004%7Cf:27/10/2004" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Resolution No. 1761/2004</a>. The change modifies <a href="https://biblioteca.arca.gob.ar/search/query/norma.aspx?p=t:RAG%7Cn:5173%7Co:3%7Ca:2022%7Cf:23/03/2022" target="_blank" rel="noopener">General Resolution No. 5173/2022</a>.</p>
<p>For mining companies, this matters because exploration typically generates VAT costs before the project generates revenue. The revised process lets these companies reclaim accumulated VAT credits earlier, improving cash flow during pre-production phases when sales haven&#8217;t yet offset expenses.</p>
<p><strong>Who is eligible and what are the requirements?</strong></p>
<p>Three conditions must be satisfied for the refund to apply.</p>
<ul>
<li>First, at least 12 tax periods must have elapsed since the VAT credit was generated.</li>
<li>Second, the credits must represent a genuine balance in favour for the taxpayer—not a theoretical claim.</li>
<li>Third, the goods and services must have been pre-approved by the mining authority as directly related to exploration activities.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Operating form and documentation requirements</strong></p>
<p>To streamline the application process, the authorities have introduced a dedicated annex and Form F.8147. While the new procedure standardises submissions, applicants must still provide comprehensive supporting documentation.</p>
<p>Required documentation includes:</p>
<ul>
<li>Purchase records: Purchase or import invoices together with the corresponding payment receipts.</li>
<li>Technical information: A detailed description of the exploration activities, including the geographical location, work schedule, and environmental impact studies.</li>
<li>Operational details: A breakdown of goods purchased and services contracted that are directly related to prospecting activities.</li>
</ul>
<p>This regulation will come into force on the day of its publication in the Official Gazette. This regulation is mandatory for recovery applications corresponding to the period from March 2026 onwards.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Netherlands Ministry of Finance has published a <a href="https://zoek.officielebekendmakingen.nl/stcrt-2026-22425.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">policy rule </a>on 13 July 2026 outlining new administrative fine policies regarding the registration of ultimate beneficial owners (UBOs) for trusts and similar legal arrangements.</p>
<p>Effective from 1 June 2026, the regulation empowers the Ministry of Finance to penalise trustees who fail to provide accurate or timely information to the national UBO register.</p>
<p>The key details are as follows:</p>
<p><strong>Fine structure and escalating penalties </strong></p>
<p>By law, the statutory maximum for these violations is tied to a fourth-category criminal fine, which currently stands at EUR 27,500. First offence costs 10% of the statutory max — EUR 2,750.</p>
<p>After that, the fine doesn&#8217;t just climb; it doubles each time: EUR 5,500 for a second violation, EUR 11,000 for a third, EUR 22,000 for a fourth, and EUR 27,500 (the full statutory ceiling) for a fifth or any repeat after that.</p>
<p>A violation only counts as &#8220;repeat&#8221; if it falls within five years of a prior fine or sanction becoming final and irrevocable — past that window, the count resets to zero.</p>
<p><strong>Nuances and mitigating factors </strong></p>
<p>Two practical rules on top of the fine structure.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Multiple violations:</strong> If one act breaches several obligations at once, say failing to register a UBO while also failing to keep the existing record accurate, the trustee gets a single fine, not stacked penalties for each broken rule. The multiple breaches can still push that one fine higher, but they don&#8217;t multiply into separate charges.</li>
<li><strong>Mitigating circumstances:</strong> The Ministry may lower the fine based on specific circumstances, namely the financial capacity of the violator, the extent to which they cooperate during the investigation, and any corrective measures they implement to prevent the violation from continuing or recurring. However, the policy explicitly states that these factors can only be used to reduce the fine, and the burden of proof lies entirely on the violator to demonstrate why a reduction is justified.</li>
</ul>

Conversely, certain non-profit organisations, such as associations and political parties, remain part of the obligatory registry if they engage in economic activities.</p>
<p>The modifications introduced by Law No. 88 regarding both the mandatory and optional RO e-Factura registries come into effect on 1 June 2026.</p>
<p><strong>Updates to Form 082 (Mandatory Registry)</strong></p>
<p>Romania has exempted individual farmers and suppliers identified by personal identification number (CNP) from mandatory use of the RO e-Factura electronic invoicing system.</p>
<p>Entities previously forced to register can now request deregistration via Form 082, effective the first day of the following month.</p>
<p>Going forward, Form 082 will primarily serve NGOs, associations, foundations, political parties, and religious institutions not registered for VAT—these must request mandatory enrollment within 3 days before commencing economic activities launched after 30 June 2025.</p>
<p><strong>Updates to Form 081 (Optional Registry)</strong></p>
<p>Romania is expanding and tightening rules around its e-Factura electronic invoicing system. Foreign cultural institutes and individual farmers can now permanently opt in to the system voluntarily.</p>
<p>CNP-identified suppliers can formally opt in using Form 081, with enrollment taking effect the first day of the following month.  The form is being updated to also allow entities to withdraw from optional use.</p>
<p>NGOs, foundations, political parties, and religious institutions are being moved from optional to mandatory use—they had a one-year grace period ending 30 June 2025, but must now use e-Factura for all invoicing.</p>

The legislation modernises the national RO e-Invoice system by updating digital invoicing rules for businesses and individuals and introducing several new exemptions.</p>

		<link>https://regfollower.com/poland-sejm-introduces-new-vat-warehousing-regime-tightens-abuse-rules/?utm_source=rss&#038;utm_medium=rss&#038;utm_campaign=poland-sejm-introduces-new-vat-warehousing-regime-tightens-abuse-rules</link>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Mohammed Al Mamun]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Fri, 24 Jul 2026 15:17:45 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Administrative Obligations]]></category>
