					<description><![CDATA[Poland’s Sejm (lower house of the parliament) has enacted the draft law of 17 July 2026, which introduces a comprehensive set of amendments to the Polish VAT Act (the Act of 11 March 2004), encompassing the new VAT warehousing regime, compliance simplifications, anti-abuse measures, and alignment with CJEU case law. The key changes introduced by...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Poland’s Sejm (lower house of the parliament) has enacted the <a href="https://orka.sejm.gov.pl/opinie10.nsf/nazwa/2677_u/$file/2677_u.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">draft law of 17 July 2026</a>, which introduces a comprehensive set of amendments to the Polish VAT Act (the Act of 11 March 2004), encompassing the new VAT warehousing regime, compliance simplifications, anti-abuse measures, and alignment with CJEU case law.</p>
<p>The key changes introduced by the draft law are:</p>
<p><strong>Introduction of the VAT warehousing regime</strong></p>
<p>A new Chapter 11 to the VAT Act establishes a warehousing procedure for specified goods (cereals, tea, coffee, chemicals, metals, and others per Annex 17).</p>
<p>Operators must obtain authorisation from the tax office and meet requirements including 12 months of prior VAT taxpayer status, no significant tax arrears, legal warehouse ownership, and clean financial/fraud records.</p>
<p>Stored goods—capped at 24 months—can only undergo processing that preserves their combined nomenclature classification; retail sales to non-business individuals, flat-rate farmers, and consumption on-site are prohibited.</p>
<p>Suppliers and purchasers both holding authorisation receive 0% VAT on warehouse supplies and intra-EU acquisitions, provided the supplier holds documentation confirming goods entry into the warehouse.</p>
<p><strong>Measures aimed at simplifying VAT compliance</strong></p>
<p>Two VAT amendments simplify compliance for businesses winding down operations and acquiring transport across the EU. The draft law now allows taxpayers dissolving partnerships or ceasing activities to report unsold goods inventory values directly in their standard VAT return for the cessation period, eliminating the need for separate filings. Separately, taxpayers acquiring new transport means from other EU member states must submit required information electronically to their tax office by the standard VAT return deadline for that period.</p>
<p><strong>Split payment and joint liability </strong></p>
<p>The draft restricts the protective shield of the split payment mechanism. While split payment typically shields buyers from joint liability for a seller&#8217;s unpaid taxes, the new rules eliminate this protection if invoices document activities constituting &#8220;abuse of law&#8221; under the VAT Act. Joint liability will also now apply to service purchases with individual invoices below PLN 15,000 if monthly acquisitions from the same vendor total over PLN 50,000.</p>
<p><strong>Implementation of CJEU judgments</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>C-697/20 (Agricultural activity):</strong> The draft law is tightening rules on tax breaks for farmers. If multiple farmers jointly operate one farm but at least one chooses not to use the exemption, none of them can claim it. Those farmers now have to keep detailed records of all sales and expenses for five years.</li>
<li><strong>C-114/22 (Right to deduct):</strong> The draft law is closing a loophole where businesses deducted input taxes on invoices that were actually part of tax-dodging schemes. Going forward, you can&#8217;t claim that deduction if the transaction was designed primarily to exploit tax rules rather than for legitimate business reasons.</li>
<li><strong>C-273/16 (Zero-rating of import-related services):</strong> The draft law clarifies that services related to importing goods qualify for zero tax—but only if the cost of those services is already included in what you&#8217;re paying for the goods themselves. You can&#8217;t double-count the service cost.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Entry into force </strong></p>
<p>Poland&#8217;s VAT law rolls out in stages from December 2026 to July 2028, with most provisions starting 1 January 2027. Cash registers get new rules; e-terminals for tax-free exports arrive in July 2028.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

The latest peer review results on preferential tax regimes highlight jurisdictions’ continued efforts to address harmful tax...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The OECD has <a href="https://www.oecd.org/en/about/news/announcements/2026/07/beps-action-5-jurisdictions-make-further-progress-in-addressing-harmful-tax-practices-under-new-review-methodology.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">released</a> the latest peer review results on preferential tax regimes under BEPS Action 5, incorporating new conclusions on 13 tax regimes reviewed during the Forum on Harmful Tax Practices (FHTP) meeting held in May 2026.</p>
<p>The <a href="https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/topics/policy-sub-issues/harmful-tax-practices/harmful-tax-practices-peer-review-results-on-preferential-regimes.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">latest peer review results on preferential tax regimes</a> highlight jurisdictions’ continued efforts to address harmful tax practices through the implementation of the BEPS Action 5 minimum standard.</p>
<p>At its 65th meeting held in May 2026, the OECD Forum on Harmful Tax Practices (FHTP) applied for the first time the <a href="https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/topics/policy-issues/beps/note-on-burden-reduction-in-the-beps-minimum-standards.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">revised BEPS Action 5 peer review methodology.</a> Under this approach, regimes are first subject to a BEPS impact assessment to determine whether a full legislative review is needed or whether the BEPS impact is expected to be low.</p>
<p>The FHTP reached new conclusions on 13 regimes. For seven regimes (one from Azerbaijan, four from Fiji, one from Japan, and one from Peru), a conclusion of “not harmful” was reached, and for six regimes (three from Azerbaijan, one from Malaysia, one from Peru, and one from Serbia), it was concluded that the regimes would be kept “under review”.</p>
<p>The total number of regimes reviewed by the FHTP since the start of the BEPS Project is now 347, with over 40% of those regimes being (or in the process of being) abolished.</p>

US Trade Representative (USTR) Jamieson Greer held talks this week with Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard, focusing on vehicles, steel, aluminium, labour standards,...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The US and Mexico will meet for a fourth negotiating round in early September 2026 to work through disagreements on revamping the 26-year-old North American trade agreement (USMCA).</p>
<p>US Trade Representative (USTR) Jamieson Greer held <a href="https://regfollower.com/us-mexico-to-convene-for-third-round-of-usmca-negotiations-tomorrow/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">talks</a> this week with Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard, focusing on vehicles, steel, aluminium, labour standards, and agricultural trade across the bloc&#8217;s USD 1.6 trillion annual commerce.</p>
<p><strong>The auto content standoff</strong></p>
<p>The negotiations hinge on a sharp disagreement over vehicle manufacturing rules. The US is pushing for 50% of content in cars to be US-made to qualify for preferential tariff treatment. Mexico has flatly rejected the demand, with negotiators refusing to accept even a 1% US-specific requirement, arguing it creates a precedent for further demands down the line.</p>
<p>The current pact requires 75% North American content overall, with 40% of that produced by workers earning at least USD 16 per hour—a wage floor met only in the US and Canada.</p>
<p>Notably, the agreement doesn&#8217;t mandate that any fixed share originate from a single country. Japan, South Korea, and the EU face a 15% tariff on US auto exports with zero regional content requirements, giving those competitors a significant cost edge over Mexican factories.</p>
<p><strong>Mexico&#8217;s counterplay and the tariff trap</strong></p>
<p>Mexico wants the Trump administration to first reduce Section 232 national security tariffs: 25% on autos and 50% on steel and aluminium. Trump has shown no appetite for rolling back those levies. The US has asked Mexico to propose alternative ways to meet Trump&#8217;s goal of shifting more auto production northward and cutting the US trade deficit with Mexico.</p>
<p>On 1 July 2026, President Donald Trump <a href="https://regfollower.com/us-walks-away-from-usmca-renewal-eyes-major-trade-overhaul/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">declined </a>to extend the USMCA, triggering a ten-year wind-down clock unless negotiators reach agreement.</p>
<p>Greer told Senate lawmakers he aims to finalise<a href="https://regfollower.com/us-targets-interim-usmca-deals-with-mexico-canada-by-year-end-as-full-overhaul-slips-to-2027/" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> interim trade deals</a> this year while punting harder USMCA changes—auto content, labour, environmental rules—to 2027.</p>
<p><a href="https://regfollower.com/us-mexico-square-off-over-automotive-content-in-usmca-overhaul/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Earlier,</a> the US and Mexico began formal negotiations to revise the USMCA, with the US seeking stricter regional content requirements, including new rules for automotive components. The first two rounds of negotiations were held in Washington and Mexico City.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Belgium&#8217;s Council of Ministers <a href="https://news.belgium.be/fr/instauration-de-lobligation-de-rapportage-electronique-des-donnees-de-facturation" target="_blank" rel="noopener">approved </a>a preliminary draft law amending the Value Added Tax Code on 18 July 2026, requiring companies to report invoice data electronically in near real time to tax authorities starting in 2028.</p>
<p>The measure extends an existing e-invoicing mandate for domestic B2B transactions that took effect on 1 January 2026, moving toward dual reporting requirements that will tighten the government&#8217;s ability to track business transactions.</p>
<p>Since 1 January 2026, a general obligation to issue structured electronic invoices or equivalent documents between taxable persons has been introduced. As a continuation of this obligation, the draft bill provides for a &#8220;near real-time&#8221; electronic reporting system under which certain mandatory invoice data must be reported electronically to the tax authorities by both the supplier or service provider and the customer.</p>
<p>This bilateral electronic reporting system aims to:</p>
<ul>
<li>Improve taxpayer compliance by digitising and automating data flows, resulting in the transmission of more reliable information.</li>
<li>Enhance tax administration and enforcement by enabling faster access to more detailed and reliable data, improving risk analysis, strengthening existing control techniques, facilitating quicker action against specific fraud schemes, and increasing the efficiency and effectiveness of tax audits.</li>
</ul>
<p>The introduction of this electronic reporting obligation also eliminates the requirement to file the annual list of taxable customers under the Value Added Tax Code for taxable persons subject to the new reporting obligation.</p>
<p>The preliminary draft has been submitted to the Data Protection Authority and the Council of State for review.</p>
<p><a href="https://regfollower.com/belgium-issues-clarification-on-2026-b2b-e-invoicing-rules/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Earlier</a>, Belgium published a decree requiring mandatory structured e-invoicing for B2B transactions between VAT-registered taxpayers from 2026, implementing the Act of 6 February 2024.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney told provincial premiers on 23 July 2026 that Canada would retaliate against new US tariffs if negotiations fail. 		<title>Hungary: NAV cuts corporate allowances and tax types to meet RRF commitments, scraps trust and foundation tax exemptions </title>
		<link>https://regfollower.com/hungary-nav-cuts-corporate-allowances-and-tax-types-to-meet-rrf-commitments-scraps-trust-and-foundation-tax-exemptions/?utm_source=rss&#038;utm_medium=rss&#038;utm_campaign=hungary-nav-cuts-corporate-allowances-and-tax-types-to-meet-rrf-commitments-scraps-trust-and-foundation-tax-exemptions</link>

				<category><![CDATA[Computation of taxable income]]></category>

		<category><![CDATA[Investment Tax Credits]]></category>

					<description><![CDATA[Hungary’s government has submitted Draft Law T/387 to the parliament on 17 July 2026 to implement commitments under the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) plan by August 31, 2026, alongside other government programs. This legislative document details a comprehensive tax reform proposal submitted by the Hungarian government in July 2026 to fulfil requirements for European...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Hungary’s government has submitted <a href="https://www.parlament.hu/irom43/00387/00387.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Draft Law T/387</a> to the parliament on 17 July 2026 to implement commitments under the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) plan by August 31, 2026, alongside other government programs.</p>
<p>This legislative document details a comprehensive tax reform proposal submitted by the Hungarian government in July 2026 to fulfil requirements for European Union recovery funding. The core reforms include scrapping tax exemptions for trust management and private foundations, cutting the overall number of tax types, and unifying the conditions applied to retail taxes, all framed as competitiveness measures. The bill also restructures how the National Tax and Customs Administration&#8217;s leadership is appointed and paid, pushes forward business digitalisation, and introduces formal definitions for cryptocurrencies so they fit into the existing fiscal framework rather than sitting outside it.</p>
<p>The key tax reforms are as follows:</p>
<p><strong>Reduction of the number of corporate tax allowances </strong></p>
<p>To increase corporate tax revenues, Hungary committed to reducing the number of preferential tax elements. The phase-out includes:</p>
<ul>
<li>Monument projects: The corporate tax base allowance for monument projects will be phased out from 1 January 2027. The 2026 tax year will be the last time this tax base reduction can be utilised, and any unused credits cannot be carried forward to subsequent years.</li>
<li>Growth tax credit: This credit will also be abolished starting 1 January 2027. For credits generated before 2027, the tax obligations and investment conditions must be fulfilled based on the rules in effect on December 31, 2026, but the credit cannot be used to reduce taxes due on instalments after 2026.</li>
<li>Public interest asset management foundations: The 300% tax base allowance for supporting these foundations, or higher education institutions maintained by them, will be repealed and can be applied for the last time in the 2027 tax year, effective 1 August 12027).</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Reduction of number of tax types </strong></p>
<p>To simplify the tax system and meet RRF commitments, several taxes and contributions are being completely abolished:</p>
<ul>
<li>Immigration tax</li>
<li>Dog contribution</li>
<li>Municipal tax</li>
<li>Carbon quota tax (abolished retroactively from 7 October 2023). Taxpayers can claim a refund of previously paid tax and related interest within 90 days.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Retail tax </strong></p>
<p>To unify competition conditions within the retail tax sector, the draft law repeals Title 5 of the Retail Tax Act. This modification is applicable starting from the 2026 tax year.</p>
<p>Ending the tax exemption for trusts and private foundations</p>
<p>Hungary&#8217;s RRF-linked reform removes the personal income tax exemption that trusts (fiduciary asset management) and private foundations have relied on.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Taxation adjustments:</strong> There&#8217;s no new entry tax on assets transferred into a trust at the outset. Capital gains are where the rules bite: if an asset changes form inside the trust (say, stock sold for cash) and the yield gets distributed, it&#8217;s taxed as a dividend. Distribute the asset in its original form instead, and that transfer is tax-free, but the beneficiary picks up the asset&#8217;s original historical acquisition cost, so any future sale triggers capital gains tax on the full gain since that original acquisition, not just the gain since distribution.</li>
<li><strong>Expanded data reporting and audits:</strong> Reporting duties expand sharply. Trustees and private foundations must report annually by 31 January on the registered value of managed assets, detailed asset value increments, and closing values of separate registers. The first such report, covering the partial 2026 year, is due 31 March 2027. On the enforcement side, the tax authority will run mandatory audits on every trust formed before 12 September 2023, then move to comprehensive audits of all trusts starting in 2028.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Status of the president of the tax authority (NAV) </strong></p>
<p>The draft law actually abolishes the State Secretary status of the NAV President. Instead, the President will become an employee of the NAV, with their unified personal salary set by the minister, while continuing to receive benefits identical to those of a state secretary. The minister will continue to appoint and dismiss the President, while the President will exercise operational employer rights over the vice-presidents to provide greater legal clarity.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Chilean tax authority (SII) has released Letter <a href="https://drive.google.com/file/d/1_rCTzWFPNDbdO67dUdDVvt8DbxysOzYR/view?usp=drive_link" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Ruling No. 1801</a>, dated 20 July 2026, in response to a taxpayer inquiry on whether the DEMPE analysis set out in Chapter VI of the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines is an appropriate method for determining the arm&#8217;s length value of intangibles under Article 64 of the Tax Code.</p>
<p>The taxpayer argued that the comparability factors listed in Article 64 of the Tax Code are illustrative rather than exhaustive, and that they align with the arm&#8217;s length principle established in Article 41 E of the Income Tax Law.</p>
<p>In its ruling, the SII provided several important clarifications regarding the valuation of intangibles under Article 64:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Definition of normal market value: </strong>The second paragraph of Article 64 defines normal market values as the prices that unrelated parties would have agreed upon in comparable operations and circumstances.</li>
<li><strong>Comprehensive comparability factors:</strong> To determine this value, taxpayers and authorities must consider industry characteristics, the specific functions, assets, and risks assumed by the parties, as well as the specific characteristics and components of the goods, services, or contracts in question.</li>
<li><strong>Flexibility in the absence of comparables: </strong>The SII explicitly noted that the law allows for the consideration of any relevant circumstance for a particular case. Importantly, this includes determining values in situations where there is no existing market or direct comparable.</li>
<li><strong>Conditional approval of DEMPE: </strong>The SII concluded that, in principle, the DEMPE analysis can indeed be used to evaluate intangibles. However, it established a clear caveat: the actual suitability of the DEMPE framework for any specific case must be verified during tax audits, and its acceptance will depend heavily on the concrete circumstances of the transaction being analysed.</li>
</ul>
<p>Furthermore, the ruling outlines procedural expectations for both the tax authority and the taxpayer. If the tax authority exercises its appraisal powers to determine a value, the administrative act must clearly indicate the parameters used and adequately justify the valuation.</p>
<p>Conversely, under Article 21 of the Tax Code, taxpayers maintain the right to prove their market values using all legally established evidentiary methods.</p>

		<category><![CDATA[US]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://regfollower.com/?p=85347</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[The United States Trade Representative (USTR) has announced on 23 July 2026 the final tariff measures following its Section 301 investigations into 60 countries and economies launched in March 2026 to determine whether foreign governments had taken adequate steps to prevent the importation of goods produced with forced labour. The action comes after the Office...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The United States Trade Representative (USTR) has <a href="https://ustr.gov/about/policy-offices/press-office/press-releases/2026/july/ustr-takes-action-forced-labor-section-301-investigations" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced</a> on 23 July 2026 the final tariff measures following its Section 301 investigations into 60 countries and economies launched in March 2026 to determine whether foreign governments had taken adequate steps to prevent the importation of goods produced with forced labour.</p>
<p>The action comes after the Office of the United States Trade Representative’s (USTR) investigations, which included two rounds of public hearings, more than 2,100 public comments, and engagement with our trading partners to remedy these longstanding concerns.</p>
<p>“President Trump recognises that decades of moral suasion have not eradicated forced labour from global supply chains.  The United States has had a forced labour import ban for nearly a century, and rigorously enforces it; it’s well past time for our trading partners to do the same,” said Ambassador Greer.  “Today’s action will begin to correct what is both a human rights abuse and a distortive trade practice to improve the welfare of workers everywhere.  I am encouraged by the trading partners who have moved quickly to adopt forced labour import prohibitions, and look forward to ensuring their effective enforcement.”</p>
<p>To view the pre-publication version of the Federal Register Notice, click <a href="https://ustr.gov/sites/default/files/files/Press/Releases/2026/FLIP%20301%20Investigation%20Final%20Action%20FRN%207-23-26%20FINAL.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">here</a>.</p>
<p>To read USTR’s Fact Sheet, click <a href="https://ustr.gov/about/policy-offices/press-office/fact-sheets/2026/july/fact-sheet-ustr-section-301-action-response-failure-60-economies-ban-imports-produced-forced-labor" target="_blank" rel="noopener">here</a>.</p>
<p><strong>Background</strong></p>
<p>Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (Trade Act), is designed to address unfair foreign practices affecting US commerce.  Section 301 may be used to respond to unjustifiable, unreasonable, or discriminatory foreign government acts, policies, or practices that burden or restrict US commerce.  A Section 301(b) investigation examines whether the acts, policies, or practices are unreasonable or discriminatory and burden or restrict US commerce.</p>
<p>At the specific direction of the President, on 12 March 2026, the US Trade Representative initiated 60 investigations related to the failure of various economies to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labour.</p>
<p>On 28 April and 29 April 2026, USTR and the Section 301 Committee convened public hearings regarding these investigations.  Pursuant to Section 303(a) of the Trade Act, USTR also held consultations with more than 45 of the governments of the economies subject to the investigations.</p>
<p>On 2 June 2026, the US Trade Representative determined under Section 301 of the Trade Act that the acts, policies, and practices of the 60 investigated economies related to the failure to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor is unreasonable and burdens or restricts US commerce, and are thus actionable under Section 301(b) of the Trade Act.  As a result of this determination, the US Trade Representative proposed responsive action and invited the public to provide written comments on the proposed action by 6 July 2026.  USTR received, reviewed, and analysed over 1,600 written comments on the proposed responsive action.</p>
<p>From 7 July to 9 July, USTR also held public hearings regarding proposed responsive action in the investigations, at which over 100 witnesses provided testimony and responded to questions.</p>
<p>Consistent with the specific direction of the President, the US Trade Representative has made the following determinations:</p>
<ul>
<li>10% is the appropriate rate of Section 301 duties for investigated economies that (i) impose a forced labour import prohibition; (ii) have committed to impose and enforce such a prohibition through an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade; or (iii) have imposed a partial regime with the effect of preventing the importation of certain forced labour goods.  These economies are: Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Canada, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Indonesia, Jordan, Malaysia, Mexico, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Trinidad and Tobago, and the United Kingdom;</li>
<li>10%  or 12.5%, net of Most-Favored-Nation (MFN) rate, is the appropriate rate of Section 301 duties for certain products of the European Union, Taiwan, Japan, Korea, and Switzerland that are not otherwise exempted, as explained in greater detail in the Federal Register Notice; and</li>
<li>12.5%  is the appropriate rate of Section 301 duty for all other investigated economies.</li>
</ul>
<p>The US Trade Representative has also determined, in accordance with the specific direction of the President, that product exemptions are appropriate for: (a) raw materials that if subject to these tariffs could lead to the unavailability of domestic supply; (b) products that could cause economy-wide disruptions if subject to these tariffs; (c) products that cannot be grown or produced in sufficient quantities or at reasonable prices in the United States or obtained from other sources; (d) certain products of Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Ecuador, El Salvador, the European Union, Guatemala, Indonesia, Jordan, Malaysia, Switzerland, Taiwan, or the United Kingdom that would encourage these economies to fulfill commitments regarding forced labor import prohibitions or to enact and effectively enforce a forced labor import prohibition; or (e) articles for which these tariffs may not contribute substantially to the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices of found to be actionable in the investigations.</p>

<p>The additional 20% reduction from 2027/28 will be applied on top of that support.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Luxembourg&#8217;s Government Council has <a href="https://gouvernement.lu/fr/actualites/toutes_actualites/communiques/2026/07-juillet/17-conseil-gouvernement1.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">approved</a> a draft law to extend mandatory electronic invoicing to domestic business-to-business (B2B) transactions between businesses established in the country. The proposal, approved on 17 July 2026, remains subject to parliamentary approval before it can enter into force.</p>
<p>The draft law would expand the existing electronic invoicing requirement, which currently applies to public procurement and concession contracts, by introducing the obligation for domestic B2B transactions. The measure is intended to align Luxembourg&#8217;s legislation with Article 1 of Council Directive (EU) 2025/516 of 11 March 2025, which amends Directive 2006/112/EC on VAT rules adapted to the digital age. It also forms part of the country&#8217;s broader digitalisation strategy for administrative and financial processes.</p>
<p>Implementation timetable</p>
<p>The draft legislation sets out a three-stage implementation schedule:</p>
<ul>
<li>1 January 2028: Mandatory receipt of electronic invoices for all businesses.</li>
<li> 1 July 2028: Mandatory issuance of electronic invoices for large and medium-sized businesses.</li>
<li>1 January 2029: Mandatory issuance extended to all remaining businesses, including smaller enterprises.</li>
</ul>
<p>The timetable will be confirmed during the parliamentary process.</p>
<p>Technical framework</p>
<p>Alongside the draft law, the Government Council endorsed a draft regulation establishing the technical framework for a common delivery network and alternative transmission methods for electronic invoices.</p>
<p>The proposed framework adopts a four-corner model based on the Peppol network, building on Luxembourg&#8217;s existing public sector infrastructure. It is designed to provide a common delivery network for the issuance, transmission and receipt of electronic invoices, avoiding the need for businesses to deploy separate, non-interoperable technical solutions.</p>
<p>Business support measures</p>
<p>To assist businesses with the transition, the Chamber of Commerce plans to organise information sessions and practical workshops, while also updating its practical guide to electronic invoicing.</p>
<p>Financial assistance will also be made available to help businesses acquire software that complies with the new electronic invoicing requirements.</p>
<p>Next steps</p>
<p>The draft law will now proceed through Luxembourg&#8217;s parliamentary process, where lawmakers will finalise the implementation dates, scope and technical standards before the legislation is adopted and enters into force.</p>

<p>The ATO has set the Division 7A benchmark interest rate at 8.77% for the income year ending 30 June 2027, based on the Reserve Bank of Australia&#8217;s variable housing loan rate published on 6 June 2026. This is an increase from 8.37% for the previous income year ending 30 June 2026.</p>
<p>Under Division 7A of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936, the benchmark interest rate for an income year is based on the Reserve Bank of Australia&#8217;s standard variable home loan rate for owner-occupiers, as published before the start of that income year. Once set, the benchmark rate remains unchanged for the year, even if the Reserve Bank later revises the published rate.</p>
<p>The update also includes benchmark interest rates for prior income years back to 2021, guidance for substituted accounting periods, and access to a Division 7A calculator and decision tool.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[Thailand&#8217;s Cabinet approved in principle a draft Royal Decree under the Revenue Code at its meeting on 21 July 2026, revising tax measures supporting Social Enterprises through amendments to Royal Decree (No. 735) B.E. 2564 (2021). According to Press Release No. PR 17/2026, issued on 21 July 2026, the proposed amendments are designed to strengthen...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Thailand&#8217;s Cabinet approved in principle a draft Royal Decree under the Revenue Code at its meeting on 21 July 2026, revising tax measures supporting Social Enterprises through amendments to Royal Decree (No. 735) B.E. 2564 (2021).</p>
<p>According to <a href="https://rd.go.th/fileadmin/user_upload/news/2569thai/news17_2569.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Press Release No. PR 17/2026</a>, issued on 21 July 2026, the proposed amendments are designed to strengthen tax support for Social Enterprises and broaden access to existing incentives.</p>
<p>The Revenue Department said the measures reflect the government&#8217;s commitment to supporting organisations that address social challenges while contributing to Thailand&#8217;s progress towards the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).</p>
<p><strong>Permanent tax deduction for corporate supporters</strong></p>
<p>Under the draft Royal Decree, corporate entities that provide money or property to support Social Enterprises will continue to be entitled to a 100% tax deduction (equal to the amount contributed).</p>
<p>The proposal removes the previous 31 December 2023 expiry date, making the incentive available on an ongoing basis rather than for a limited period.</p>
<p><strong>New tax benefit for individual donors</strong></p>
<p>The draft also introduces a new incentive for individual taxpayers.</p>
<p>Individuals who make monetary contributions to support Social Enterprises will be eligible to claim a 100% tax deduction, with no expiry date attached to the relief.</p>
<p>This represents a significant expansion of the existing framework by extending tax support beyond corporate contributors.</p>
<p>Enhanced deduction for donations to the Social Enterprise Promotion Fund</p>
<p>The Cabinet also approved an enhanced incentive for donations to the Social Enterprise Promotion Fund.</p>
<p>Under the proposal, deductions for donations of money or property to the Fund will increase from 100% to 200% for donations made between 1 January 2024 and 31 December 2028.</p>
<p>To qualify for the tax benefits available to corporate supporters, individual supporters and donors to the Fund, all contributions must be made through the Revenue Department&#8217;s electronic donation (e-Donation) system.</p>
<p><strong>Property transfer tax exemptions extended indefinitely</strong></p>
<p>The draft Royal Decree also removes the expiry date for tax exemptions relating to qualifying property transfers.</p>
<p>The exemptions from:</p>
<ul>
<li>Personal income tax;</li>
<li>Corporate income tax;</li>
<li>Value added tax (VAT);</li>
<li>Specific business tax; and</li>
<li>Stamp duty</li>
</ul>
<p>will continue indefinitely for individuals, companies and juristic partnerships transferring property to Social Enterprises or donating property to the Social Enterprise Promotion Fund through the e-Donation system.</p>
<p>Previously, these exemptions were scheduled to expire on 31 December 2023.</p>
<p><strong>More flexible notification requirements</strong></p>
<p>The proposal also eases administrative requirements for Social Enterprises seeking tax incentives.</p>
<p>Under the revised rules, Social Enterprises will be permitted to notify the Director-General of the Revenue Department of their intention to claim tax incentives after the statutory filing deadline.</p>
<p>However, both the Social Enterprise and its supporters will become eligible for the tax benefits only from the accounting period or tax year following the period in which the notification is submitted.</p>
<p><strong>Investment incentive rules to be relaxed</strong></p>
<p>Revenue Department Director-General Somsak Anantawat said that, once the Royal Decree comes into force, the Department will amend Director-General&#8217;s Notification No. 38 to relax the conditions for investment-related tax deductions.</p>
<p>Currently, investors claiming deductions for investments in shares or partnership interests used to establish or increase the capital of a Social Enterprise must hold those investments indefinitely.</p>
<p>Under the revised rules, investors will instead be required to retain their shares or partnership interests for at least 10 years from the date of investment.</p>
<p>The amendment will also apply retrospectively to qualifying investments made before the new Royal Decree takes effect.</p>
<p><strong>Supporting long-term social development</strong></p>
<p>Commenting on the proposal, Director-General Somsak Anantawat said the Revenue Department recognises the important role Social Enterprises play in addressing social challenges and advancing Thailand&#8217;s sustainable development objectives.</p>
<p>He said the revised measures are intended to ensure that government support for Social Enterprises is broader, more comprehensive and available on a long-term basis by expanding eligibility, enhancing incentives and removing time limits on key tax benefits.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>US President Donald Trump has signed a new proclamation on 20 July 2026, adjusting tariffs on aluminium imports to address the gap between US demand and domestic production capacity.</p>
<p>The administration cited aluminium as critical to the economy and defence industrial base, noting that current US smelting facilities cannot meet demand.</p>
<p>This <a href="https://regfollower.com/us-trump-administration-adjusts-steel-aluminium-tariffs-in-new-proclamation/">follows</a> after Trump signed a proclamation revising his Section 232 national security tariffs on steel, aluminium, and copper imports on 1 June 2026.</p>
<p>Under the new policy, the Commerce Secretary will launch an incentive program offering companies reduced tariff rates for primary aluminium imports—set at half the standard Section 232 rate—in exchange for approved plans to build, expand, or refurbish aluminium smelters in the US. The tariff reduction is tied to the company&#8217;s onshoring capacity: the more aluminium a company commits to producing domestically, the higher its import allowance at the reduced rate.</p>
<p>The proclamation invokes Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, which authorises presidential tariff adjustments on imports deemed to threaten national security. Trump&#8217;s move aims to shift aluminium supply chains onshore while using tariff incentives rather than blanket restrictions to drive investment.</p>
<p>Below is the<a href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-sheets/2026/07/fact-sheet-president-donald-j-trump-takes-further-action-to-adjust-imports-of-aluminum-into-the-united-states/" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> fact sheet</a> of the signed proclamation:</p>
<p><strong>Fact Sheet: President Donald J. Trump Takes Further Action To Adjust Imports Of Aluminum Into The United States</strong></p>
<p><strong>BOLSTERING DOMESTIC MANUFACTURING OF PRIMARY ALUMINUM:</strong> Today, President Donald J. Trump signed a Proclamation using his authority under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 to address the national security threat posed by imports of aluminium into the United States and drive new investment into the US aluminium industry.</p>
<ul>
<li>The Proclamation authorises and directs the Secretary of Commerce to establish an incentive program for companies that will invest in building, expanding, or refurbishing aluminium smelters in the United States.
<ul>
<li>The program will request onshoring plans from companies that, if approved, will be eligible to import a commensurate level of primary aluminium into the United States at a reduced tariff rate equal to half of the otherwise applicable Section 232 rate.</li>
<li>The Secretary will monitor and enforce all approved onshoring plans and, if a company fails to meet its agreed-upon commitments, may stop and rescind the tariff benefits, including retroactively.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>STRENGTHENING ECONOMIC AND NATIONAL SECURITY:</strong>  President Trump has utilised tariffs on imported aluminium to protect the national security of the United States and its defence and defence-adjacent industrial base.</p>
<ul>
<li>Aluminium is a key input for the production of US military systems, including armoured vehicles, naval vessels, spacecraft, and missiles, as well as other key strategic products.</li>
<li>These products and their components are manufactured using high-strength advanced aluminium alloys, which can only be produced using primary aluminium.</li>
<li>US demand for primary aluminium currently outpaces the primary aluminium production capacity of US smelting facilities; therefore, this proclamation encourages increased reshoring of primary aluminium production.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>BUILDING ON A RECORD OF SECURING CRITICAL INDUSTRIES:</strong> President Trump has long recognised that America’s national security and economic strength depend on rebuilding key sectors of our industrial base.</p>
<ul>
<li>In his first term, President Trump revolutionised international trade by using Section 232 to address decades of short-sighted, globalist trade policies that had allowed our domestic steel and aluminium industries to weaken, impairing our national security.</li>
<li>Since returning to office, President Trump has continued taking actions under Section 232 to protect and strengthen domestic manufacturing critical to our national and economic security, including imposing and strengthening tariffs on key goods such as steel, aluminium, copper, trucks, automobiles, timber, lumber, and pharmaceuticals.</li>
<li>Through negotiations with foreign trading partners and the strategic use of tariffs, President Trump has secured trillions in private and foreign investment to bring American jobs and manufacturing back to the United States while diversifying global supply chains and reducing dependence on adversarial nations.</li>
</ul>

					<description><![CDATA[Italian investors holding shares in collective investment funds can now participate in cross-border UCITS (undertakings for collective investment in transferable securities) mergers tax-free. The Italian Revenue Agency confirmed this position on 20 July 2026 in Response no. 149, ruling on a transaction where Irish funds were being absorbed into Luxembourg sub-funds under the same management...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Italian investors holding shares in collective investment funds can now participate in cross-border UCITS (undertakings for collective investment in transferable securities) mergers tax-free. The Italian Revenue Agency <a href="https://www.fiscooggi.it/portale/-/fusione-di-fondi-transfrontalieri-fisco-neutrale-per-gli-investitori" target="_blank" rel="noopener">confirmed</a> this position on 20 July 2026 in <a href="https://www.agenziaentrate.gov.it/portale/documents/20143/10196933/Risposta+n.+149_2026.pdf/41f6222e-e897-1924-b50b-4fddabb0d745?t=1784533638761" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Response no. 149</a>, ruling on a transaction where Irish funds were being absorbed into Luxembourg sub-funds under the same management company.</p>
<p>The answer was no. Under Directive 2009/65/EC and Article 10-ter of Law No. 77/1983, which governs taxation of foreign investment schemes, the share allocation doesn&#8217;t trigger capital gains or the standard 26% withholding tax.</p>
<p><strong>How the merger works and why it&#8217;s tax-neutral</strong></p>
<p>The absorbed Irish funds are dissolved without liquidation, with all assets and liabilities flowing into the absorbing Luxembourg funds. Investors receive shares in the new funds at a fixed 1:1 exchange rate, maintaining their economic position unchanged.</p>
<p>The key question for the Revenue Agency was whether this share allocation constitutes a taxable event under Article 10-ter of Law No. 77/1983, which governs taxation of income from foreign harmonised collective investment schemes.</p>
<p>Italian tax law specifies the circumstances that trigger taxation: distributions of income during ownership, redemptions, sales of units, liquidations, and conversions between fund compartments (treated as a redemption followed by a new subscription). Fund mergers are not among these taxable events.</p>
<p>The reason is fundamental: a merger involves no divestment by the investor. The shareholder does not sell shares, receives no cash, and earns no income. The existing shares are simply replaced with shares of equal value in the absorbing fund.</p>
<p>EU legislation defines a merger as dissolution &#8220;without liquidation&#8221;—a transition that preserves the continuity of the investment relationship rather than ending it. A merger therefore cannot be treated as a transfer or liquidation of shares.</p>
<p>The Revenue Agency&#8217;s position aligns with its previous guidance in responses nos. 206/2024, 56/2026, and 69/2026, which confirmed tax neutrality for similar mergers between collective investment undertakings. This principle now extends explicitly to cross-border UCITS mergers between different Member States.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Irish Department of Finance and Revenue published the <a href="https://www.revenue.ie/en/corporate/press-office/press-releases/2026/pr-072226-ewht-report.aspx" target="_blank" rel="noopener">report </a>on the public consultation on the proposed electronic withholding tax (eWHT) model on 22 July 2026.</p>
<p>The consultation, which ran from 5 December 2025 , invited views from businesses, taxpayers, representative bodies, software providers, tax professionals and other stakeholders on proposals to modernise the operation of withholding taxes through greater digital integration, automation and real-time reporting.</p>
<p>A total of 233 responses were received from a broad range of respondent groups. In addition to representative organisations, the consultation attracted participation from businesses and individual taxpayers with direct experience of the current Relevant Contracts Tax (RCT) and Professional Services Withholding Tax (PSWT) regimes.</p>
<p>Respondents identified recurring themes including opportunities associated with automation and systems integration, as well as issues relating to administrative burden, cashflow impacts, implementation, withholding rates and compliance processes.</p>
<p>The report presents the views expressed by respondents and does not make policy recommendations. The findings will inform the ongoing consideration of the proposed eWHT model.</p>
<p>The consultation closed on 30 January 2026, and the Department of Finance and Revenue said the feedback received will inform the ongoing consideration of the proposed eWHT model.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Taiwan’s Northern Region National Taxation Bureau of the Ministry of Finance <a href="https://www.mof.gov.tw/singlehtml/384fb3077bb349ea973e7fc6f13b6974?cntId=7e55da4a926d4dccaa2c7de816b5d96e" target="_blank" rel="noopener">stated</a>, on 23 July 2026, that, with the rapid growth of social media platforms and online self-media, it has become increasingly common for influencers to receive revenue-sharing income from platforms.</p>
<p>On 10 September 2025, the Ministry of Finance issued the &#8220;Operational Guidelines for the Imposition of Business Tax on Individuals Who Regularly Publish Creative Works or Share Information Online&#8221;, clarifying that influencers who have a fixed physical place of business in Taiwan, operate under a business name, employ staff to assist with sales, or conduct sales through the internet must register for tax purposes and pay Business Tax if their monthly sales reach the Business Tax registration threshold.</p>
<p>The current thresholds are TWD 100,000 for the sale of goods and TWD 50,000 for the provision of services.</p>
<p>The Bureau explained that, under Article 28 of the Value-added and Non-value-added Business Tax Act, influencers with a fixed place of business in Taiwan must apply for tax registration before commencing business.</p>
<p>For those who sell goods or services exclusively through the internet, the Ministry of Finance Order Tai-Cai-Shui No. 10904512340, dated 31 January 2020, provides that they are temporarily exempt from applying for tax registration with the local tax authority if their monthly sales do not reach the Business Tax registration threshold. However, once monthly sales reach the threshold, they must immediately apply for tax registration with the competent tax authority.</p>
<p>The Bureau urged influencers and self-media creators to regularly review the nature of their income and the scale of their business activities. If they fail to register for tax purposes or underreport sales due to oversight, they may avoid penalties under Article 48-1 of the Tax Collection Act, provided they voluntarily complete tax registration with the competent National Taxation Bureau and file and pay the outstanding tax together with accrued interest before the case is reported by another person or before an investigation is initiated by the tax authority or investigators designated by the Ministry of Finance.</p>

The changes flow from the government&#8217;s broader deregulation agenda and take effect in stages through 2027. Penalties scrapped...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Polish Council of Ministers <a href="https://www.gov.pl/web/finanse/rzad-przyjal-rozwiazania-ulatwiajace-realizacje-obowiazkow-podatkowych" target="_blank" rel="noopener">approved</a> amendments to the Personal Income Tax Act and Corporate Income Tax Act on 21 July 2026, designed to cut red tape around transfer pricing disclosures and reduce penalties for misfiled payments.</p>
<p>The changes flow from the government&#8217;s broader deregulation agenda and take effect in stages through 2027.</p>
<p><strong>Penalties scrapped for off-list payments</strong></p>
<p>Companies will no longer face sanctions or lose expense deductions if they pay contractors outside the VAT whitelist or circumvent the split payment mechanism. Previously, using an account not on the tax authority&#8217;s registered VAT payer list could trigger costly penalties, even when the underlying transaction was legitimate.</p>
<p><strong>Transfer pricing forms get simpler</strong></p>
<p>The TPR form—which reports settlements between related entities—no longer requires a board member or certified professional to sign it. Any authorised company representative can now sign under the same rules as standard tax returns, cutting friction in the approval process.</p>
<p>Micro and small entrepreneurs will no longer be required to provide indicators describing the company&#8217;s financial situation in their TPR reports. This will make document preparation simpler and less time-consuming.</p>
<p><strong>Timeline</strong></p>
<p>The amendments take effect 14 days after publication in the Journal of Laws.</p>
<p>Transfer pricing simplifications apply to reports filed for the 2026 tax year.</p>
<p>The penalty changes take effect on 1 January 2027.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Poland&#8217;s Council of Ministers <a href="https://www.gov.pl/web/finanse/rzad-przyjal-projekt-porzadkujacy-zasady-opodatkowania-papierosow-elektronicznych-i-urzadzen-do-waporyzacji" target="_blank" rel="noopener">approved</a> an amendment to the Excise Duty Act on 21 July 2026, closing loopholes in how the government taxes e-cigarettes and vaping equipment.</p>
<p>The new rules treat all vaping devices the same way regardless of their design, and they substantially raise excise rates across the board.</p>
<p><strong>What&#8217;s changing</strong></p>
<p>The excise tax on e-cigarettes, heaters, and multifunction devices climbs from PLN 40 to PLN 50 per unit. That same PLN 50 rate now applies to component kits sold separately—a deliberate move to prevent manufacturers from sidestepping taxes by selling e-cigarettes in pieces.</p>
<p>Disposable devices face matching taxation with reusable ones under the revised rules.</p>
<p>E-cigarette liquid gets the steepest increase: the rate rises from PLN 1.80 to PLN 2.20 per millilitre.</p>
<p>Liquid sold in disposable devices also moves to PLN 50 per unit (up from PLN 40), aligning its treatment with standalone reusable devices.</p>
<p><strong>Timeline and scope</strong></p>
<p>Most of the new rates take effect 14 days after publication in the Journal of Laws and initially run for three months—a trial period.</p>
<p>The only exception is the liquid tax increase, which doesn&#8217;t begin until 1 January 2027, giving manufacturers and retailers a longer runway to adjust pricing.</p>
<p>The revised definition of e-cigarettes is deliberately broad, covering any device used to vaporise liquids no matter how it&#8217;s built or what technology powers it. That breadth stops manufacturers from inventing new hardware designs to circumvent the law.</p>

Importers skip the VAT certificate step Companies no longer need to submit proof of active VAT...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Poland’s Council of Ministers <a href="https://www.gov.pl/web/finanse/rada-ministrow-zaakceptowala-projekt-upraszczajacy-przepisy-dotyczace-podatku-vat" target="_blank" rel="noopener">approved</a> draft amendments to the Goods and Services Tax Act on 21 July 2026. The changes target three pain points: redundant paperwork for importers, manual customs processes, and disagreements with tax authorities over export documentation.</p>
<p><strong>Importers skip the VAT certificate step</strong></p>
<p>Companies no longer need to submit proof of active VAT payer status to customs when claiming simplified import settlement. The tax office will verify registration directly without requiring additional paperwork. For shipments under EUR 150, businesses can now use simplified VAT rules despite recent shifts in EU customs regulations, making small cross-border purchases administratively lighter.</p>
<p><strong>Electronic-only declarations and flexible export proof</strong></p>
<p>All customs clearance declarations must now be filed electronically rather than on paper, cutting processing time and reducing back-and-forth with administrators.</p>
<p>On the export side, companies gain flexibility. Businesses will be allowed to rely on a wider range of documents to prove that goods have been exported outside the EU. Rather than requiring a single prescribed document, alternative evidence that reliably demonstrates the export may be used to support the application of the 0% VAT rate, helping reduce disputes with tax authorities.</p>
<p><strong>EU alignment for B2B shipments</strong></p>
<p>Poland is aligning with a European Court of Justice ruling to expand VAT exemptions on imports. The new rules let businesses send goods to individuals in other EU member states and claim the same exemptions they&#8217;d get for domestic B2B transfers, rather than being confined to Poland-only transactions.</p>
<p>The regulations will take effect 14 days after they are published in the Journal of Laws.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Greece’s The Independent Authority for Public Revenue (AADE) has simplified the application process for the alternative taxation regime for foreign-source income for new tax residents investing in Greece under Article 5A of the Income Tax Code (ITC).</p>
<p>The changes were introduced through <a href="https://www.aade.gr/deltia-typoy-anakoinoseis/deltio-typoy-20072026-0" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Decision A.1147/2026</a>, issued by AADE Governor George Pitsilis on 20 July 2026.</p>
<p>Under the revised procedure, taxpayers may submit applications and supporting documents digitally through the myAADE portal, by registered mail or courier, or in person by appointment via the My Appointments application on the myAADE digital portal.</p>
<p>Supporting documents completing an application file may be submitted no later than 31 October of the tax year for which registration is requested.</p>
<p>The decision also clarifies application deadlines.</p>
<p>Individuals arriving in Greece may apply by 30 September of the year of arrival to be covered by Article 5A from that year, or by 30 September of the following tax year to be covered from the year after arrival.</p>
<p>Those transferring their tax residence to Greece on or before 2 July may choose either option, while individuals relocating after 2 July must apply for the year following their arrival.</p>
<p>Applicants may also request that the regime be extended to related persons, including a spouse, parents or children, either with the initial application or at a later stage.</p>
<p>Under the regime, an administrative tax assessment for the fixed tax amount is issued by the last working day of November. The annual fixed tax is EUR 100,000, with an additional EUR 20,000 for each related person. The tax must be paid by the last working day of December, after which it fully satisfies all tax obligations relating to foreign-source income.</p>
<p>The new provisions apply to new applications, applications currently pending review, and administrative tax assessment decisions for the 2026 tax year where the fixed tax amount had not been paid when Decision A.1147/2026 entered into force.</p>
<p>To qualify under Article 5A of the Income Tax Code (ITC), an individual must not have been a tax resident of Greece for seven of the eight years preceding the transfer of tax residence, must make an investment of at least EUR 500,000 in eligible assets in Greece, and complete the investment within three years from submitting the application. Proof that the minimum investment amount has been transferred must accompany every application.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) <a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/business-bulletins-newsroom/early-stage-innovation-company-reports-due-31-july" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced</a>, on 22 July 2026, that the annual information reporting deadline for early stage innovation companies is nearly here.</p>
<p>Companies that issued new shares during 2025–26 must lodge their information report by 31 July 2026.</p>
<p>Companies are required to complete an early stage innovation company report if new shares are issued to one or more investors during a financial year that could lead to an investor being entitled to access the early stage investor tax incentives. <p>For each investment received during the year that may give rise to an investor accessing the tax incentives, companies should keep the following information to report to the ATO:</p>
<ul>
<li>ABN, name and address for the investor (plus the date of birth for investors that are individuals)</li>
<li>number of new shares issued to the investor</li>
<li>amount paid for the new shares</li>
<li>date the shares were issued</li>
<li>percentage of shares in the company held by the investor immediately after the shares were issued</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>How to report</strong></p>
<p>Companies need to report this information electronically. 										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Brazil’s tax authority, the Federal Revenue Service (RFB) <a href="https://www.gov.br/receitafederal/pt-br/assuntos/noticias/emissao-do-cnpj-e-de-documentos-fiscais-por-pessoas-fisicas-contribuintes-da-cbs-comecara-em-1o-de-janeiro-de-2027" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced</a>, on 22 July 2026, the publication of <a href="https://www.in.gov.br/web/dou/-/decreto-n-13.075-de-21-de-julho-de-2026-720537748" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Decree No. 13,075, of 21 July 2026</a>, formalising the change in the implementation schedule for registration and documentary obligations applicable to individuals under the Contribution on Goods and Services (CBS).</p>

<ul>
<li>the individual acting as a taxpayer or tax-responsible party; and</li>
<li>the individual rural producer referred to in article 239 of the CBS regulations.</li>
</ul>
<p>The change gives taxpayers, tax authorities, and system developers more time to adapt to the new requirements arising from the Consumption Tax Reform.</p>
<p>The Federal Revenue Service and the IBS Management Committee have confirmed that the existing tax identification mechanisms for individuals covered by the CBS regulations will remain valid until 31 December 2026, in line with the joint statement issued in June 2026.</p>
<p>The extension also gives the government more time to finish a simplified CNPJ registration process for individuals, modelled on the one already used for the Individual Microentrepreneur (MEI). It also allows for the gradual rollout of operational guidelines, testing environments, and technical manuals to help taxpayers and document issuers adapt.</p>
<p>Decree No. 13,075 entered into force on the date of its publication, 21 July 2026.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[The Parliament of Tanzania has enacted the Finance Act 2026, introducing a broad package of tax and revenue measures affecting excise duty, export taxes, Value Added Tax (VAT), tax administration and public finance. The Act received presidential assent from President Samia Suluhu Hassan on 30 June 2026. The legislation amends several laws governing the collection...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Parliament of Tanzania has enacted the<a href="https://www.tra.go.tz/images/uploads/acts/THE_FINANCE_ACT%2C_2026.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> Finance Act 2026</a>, introducing a broad package of tax and revenue measures affecting excise duty, export taxes, Value Added Tax (VAT), tax administration and public finance.</p>
<p>The Act received presidential assent from President Samia Suluhu Hassan on 30 June 2026.</p>
<p>The legislation amends several laws governing the collection and management of public revenues while introducing new compliance obligations, revising tax rates and establishing new funding arrangements for infrastructure and sector-specific programmes.</p>
<p><span style="text-decoration: underline"><strong>Export tax Act:</strong></span></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Annual rate adjustments: </strong>Specific excise duty rates are now adjusted annually based on the year-on-year actual inflation rate for the period ending March, plus 2%.</li>
<li><strong>Electronic services: </strong>Excise duty is levied on services provided or delivered by non-residents through the internet or other electronic forms to residents.</li>
<li><strong>Imported vehicles:</strong> New excise rates are established for imported vehicles based on their age: 18% for vehicles eight to 10 years old, 35% for vehicles over 10 to 20 years old, and 40% for those exceeding 20 years.</li>
<li><strong>Specific goods update: </strong>Specific excise rates were updated for a wide range of goods, including margarine, sugar confectionery, chocolate, biscuits, bottled water, beer, wine, spirits, tobacco products, and cement.</li>
<li><strong>New export taxes: </strong>New export tax items were added to the schedule, including waste and scrap paper (30% of FOB or TZS 200/kg), various types of bran (TZS 50/kg), and quartz sands or feldspar (10% of FOB or TZS 200/kg).</li>
</ul>
<p><span style="text-decoration: underline"><strong>Sector-Specific Revenue Management</strong></span></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Mining:</strong> The Act establishes the Mineral Survey Fund to finance geoscientific surveys, funded by 10% of revenues collected from royalties and fees. It also provides for excise duty remissions and VAT exemptions for mining projects with government ownership interest during their construction phase.</li>
<li><strong>Gaming:</strong> Revenue distribution from land-based casinos (7%) and sports betting (13%) is split: 70% to the AIDS Trust Fund and 30% to the Universal Health Insurance Fund.</li>
<li><strong>Forestry: </strong>Resident individuals receiving payments for the sale of forest produce (timber, logs, resin, etc.) must now pay a single instalment income tax of 2% of the gross payment.</li>
</ul>
<p><span style="text-decoration: underline"><strong>Infrastructure and development funding</strong></span></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Railways: </strong>The railway development levy is distributed as follows: 70% to the Railway Fund, 25% to the Consolidated Fund, and 5% for supportive infrastructure for industrial parks and special economic zones.</li>
<li><strong>Roads and fuel tolls:</strong> Fuel tolls on petrol and diesel (TZS 363 per litre) are distributed among TARURA (TZS 100), the Road Fund Board, the Consolidated Fund, and infrastructure for special economic zones. Additional fuel tolls support the National Water Fund, AIDS Trust Fund, and Universal Health Insurance Fund.</li>
<li><strong>National planning: </strong>The Act mandates that no national development project shall be included in the government budget unless it has undergone professional technical, financial, and economic evaluations.</li>
</ul>
<p><span style="text-decoration: underline"><strong>Local government and land administration</strong></span></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Land rent: </strong>All land rent collected is deposited into the Consolidated Fund, with 10% disbursed back to the Ministry for land surveys and 10% to the local government authority for collection and recovery efforts.</li>
<li><strong>Rating authorities:</strong> Every Council is designated as the rating authority for its area of jurisdiction. Property rates can now be paid at the time of payment for electricity or through other prescribed means.</li>
<li><strong>Revenue allocation:</strong> Local government authorities are required to set aside 15% of their own source revenue: 10% for funding registered groups of women, youth, and persons with disabilities, and 5% for the construction and renovation of markets and business centres.</li>
</ul>
<p><span style="text-decoration: underline"><strong>Tax Administration and compliance</strong></span></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Electronic payments: </strong>The Minister for Finance may mandate certain payments be made through electronic means; proof of such payment is a mandatory requirement for the transfer of assets like land, buildings, and motor vehicles.</li>
<li><strong>TIN registration: </strong>Individuals must apply for a Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN) within fifteen days of commencing business, employment, or investment activities.</li>
<li><strong>Disclosure requirements:</strong> Entities in the construction and extractive industries must disclose details of all contracted and sub-contracted persons to the Commissioner General electronically within 30 days of executing a contract.</li>
<li><strong>Offenses and penalties:</strong> A new offense is established for the abuse of tax exemptions or remissions granted under framework agreements, with a fine equal to 100%of the tax shortfall.</li>
</ul>
<p><span style="text-decoration: underline"><strong>Value Added Tax (VAT) adjustments</strong></span></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Withholding VAT:</strong> For supplies with both goods and services, the taxable value subject to withholding is apportioned at a ratio of 3:2 respectively.</li>
<li>Digital intermediaries: Operators of online intermediation services or digital marketplaces are deemed the suppliers when electronic services are provided to unregistered persons in Mainland Tanzania.</li>
<li><strong>New exemptions: </strong>VAT exemptions were added or extended for locally manufactured fishing nets, specific aircraft parts, and locally manufactured garments made from domestic cotton.</li>
</ul>
<p>The measures took effect on 1 July 2026 unless otherwise specified in the Act.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) has updated its <a href="https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/corporate-income-tax/corporate-income-tax-compliance/getting-companies-to-comply" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Getting Companies to Comply</a> guidance, adding the timely and accurate filing of the Form for Reporting Related Party Transactions (RPT Form) as a new ongoing area of corporate tax compliance focus.</p>
<p>Companies are required to complete the RPT Form where the value of related party transactions disclosed in their financial statements for the relevant financial period exceeds SGD 15 million. The form, which forms part of the Corporate Income Tax Return (Form C), provides IRAS with information to assess transfer pricing risks. Companies are encouraged to review their internal processes and controls to ensure that RPT Forms are filed accurately and on time.</p>
<p>The overall guidance outlines IRAS&#8217; corporate tax compliance strategy, which combines risk-based and random audits supported by data analytics and other tools to identify non-compliance across industries.</p>
<p>Upcoming compliance programmes will focus on claims under the Enterprise Innovation Scheme (EIS) and compliance with withholding tax obligations. IRAS encourages businesses that identify errors to make voluntary disclosures, which may qualify them for reduced penalties.</p>
<p>IRAS&#8217; ongoing compliance efforts continue to cover timely filing of corporate income tax returns, claims for private or non-deductible expenses, the classification of income and expenses subject to concessionary tax rates, recognition of income from construction contracts, the tax treatment of property disposal gains, digital economy businesses, deductibility of interest expenses and borrowing costs, and related party transaction reporting.</p>
<p>The guidance also highlights recurring areas of non-compliance, including the abuse of tax exemption schemes, incorrect capital allowance claims, related party services that are not priced at arm&#8217;s length, the tax treatment of investment dealing companies, and companies that recommence business after being exempted from filing corporate income tax returns without notifying IRAS.</p>
<p>IRAS emphasises the importance of maintaining proper business records, meeting filing obligations on time, voluntarily disclosing errors, and reporting suspected tax evasion as part of its broader strategy to promote voluntary compliance and safeguard Singapore&#8217;s tax system.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[China&#8217;s State Taxation Administration (STA) has issued Announcement No. 13 of 2026 on 8 July 2026, introducing rules on the special tax treatment applicable to corporate restructuring transactions, including mergers and demergers. China has simplified access to deferral tax treatment for mergers and spin-offs, reducing the shareholder approval threshold to 50% from a previous consensus...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>China&#8217;s State Taxation Administration (STA) has issued <a href="https://fgk.chinatax.gov.cn/zcfgk/c100012/c5251155/content.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Announcement No. 13 of 2026</a> on 8 July 2026, introducing rules on the special tax treatment applicable to corporate restructuring transactions, including mergers and demergers.</p>
<p>China has simplified access to deferral tax treatment for mergers and spin-offs, reducing the shareholder approval threshold to 50% from a previous consensus requirement. The change takes effect for all restructuring transactions dated 1 January 2026 onwards as per the Announcement No. 13 of 2026.</p>
<p><strong>What qualifies for special treatment</strong></p>
<p>Under the modified rules in Announcement No. 13, which implement provisions of the Enterprise Income Tax Law alongside Notices Cai Shui [2009] No. 59 and Cai Shui [2014] No. 109, restructuring gains are deferred when the relevant conditions are met.</p>
<p>If resident enterprise shareholders holding more than 50% of shares in a merged or divided enterprise agree to special treatment, their acquired equity and the corresponding assets and liabilities qualify for deferral. The remaining shareholders default to standard tax treatment.</p>
<p>When assets acquired by the reorganised enterprise fall under standard treatment, companies may elect to preserve the original tax basis and spread the difference between that basis and fair market value across a 10-year depreciation period from the reorganisation year. This election is permanent once made.</p>
<p><strong>Lock-up and shareholder constraints</strong></p>
<p>Resident shareholders owning 5% or more of the merged or divided enterprise on the restructuring date must sign onto the special treatment agreement. The same requirement applies to the top ten resident shareholders by stake.</p>
<p>All locked-in parties cannot transfer their shares for 12 consecutive months following the restructuring—a breach disqualifies the entire transaction from special treatment.</p>
<p>If other shareholders sell within 12 months and push the consenting bloc below 50%, special treatment also becomes unavailable, triggering retroactive adjustments.</p>
<p><strong>Who counts as a shareholder?</strong></p>
<p>Shareholders can be individuals, partnerships, contractual asset management products, or non-resident enterprises. Each category follows its own applicable income tax rules; the reorganisation rules don&#8217;t override those requirements.</p>

Speaking before the Senate Finance Committee on 22 July 2026, Greer said he aimed to lock in separate interim deals with Mexico and Canada by year-end, while deferring the complex questions—auto...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>US Trade Representative (USTR) Jamieson Greer signalled this week that the Trump administration has abandoned hope of completing a full USMCA overhaul this year.</p>
<p>Speaking before the Senate Finance Committee on 22 July 2026, Greer said he aimed to lock in separate interim deals with Mexico and Canada by year-end, while deferring the complex questions—auto content rules, labour standards, environmental compliance—to 2027.</p>
<p><em>“I’m hopeful that before the end of the year, we could have at least options for President Trump and the leaders of Canada and Mexico to consider potential interim arrangements or things that Canada can do on the one hand and Mexico can do on the other hand to strengthen enforcement and to improve their commitments toward us,” Greer told the Senate Finance Committee on 22 July, adding that US proposals for stricter rules of origin and labour-related provisions are expected to be addressed next year. </em></p>
<p><em>&#8220;I would love to have by the end of the year at least some arrangements — one with Canada, one with Mexico,&#8221; Greer told a Senate Finance Committee hearing.</em></p>
<p>The United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) is now subject to annual reviews after the US <a href="https://regfollower.com/us-walks-away-from-usmca-renewal-eyes-major-trade-overhaul/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">declined</a> to extend the trade pact for another 16 years.</p>
<p>While Canada remains a key US supplier of steel, aluminium, lithium, natural gas, oil and electricity, and Mexico supplies significant amounts of silver and steel, the latest US<a href="https://regfollower.com/us-trump-administration-invokes-century-old-law-to-hit-canada-with-50-tariffs/" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> tariffs imposed on Canadian goods </a>on 20 July largely exempted metals.</p>
<p>The timeline amounts to a public acknowledgement that business uncertainty will persist well into next year.</p>
<p>Mexico and Canada have been pressing for quick wins, particularly relief from Section 232 tariffs Trump imposed last year: 25% on autos, 50% on steel and aluminium. This week alone, Trump escalated by threatening 50% duties on roughly USD 20 billion in Canadian imports including beer, dairy, and hockey sticks.</p>
<p><strong>What&#8217;s negotiable now, what isn&#8217;t</strong></p>
<p>Greer said he would present options to Trump, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney by December. Mexico broadly backs the US push to raise regional auto content (a stated effort to keep Chinese components out of North American vehicles), but wants tariff cuts first.</p>
<p>Canada sits on the sidelines for now—excluded from the bilateral <a href="https://regfollower.com/us-mexico-to-convene-for-third-round-of-usmca-negotiations-tomorrow/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Mexico City talks</a>, a positioning that risks forcing it to swallow terms it didn&#8217;t shape.</p>
<p>Trump is also tying trade concessions to unrelated demands: stricter Mexican border security and compliance with a 1944 Rio Grande water treaty that obligates Mexico to supply Texas irrigation water. Greer made plain that without movement on those fronts, the president will resist even a modest interim agreement.</p>
<p>The six-year-old USMCA underpins roughly USD 1.6 trillion in regional trade.</p>
<p>On 1 July 2026, Trump chose not to renew the pact, triggering a 10-year countdown to its expiration unless all three countries agree to changes. That countdown clock is now running.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The German Federal Ministry of Finance has released updated VAT registration forms for non-resident businesses, along with revised annexes and guidance notes, replacing versions issued in 2021 and 2023. The forms, published in July 2026, are available in German, English and French.</p>
<p>The revised &#8220;Fragebogen zur umsatzsteuerlichen Erfassung von im Ausland ansässigen Unternehmern&#8221; applies to businesses established outside Germany with no fixed establishment in the country that carry out activities subject to German VAT. Registration is generally required for businesses providing taxable services, importing or exporting goods, or selling goods to German customers through online shops or electronic marketplaces.</p>
<p>The updated registration package requires businesses to provide information on their legal identity, tax representatives, taxable activities and expected turnover. It also includes provisions for requesting a German VAT Identification Number, an EORI number and participation in the One-Stop-Shop (OSS) schemes, where applicable.</p>
<p>According to the guidance, VAT returns must be filed electronically through the ELSTER portal and are generally due by the 10th day after the end of the monthly or quarterly reporting period. Depending on their activities, businesses may also be required to submit supplementary annexes covering areas such as online trade, passenger transport or multiple facilities in Germany.</p>
