										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>China is advancing invoice digitalisation by phasing out paper invoices and expanding fully digital e-invoices as part of broader tax administration reforms to reduce costs, improve compliance, and support digital transformation.</p>
<p><strong>Zhejiang eliminates paper invoices by June 2026</strong></p>
<p>Many taxpayers are no longer allowed to issue paper invoices after 30 June 2026, while previously issued paper invoices remain valid.</p>
<p>In Zhejiang Province, the State Taxation Administration (STA) <a href="https://zhejiang.chinatax.gov.cn/art/2026/4/3/art_8414_84495.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced</a> it is phasing out paper invoices for a full digital system. Tax authorities will stop approving new paper invoice applications from 30 April 2026, and taxpayers must stop issuing provincial paper invoices entirely by 30 June 2026—existing invoices issued before that date remain valid.</p>
<p>Digital invoices will be issued through the National Unified Standard Electronic Tax Bureau (Zhejiang) or Leqi, both verified via the State Taxation Administration&#8217;s National Value-Added Tax Invoice Verification Platform. All taxpayers must complete verification and cancellation of paper invoices with tax authorities by 31 December 2026. Any voided paper invoices that require replacement must be reissued as digital invoices.</p>
<p><strong>Dalian suspends paper invoices from 1 July 2026</strong></p>
<p>Meanwhile, Dalian Municipality STA <a href="https://dalian.chinatax.gov.cn/art/2026/6/1/art_1715_698694.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced</a> that it is discontinuing most paper invoices effective 1 July 2026, with exceptions only for certain taxi and urban transport invoices. Digital invoices will replace them, issued through the National Unified Standard Electronic Tax Bureau (Dalian) or the Leqi Platform. Taxpayers must complete verification and cancellation of paper invoices by 31 December 2026. Voided invoices follow existing rules; replacements must be digital.</p>
<p><strong>Synthesised China&#8217;s digital invoice rollout and future trajectory</strong></p>
<p>China&#8217;s fully digital invoice system, implemented nationwide on 1 December 2024, uses unified numbering and automated issuance with direct data exchange to tax authorities through digital accounts. Tax authorities are now encouraging taxpayers to migrate to digital invoices, signalling a strategic shift toward phasing out paper-based invoicing entirely as part of broader <a href="https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/2021-03/24/content_5595384.htm" target="_blank" rel="noopener">tax digitalisation efforts</a>. Implementation pace varies by region and industry, but the policy direction is clear: establish digital invoices as the primary method across the economy.</p>

		<title>UK: HMRC consults draft 2026 Finance Bill tax measures</title>
		<link>https://regfollower.com/uk-hmrc-consults-draft-2026-finance-bill-tax-measures/?utm_source=rss&#038;utm_medium=rss&#038;utm_campaign=uk-hmrc-consults-draft-2026-finance-bill-tax-measures</link>

					<description><![CDATA[The UK government has published a series of draft Finance Bill 2026 measures proposing changes across several indirect taxes and duties, including the Soft Drinks Industry Levy, Air Passenger Duty (APD), Alcohol Duty, Landfill Tax, VAT and Vehicle Excise Duty (VED). The proposals also include new legislation affecting electric vehicles and technical amendments to tax...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The UK government has published a series of draft Finance Bill 2026 measures proposing changes across several indirect taxes and duties, including the Soft Drinks Industry Levy, Air Passenger Duty (APD), Alcohol Duty, Landfill Tax, VAT and Vehicle Excise Duty (VED). The proposals also include new legislation affecting electric vehicles and technical amendments to tax administration.</p>
<p>Subject to consultation and parliamentary approval, the measures are scheduled to take effect between April 2027 and January 2028, providing businesses and affected sectors with advance notice of the planned legislative changes.</p>
<p><a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/changes-to-the-soft-drinks-industry-levy" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Draft soft drinks industry levy amendments 2028</a></p>
<p>This legislation outlines upcoming adjustments to the Soft Drinks Industry Levy, specifically detailing changes to how sugar content is calculated and which beverages are taxed. A key modification includes lowering the sugar threshold from 5 grams to 4.5 grams per 100 milliliters, a change set to take effect on 1 January 2028.</p>
<p>It also clarifies the status of milk-based drinks and plant-based alternatives, specifying that while natural lactose is generally excluded from sugar counts, certain additions like added sugar or lactase-treated sugars may still trigger the levy. Furthermore, drinking yoghurts are explicitly defined as non-beverages to exempt them from the tax, provided they meet specific fermentation standards.</p>
<p>These draft measures grant tax commissioners the authority to regulate how quantities are measured and how specific liquids are classified under the law.</p>
<p><a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/air-passenger-duty-and-private-jets" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Air passenger duty: business jet higher rate legislation</a></p>
<p>This draft legislation outlines upcoming changes to the Air Passenger Duty, specifically targeting the use of private aviation.</p>
<p>Starting in April 2027, a significantly higher tax rate will be applied to individuals traveling on business jets, with costs varying based on the flight&#8217;s destination. The legislation provides a legal definition for these aircraft, identifying them as non-scheduled planes where departure details are specifically arranged for the traveler. Additionally, it clarifies that certain tax exemptions for children will not apply if they are flying on these private vessels.</p>
<p><a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/alcohol-duty-penalties-for-late-filing-and-late-payments" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Alcohol duty: penalties for non-compliance and late payment</a></p>
<p>This legislative draft outlines structural updates to the legal framework governing financial penalties for alcohol-related tax non-compliance.</p>
<p>By amending the Finance Acts of 2009 and 2021, the legislation transitions the enforcement of alcohol duty returns and payments into a modernised regulatory system. It specifies precise deadline requirements for tax submissions and establishes how HMRC assessments will trigger fines if obligations are missed.</p>
<p>Furthermore, it grants the Treasury the authority to determine exactly when these new administrative rules will officially take effect.</p>
<p><a href="https://www.gov.uk/guidance/rates-and-allowances-for-air-passenger-duty" target="_blank" rel="noopener">UK air passenger duty rates and guidance</a></p>
<p>This official government guidance outlines the Air Passenger Duty (APD) rates that aircraft operators must pay for travelers departing from the United Kingdom. The total tax is determined by the final destination of the passenger&#8217;s journey, which is categorised into four distinct geographic bands ranging from domestic to long-haul travel. Additionally, the amount owed is influenced by the class of travel, with different pricing for reduced, standard, and higher rates based on seat spacing and aircraft size. The legislation provides specific future pricing tables for 2026 and 2027, including unique rules for direct long-haul flights originating in Northern Ireland. Operators are instructed on how to properly calculate their liabilities and submit the necessary tax returns to HMRC.</p>
<p><a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/electric-vehicle-excise-duty-eved" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Draft finance bill: electric vehicle excise duty legislation</a></p>
<p>This draft legislation outlines the introduction of a new mileage-based tax system for electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles, referred to as the eVED charge.</p>
<p>Under these proposed amendments to existing road traffic laws, owners of these vehicles would be required to pay an additional duty calculated by multiplying their estimated annual mileage by a specific per-mile rate. The bill establishes strict protocols for mileage reporting, including provisions for adjustments, refunds, and &#8220;top-up&#8221; payments based on actual distance driven. To ensure compliance, the bill introduces new criminal offences related to odometer tampering and the use of software designed to falsify distance records. Furthermore, authorities would be granted expanded powers to inspect vehicles suspected of carrying faulty or compromised odometers. These measures essentially transition low-emission vehicles into a taxable framework that mirrors the duty traditionally collected from fossil fuel consumption.</p>
<p><a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/landfill-tax-removal-of-exemption-for-stabilisers-added-to-dredgings-when-sent-to-landfill" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Legislative amendments to dredging exemptions for landfill tax</a></p>
<p>This legal draft outlines proposed modifications to the Finance Act 1996 regarding the taxation of waste removed from waterways. The new provisions specifically address how dredged materials and non-liquid additives are categorised when they are deposited at landfill sites.</p>
<p>Under these rules, different components of a single waste deposit can be treated as separate disposals for tax calculation purposes if they meet specific criteria. This allows for a more granular assessment by authorities to ensure that tax exemptions or rates are applied accurately to the distinct types of material involved. These regulatory updates are scheduled to take effect for all relevant waste disposals occurring on or after 1 April 2027.</p>
<p><a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/vat-provisions-for-deposit-return-schemes-drs" target="_blank" rel="noopener">VAT treatment of qualifying deposit schemes</a></p>
<p>This legislation outlines a legal framework for the Value Added Tax (VAT) treatment of deposit return schemes established under environmental laws in the UK and Scotland. Under these rules, the initial deposit paid by a consumer is excluded from the taxable value of the goods at the point of sale. Instead, the scheme administrator is responsible for paying VAT specifically on the surplus funds created when deposits are collected but never reclaimed through refunds.</p>
<p>To facilitate this, the legislation mandates that administrators must register for VAT and outlines strict notification procedures for beginning or ending their operations. Furthermore, it empowers tax authorities to set regulations for record-keeping and specific methods for calculating tax obligations related to these environmental initiatives.</p>
<p><a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/vehicle-excise-duty-ved-exemption-for-search-and-rescue-vehicles" target="_blank" rel="noopener">VED exemption for search and rescue vehicles</a></p>
<p>This legislative draft outlines a new tax exemption for search and rescue vehicles under the Vehicle Excise and Registration Act 1994. To qualify for this financial relief, a vehicle must be operated by a charity and utilised primarily for lifesaving missions. Additionally, the law requires that these vehicles are clearly labeled with identifying signage on both sides to verify their official purpose. The legislation further clarifies the legal definitions of eligible organisations and activities by referencing existing value-added tax codes. These updated regulations are scheduled to be implemented for all qualifying licenses starting on 1 April 2027. This measure serves to reduce the operating costs for emergency response organizations performing essential public services.</p>
<p><strong>Consultation timeline</strong></p>
<p>Several of the draft measures remain open for technical consultation before being included in Finance Bill 2026. Consultation deadlines fall between 6 September 2026 and 7 September 2026, depending on the measure, with implementation dates ranging from 1 April 2027 to 1 January and 1 April 2028.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[The Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) has updated its guidance on Employee fringe benefits, providing additional clarification on the Goods and Services Tax (GST) treatment of benefits that employers provide to their employees. The revised guide explains that when an employer provides fringe benefits, it is regarded as making a supply and may be...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) has updated its guidance on <a href="https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/goods-services-tax-(gst)/charging-gst-(output-tax)/common-scenarios---do-i-charge-gst/employee-benefits" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Employee fringe benefits</a>, providing additional clarification on the Goods and Services Tax (GST) treatment of benefits that employers provide to their employees.</p>
<p>The revised guide explains that when an employer provides fringe benefits, it is regarded as making a supply and may be required to account for output GST on the value of those benefits. A new section has been added to address common employee benefits and clarify when output tax applies in different circumstances.</p>
<p>IRAS defines employee fringe benefits as goods or services provided free of charge or at a reduced cost as part of an employee&#8217;s remuneration package. Examples include company cars for private use, free meals, accommodation and the personal use of business mobile phones.</p>
<p><strong>Accommodation provided to employees</strong></p>
<p>Under the updated guidance, employers are not required to account for output GST when providing non-residential accommodation, such as hotels, chalets and boarding houses, for employees.</p>
<p>The same GST treatment also applies to furnished residential accommodation provided to employees, including workers&#8217; dormitories and serviced apartments.</p>
<p><strong>Mobile phones given as employee gifts</strong></p>
<p>The revised guide provides specific guidance on the GST treatment of mobile phones supplied to employees.</p>
<p>Where a mobile phone is purchased with the intention of being given as a gift and the employer has claimed input tax, output tax must be accounted for if the purchase price exceeds SGD 200. For GST purposes, employers may use the purchase price paid to the supplier as the open market value.</p>
<p>If a phone was initially acquired for business use but is subsequently given to an employee as a gift, output tax must also be accounted for where input tax has been claimed and the purchase price exceeds SGD 200. In these cases, the open market value must be determined based on the price of identical or similar goods at the time the phone is transferred.</p>
<p><strong>Mobile phones retained as business assets</strong></p>
<p>No output tax is required where a mobile phone remains a business asset and is provided to an employee solely for temporary business use.</p>
<p>This treatment applies where the phone is used exclusively for business purposes and the employer has apportioned the input tax claimed on the purchase, claiming only the portion attributable to business use.</p>
<p><strong>Purpose of the update</strong></p>
<p>According to IRAS, the new section is intended to help employers determine when GST applies to commonly provided employee fringe benefits and how those benefits should be valued when output GST is required.</p>

Effective from 1 July 2026, the Decree sets out the framework for the creation, issuance, transmission, storage and management of electronic invoices, while replacing several earlier regulations, including Decree No. 123/2020/NĐ-CP. Scope...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Vietnam has issued <a href="https://vanban.chinhphu.vn/?pageid=27160&amp;docid=218689&amp;classid=1&amp;orggroupid=2" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Decree No. 254/2026/NĐ-CP</a>, establishing detailed regulations on electronic invoices and electronic records under the Law on Tax Administration No. 108/2025/QH15.</p>
<p>Effective from 1 July 2026, the Decree sets out the framework for the creation, issuance, transmission, storage and management of electronic invoices, while replacing several earlier regulations, including Decree No. 123/2020/NĐ-CP.</p>
<p><strong>Scope of application</strong></p>
<p>The Decree applies to a broad range of parties involved in electronic invoicing. These include enterprises, cooperatives, business households and individuals selling goods or providing services in Vietnam, as well as organisations and individuals purchasing goods or services. It also covers organisations providing electronic invoice and electronic record services, together with tax and customs authorities responsible for oversight and administration.</p>
<p><strong>Types of electronic invoices</strong></p>
<p>The Decree classifies electronic invoices into three categories.</p>
<p>Electronic invoices with a Tax Authority Code require a unique identification code issued by the tax authority before the invoice is sent to the buyer.</p>
<p>Electronic invoices without a Tax Authority Code are transmitted directly by the seller without prior coding by the tax authority and are generally intended for certain large-scale sectors, including electricity, petroleum and banking.</p>
<p>The Decree also recognises electronic invoices generated from cash registers connected to the tax authority&#8217;s database.</p>
<p><strong>Invoice content and format</strong></p>
<p>Electronic invoices must comply with prescribed data standards and include mandatory information such as the invoice name, invoice number and serial number, together with the names, addresses and tax identification numbers of the seller and buyer.</p>
<p>Invoices must also specify details of the transaction, including the description of goods or services, unit of measure, quantity, unit price, applicable tax rate and total amount.</p>
<p>The seller&#8217;s digital signature is generally required, while the buyer&#8217;s digital signature is only necessary in cases agreed between the parties. Vietnamese is the primary language for invoices, and the Vietnam Dong (đ) is the standard currency, although foreign languages and currencies may be used in certain international transactions.</p>
<p><strong>Timing of invoice issuance</strong></p>
<p>For the sale of goods, electronic invoices must be issued when ownership or the right to use the goods is transferred, regardless of whether payment has been received.</p>
<p>For services, invoices must generally be issued when the service has been completed.</p>
<p>The Decree also establishes sector-specific rules for industries including construction, electricity, telecommunications and real estate.</p>
<p><strong>Storage, reporting and compliance</strong></p>
<p>The Decree requires electronic invoices to be stored in a way that preserves their integrity, security and accessibility throughout the statutory retention period.</p>
<p>Sellers must transmit invoice data to the tax authorities either directly or through authorised service providers.</p>
<p>The regulations prohibit the use of fake invoices, &#8220;khống&#8221; invoices issued for non-existent transactions, and invoices issued by entities that have ceased operations.</p>
<p><strong>Incentives and consumer measures</strong></p>
<p>To support implementation, the Decree provides for free electronic invoice services for up to 12 months for eligible small and medium enterprises, cooperatives and business households located in difficult socio-economic areas.</p>
<p>It also introduces a framework for rewarding consumers who report sellers that fail to issue legal electronic invoices, with the aim of improving compliance.</p>
<p><strong>Transitional arrangements</strong></p>
<p>The Decree took effect on 1 July 2026, replacing several earlier regulations, including Decree No. 123/2020/NĐ-CP. It also includes transitional provisions requiring certain paper records, including specified receipts, to be converted to electronic formats by the end of 2026.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Dominican Republic has enacted Law No. 36-26, amending the General Law on Integrated Management and Co-Processing of Solid Waste (Law 225-20) by introducing a revised environmental contribution framework for corporate entities and other changes to strengthen financing for the country&#8217;s waste management system.</p>
<p>The law, promulgated by the Executive Branch on 6 July 2026 and officially notified on 14 July 2026, replaces the previous six-tier contribution structure with a progressive system covering 12 categories. <p>Law 36-26 raises the maximum contribution for the highest-income companies while requiring the State, through the General Budget, to provide funding equivalent to the amount collected by the DGII to reinforce financing for the national waste management system.</p>
<p>The legislation also updates provisions on integrated solid waste management by promoting recycling, supporting the circular economy, and strengthening waste collection, recovery and final disposal mechanisms. It further tightens restrictions on single-use plastics, including a prohibition on the importation of foam (expanded polystyrene) products and other specified foam items unless certified as biodegradable.</p>
<p>The amendment to Law 225-20 faced opposition from several business organisations during its passage through Congress, with critics arguing that the measure advanced under an accelerated legislative process and would increase compliance costs for businesses. Despite those objections, the National Congress approved the legislation and the Executive Branch subsequently promulgated Law 36-26, which will enter into force upon its publication in the Official Gazette.</p>

<p>Published on 13 July 2026, the consultations form part of the government&#8217;s wider efforts to simplify tax rules, improve investment certainty and refine existing tax reliefs.</p>

<p>Building on an earlier review of the relief&#8217;s effectiveness and robustness, the government is seeking views on reforms that would make the relief more accessible and better aligned with the practical realities of brownfield development.</p>
<p>The consultation examines proposals to change the timing of the relief, align eligible contamination expenditure with planning processes, and establish a framework for defining and providing relief for long-term derelict land.</p>

<p><strong><a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/consultations/tax-treatment-of-predevelopment-costs--2" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Tax treatment of predevelopment costs</a></strong></p>
<p>HMRC has also launched a consultation on the tax treatment of predevelopment costs, seeking evidence on the types of expenditure businesses incur before development begins, how those costs are treated under current tax rules and their impact on investment decisions.</p>
<p>The consultation follows the government&#8217;s commitment in the Corporate Tax Roadmap to provide greater certainty over capital allowances. It also comes after the UK Supreme Court&#8217;s judgment in Orsted West of Duddon Sands (UK) Ltd and others v HMRC [2026], with the government now examining whether businesses face uncertainty under the existing legislation and how that affects commercial investment.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Dominican Republic&#8217;s General Directorate of Internal Taxes (DGII) launched a <a href="https://dgii.gov.do/publicacionesOficiales/foroContribuyentes/Paginas/NG-aplicacion-amnistia-fiscal-transitoria-Ley-30-26.aspx" target="_blank" rel="noopener">public consultation</a> on 14 July 2026 on a <a href="https://dgii.gov.do/publicacionesOficiales/foroContribuyentes/Documents/Borrador-NG-aplicacion-amnistia-fiscal-transitoria-Ley-30-26%20.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">draft General Rule</a> establishing the procedures, requirements and conditions for applying the temporary tax amnesty introduced by Article 8 of Law No. 30-26 on Tax Reform.</p>
<p>The draft General Rule outlines the application process, eligibility requirements, payment options and administrative procedures for taxpayers seeking relief under the temporary amnesty.</p>
<p>The consultation will remain open until 15 September 2026.</p>
<p><strong>Scope of the amnesty</strong></p>
<p>The proposed rules would apply to individuals, legal entities, estates and entities without legal personality.</p>
<p>The temporary tax amnesty would cover all types of taxes, regardless of the fiscal period, including:</p>
<ul>
<li>Tax debts under administrative or judicial appeal at the time Law No. 30-26 entered into force.</li>
<li>Delinquent debts that have become final and irrevocable (res judicata).</li>
<li>Tax liabilities arising from omitted tax declarations.</li>
<li>Certain specific liabilities, including real estate and motor vehicle transfer taxes, inheritance taxes where the death occurred before the law entered into force, and unpaid income tax advance payments.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Application requirements</strong></p>
<p>Taxpayers would be required to submit their applications by 31 December 2026 through the DGII Virtual Office (OFV) or in person at local tax offices using the &#8220;Solicitudes de Pago Amnistía Ley núm. 30-26&#8221; form.</p>
<p>For debts that are currently under administrative or judicial appeal, applicants would have to formally withdraw those proceedings before qualifying for the amnesty.</p>
<p><strong>Payment conditions</strong></p>
<p>Under the draft rules, taxpayers would generally be required to pay the principal tax liability together with a limited amount of interest and penalties.</p>
<p>For debts under appeal, settlement would consist of a single payment of the tax due plus up to one year of interest.</p>
<p>For delinquent debts and liabilities arising from omitted declarations, taxpayers would pay the principal tax together with up to one year of late-payment surcharges and interest.</p>
<p><strong>Payment options</strong></p>
<p>Accepted applicants could either make a single payment or choose an instalment arrangement.</p>
<p>A full payment would have to be made within three calendar days after the DGII notifies the taxpayer that the application has been accepted.</p>
<p>Alternatively, taxpayers could make an initial payment followed by equal monthly instalments over a period of up to 12 months. Interest would apply to the instalments, and failure to pay three consecutive monthly instalments would result in the loss of the amnesty benefits.</p>
<p><strong>Administrative procedure</strong></p>
<p>The DGII would have up to 30 business days to issue a decision accepting or rejecting an application. If no decision is issued within that period, the application would be deemed rejected under the principle of negative administrative silence.</p>
<p>The consultation on the draft General Rule will remain open until 15 September 2026, after which the DGII is expected to consider stakeholder feedback before finalising the implementation rules for the temporary tax amnesty.</p>

		<link>https://regfollower.com/italy-clarifies-no-gift-or-inheritance-tax-on-trust-dissolution-without-beneficiary-transfer/?utm_source=rss&#038;utm_medium=rss&#038;utm_campaign=italy-clarifies-no-gift-or-inheritance-tax-on-trust-dissolution-without-beneficiary-transfer</link>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Mohammed Al Mamun]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Mon, 20 Jul 2026 11:44:32 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Gift Taxes]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Inheritance/Estate Taxes]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Europe]]></category>

					<description><![CDATA[The Italian Revenue Agency confirmed on 17 July 2026 that dissolving a trust and returning assets to the settlor triggers no gift or inheritance tax, provided no beneficiaries receive the property. Response no. 146 of 16 July 2026 clarifies a long-debated point: the mere setup of a trust doesn&#8217;t create a taxable event. Taxation only...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Italian Revenue Agency <a href="https://www.fiscooggi.it/portale/-/trust-sciolto-e-rientro-dei-beni-non-c-%C3%A8-imposta-sulle-donazioni" target="_blank" rel="noopener">confirmed</a> on 17 July 2026 that dissolving a trust and returning assets to the settlor triggers no gift or inheritance tax, provided no beneficiaries receive the property.</p>
<p><a href="https://www.agenziaentrate.gov.it/portale/documents/20143/10196933/Risposta+n.+146_2026.pdf/98b0d8fa-5cd7-b976-54ff-a3d3c3865438?t=1784205528768" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Response no. 146</a> of 16 July 2026 clarifies a long-debated point: the mere setup of a trust doesn&#8217;t create a taxable event. Taxation only arrives when beneficiaries actually take possession of assets. If the trust ends before that transfer happens, nothing is taxable.</p>
<p>This aligns with recent administrative guidance (Circular No. 34/2022; Response to Interpellation No. 165/2024) and established case law, particularly Court of Cassation Order No. 31857/2023, which held that early termination of a trust can entirely preclude the taxable event if beneficiaries never achieve enrichment.</p>
<p><strong>Background</strong></p>
<p>The ruling involved a settler who transferred bare ownership of company shares—inherited shares held in Alfa Srl and Beta SpA—into a trust while retaining usufruct. The trust conducted minimal activity, primarily holding the shares and consenting to an extraordinary shareholder meeting that approved Alfa Srl&#8217;s merger into Beta SpA.</p>
<p>Following the merger, the trust owned a 36.68% stake in the resulting entity, Beta Srl. Only in 2021 did Beta Srl distribute dividends to the settlers as a usufructuary.</p>
<p>The original designated beneficiary was the settler&#8217;s mother, who later renounced her interest. Proposed amendments to add the settlor&#8217;s adopted son failed due to legal ineffectiveness under New Zealand law (Trusts Act 2019). With no active beneficiaries and no distributions pending, all parties—settler, trustee, and guardian—agreed to dissolve the trust before its natural expiration and return the 36.68% shareholding to the settlor at no cost.</p>
<p><strong>Legislative framework</strong></p>
<p>Legislative Decree No. 139/2024 recently codified the tax treatment of trusts by inserting Article 4-bis into the Consolidated Law on Inheritance and Donation Tax (Legislative Decree No. 346/1990).</p>
<p>The decree establishes that a taxable event occurs only when the trust results in actual gratuitous enrichment of beneficiaries, with taxation triggered upon asset transfer to them. A destination restriction alone—the settlor&#8217;s decision to earmark assets for future beneficiaries—does not constitute an independent taxable event. Instead, a stable and genuinely operative transfer of assets is required.</p>
<p><strong>Income tax treatment</strong></p>
<p>Under the Income Tax Code (TUIR, Articles 9 and 67), capital gains arise only from transactions made for consideration. Since the reconveyance was free and without consideration, no taxable capital gain emerges. The Agency concluded that neither the original contribution to the trust nor the reconveyance upon dissolution produced tax-relevant transfers.</p>
<p>The transaction remains fiscally neutral for both indirect taxes (gift and inheritance tax) and direct taxes (income tax).</p>
]]></content:encoded>

The authority stated that, from 1 January 2016, income derived from house and land transactions must be filed separately and...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Taiwan&#8217;s National Taxation Bureau has <a href="https://www.mof.gov.tw/Eng/singlehtml/f48d641f159a4866b1d31c0916fbcc71?cntId=e8405aacef294b96889226b7e810538c" target="_blank" rel="noopener">clarified</a>, on 20 July 2026, that foreign taxpayers that income derived from qualifying house and land transactions must be reported separately from gross consolidated income under the Income Tax Act.</p>
<p>The authority stated that, from 1 January 2016, income derived from house and land transactions must be filed separately and must not be consolidated with gross consolidated income.</p>
<p>Foreign taxpayers who derive income from transactions involving a house, land, the house utilisation right, a presale house, or shares or capital meeting specified conditions (collectively referred to as &#8220;house and land&#8221;) are required to file an individual house and land transactions income tax return if any of the following conditions are met:</p>
<ul>
<li>The transferred house, the share of land associated with the house, or land for which a construction permit may lawfully be issued was acquired on or after 1 January 2016.</li>
<li>The transferred right of using a house by creation of superficies was acquired on or after 1 January 2016.</li>
<li>The transferred right or the presale house together with its building location was acquired on or after 1 January 2016.</li>
<li>The transaction involves shares or capital of an individual or profit-seeking enterprise directly or indirectly holding more than half of the total number of shares or the total amount of capital of an enterprise within or outside the R.O.C., where at least 50% of the value of those shares or capital is constituted by house and land within the territory of the R.O.C. This provision does not apply to transactions involving shares of companies listed on the Taiwan Stock Exchange, Taipei Exchange or the Emerging Board.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Tax calculation and rates</strong></p>
<p>The authority said taxable income from house and land transactions is calculated using the following formula:</p>
<p>Taxable income = the amount of house and land transaction income – the amount of land value increment calculated in accordance with the Land Tax Act.</p>
<p>For non-residents of the R.O.C., the applicable tax rate depends on the holding period. A 45% tax rate applies where the holding period is less than two years, while a 35% tax rate applies where the holding period exceeds two years.</p>
<p><strong>Filing deadline and penalties</strong></p>
<p>Taxpayers must file a house and land transaction income tax return with the tax collection authority within 30 days from the day following the completion of the ownership transfer registration of the house and land, or from the transaction date of the right to use a house created by superficies.</p>
<p>A foreign taxpayer who fails to file the required house and land transaction income tax return may be subject to a fine of more than TWD 3,000 and up to TWD 30,000, the authority said.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) has published a recap of its June Pillar Two information session on 14 July 2026. In June, the ATO held its fourth Pillar Two pre-lodgment information session, attended by more than 300 participants from Australia and overseas. The session supported multinational enterprise (MNE) groups and their advisers to prepare for...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) has published a <a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/business-bulletins-newsroom/pillar-two-june-information-session-recap" target="_blank" rel="noopener">recap of its June Pillar Two information session</a> on 14 July 2026.</p>
<p>In June, the ATO held its fourth Pillar Two pre-lodgment information session, attended by more than 300 participants from Australia and overseas. The session supported multinational enterprise (MNE) groups and their advisers to prepare for Pillar Two lodgment essentials and obligations.</p>
<p><strong>What was covered</strong></p>
<p>The session focused on lodgment requirements and included updates on:</p>
<ul>
<li>Australia&#8217;s Pillar Two implementation progress and milestones</li>
<li>key lodgment issues, such as whether MNE groups need to create a global and domestic minimum tax account and role before lodging</li>
<li>lodging the GloBE Information Return (GIR)</li>
<li>joint ventures.</li>
</ul>
<p>The ATO saw strong engagement during the session. Most questions were answered by information available on the ATO website. The content will be reviewed and updated over the coming months.</p>
<p>The sections below summarise the key topics and link to relevant resources.</p>
<p><strong>Registrations for Pillar Two</strong></p>
<p>MNE groups don&#8217;t need to <a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/international-tax-for-business/in-detail/multinationals/global-and-domestic-minimum-tax/lodging-paying-and-other-obligations-for-pillar-two#ato-Registration" target="_blank" rel="noopener">register </a>for Pillar Two before their first lodgment. However, some entities may need to create a Global Domestic Minimum Tax (GDMT) account and role before lodging to <a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/preparing-lodging-and-paying/agent-nomination" target="_blank" rel="noopener">nominate a tax agent</a>.</p>
<p>If a tax agent already has client-level access for income tax returns, a GDMT account and role are not required, and the agent can lodge the Combined Global and Domestic Minimum Tax Return (CGDMTR).</p>
<p>Requests to create GDMT accounts and roles are being processed, and agents don&#8217;t need to follow up on nominations.</p>
<p><strong>Lodging the CGDMTR</strong></p>
<p>The CGDMTR combines the foreign lodgment notification, Australian IIR/UTPR tax return (AIUTR) and Australian Domestic Minimum Tax return (DMTR) into one form available through ATO online services.</p>
<p>All in-scope taxpayers will receive an automatic 30-day<a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/international-tax-for-business/in-detail/multinationals/global-and-domestic-minimum-tax/lodging-paying-and-other-obligations-for-pillar-two#ato-Deferrals" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> lodgment deferral</a> for the 2024 fiscal year (AIUTR and DMTR only). Payment deferrals must be requested separately.</p>
<p>The API channel is open for onboarding. Digital Service Providers should be contacted to confirm they have completed all onboarding with the ATO.</p>
<p><strong>Lodging the GIR</strong></p>
<p>The ATO outlined the <a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/international-tax-for-business/in-detail/multinationals/global-and-domestic-minimum-tax/lodging-paying-and-other-obligations-for-pillar-two/globe-information-return-gir-xml-file-requirements" target="_blank" rel="noopener">GloBE Information Return (GIR) XML file requirements</a> and how to complete certain elements of the GIR, including:</p>
<ul>
<li>when to lodge</li>
<li>due dates</li>
<li>the GIR XML schema and validation rules.</li>
</ul>
<p>The automatic 30-day domestic lodgment deferral doesn&#8217;t apply to the GIR. However, the ATO may consider a suspension of lodgment enforcement during the transition period. This must be requested separately.</p>
<p><strong>Joint arrangements</strong></p>
<p>The ATO provided an update about GloBE<a href="https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/international-tax-for-business/in-detail/multinationals/global-and-domestic-minimum-tax/when-and-how-the-pillar-two-rules-apply" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> joint arrangements</a> and how the rules apply, including examples of whether arrangements may be subject to potential top-up tax or reporting obligations.</p>
<p>Common questions were also addressed, and attendees were invited to send complex enquiries to the ATO mailbox. Further web guidance on joint arrangements is being developed.</p>
<p><strong>Reminders and what&#8217;s next</strong></p>
<p>Pillar Two first lodgments for December 2024 balancers were due by 30 June; however, an automatic 30-day deferral for domestic lodgments is in place.</p>
<p>MNEs that are January 2025 balancers should note that Pillar Two first lodgments are due by 31 July 2026.</p>
<p>A <a href="https://share.viostream.com/bd1bdiur7iqent" target="_blank" rel="noopener">recording</a> of the information session is available for those who were unable to attend.</p>

		<pubDate>Mon, 20 Jul 2026 10:51:38 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Import Tariffs or Duty]]></category>

					<description><![CDATA[Belgium’s tax authorities, SPF Finance, announced on 14 July 2026 that starting 1 July 2026, American exporters can ship into Europe at reduced or zero customs duties under the Turnberry Agreement, inked on 27 July 2025. The rules sit in Regulation (EU) No 2026/1455. The European Commission&#8217;s guidance (OEO Information Note DD 022.835, issued 1...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Belgium’s tax authorities, SPF Finance, <a href="https://finances.belgium.be/fr/Actualites/avis-aux-importateurs-preuves-justificatives-concernant-les-preferences-tarifaires" target="_blank" rel="noopener">announced</a> on 14 July 2026 that starting 1 July 2026, American exporters can ship into Europe at reduced or zero customs duties under the<a href="https://policy.trade.ec.europa.eu/news/joint-statement-united-states-european-union-framework-agreement-reciprocal-fair-and-balanced-trade-2025-08-21_en" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> Turnberry Agreement</a>, inked on 27 July 2025.</p>
<p>The rules sit in Regulation (EU) No 2026/1455.</p>
<p>The European Commission&#8217;s guidance <a href="https://financien.belgium.be/fr/douanes_accises/entreprises/douane/origine/usa" target="_blank" rel="noopener">(OEO Information Note DD 022.835, issued 1 July 2026)</a> makes clear that importers must prove non-preferential origin themselves. No certificates of origin, no EUR.1 movement documents, no official paperwork issued by the US. Just the importer, the supplier&#8217;s invoices, and whatever evidence can be gathered.</p>
<p><strong>What counts as proof—and what doesn&#8217;t</strong></p>
<p>A product qualifies as American if it was entirely made there (harvesting, extraction, fishing) or underwent substantial transformation on US soil when inputs came from multiple countries.</p>
<p>Certificates of origin and &#8220;Made in USA&#8221; declarations on invoices don&#8217;t count, even if they&#8217;re legitimate-looking. The EU&#8217;s position is straightforward: a certificate from a US issuer doesn&#8217;t guarantee accuracy because US rules of origin might differ, and there&#8217;s no bilateral agreement to verify claims. They can be presented as supporting material, but they can&#8217;t stand alone.</p>
<p><strong>What importers actually need</strong></p>
<p>The principle of free presentation of evidence applies. This means the importer is responsible for correctly determining the origin of the goods and must possess the information and documents necessary to substantiate that origin. Depending on the applicable rule of origin, this information may include:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>For wholly obtained goods: </strong>Documents confirming that the products and all materials or components used were wholly obtained in the country of origin.</li>
<li><strong>For a change in tariff classification: </strong>Information relating to the production process and the tariff classifications of the materials and components used.</li>
<li><strong>For a specific operation criterion:</strong> Production records demonstrating that the required manufacturing or processing operation has been carried out.</li>
<li><strong>For the value-added criterion:</strong> Information on the materials used, their value, and their origin (often in the form of a bill of materials). It should also be possible to provide a detailed breakdown of production costs, labour costs, and other elements contributing to the added value of the finished product.</li>
</ul>
<p>This list is not exhaustive, and customs authorities may request any additional documentary evidence considered necessary to verify the origin of the goods.</p>
<p>In addition, each request must be supported by proof of direct transport/non-manipulation.</p>
<p>Importers are advised to obtain all relevant origin-related information and supporting documentation from the exporter and/or manufacturer established in the United States before submitting a claim for preferential tariff treatment.</p>
<p>Without this information, the origin of the goods cannot be substantiated, and preferential treatment cannot be claimed. The importer is responsible for collecting, retaining, and, upon request, presenting sufficient evidence of the origin of the goods to the customs authorities.</p>
<p><a href="https://regfollower.com/eu-finalises-trade-deal-with-us-under-trumps-july-deadline-threat/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Earlier</a>, the European Union reached a provisional agreement on 20 May 2026 to remove import duties on US goods, aiming to avoid threatened US tariffs after months of negotiations.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Austria’s Federal Council (Bundesrat) <a href="https://www.parlament.gv.at/aktuelles/pk/jahr_2026/pk0748#BR_BRSITZ_00994" target="_blank" rel="noopener">approved </a>the <a href="https://www.parlament.gv.at/dokument/XXVIII/I/523/fname_1763421.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Budget for 2027 and 2028</a>, including a range of tax measures, on 16 July 2026.</p>
<ol>
<li><span style="text-decoration: underline"><strong>Financial and tax reforms</strong></span></li>
</ol>
<p>The Budget detail several significant changes to the Austrian tax and financial landscape:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Parcel tax: </strong>A new tax is introduced for the delivery of parcels from mail-order businesses. Starting 1 October 2026, a tax of EUR 2 per parcel will be charged to “mail-order retailers” whose domestic turnover exceeded EUR 100 million in the previous year.</li>
<li><strong>Corporate tax: </strong>While the standard corporate tax rate remains at 23%, a higher rate of 24% will be introduced for income exceeding EUR 1 million starting in 2028.</li>
<li><strong>Alcohol tax:</strong> The alcohol tax rate will increase to EUR 1,560 per 100 liters of pure alcohol, effective 1 January 2027.</li>
</ul>
<ul>
<li><strong>Income tax adjustments:</strong>
<ul>
<li>Employees can claim up to EUR 300 annually for ergonomically suitable home office furniture (e.g., desks, chairs, lighting) starting in 2027.</li>
<li>The Family Bonus Plus rules are adjusted regarding how the bonus is split between parents depending on the age of the child and who receives family allowance [68–73].</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><strong>Stability levy for banks:</strong> The rates for the stability levy on credit institutions are adjusted for 2027–2029 (0.033% to 0.041%) and set for 2030 onwards (0.024% to 0.029%).</li>
</ul>
<p><span style="text-decoration: underline">2.<strong>Social affairs, labor, and pensions</strong></span></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Pension adjustment 2027:</strong> For the year 2027, pensions will be increased by 2.95% for monthly pension incomes up to EUR 6,930. For incomes above this threshold, a flat increase of EUR 204.44 will apply.</li>
<li><strong>Maximum contribution base: </strong>The maximum social security contribution base (Höchstbeitragsgrundlage) is specifically adjusted and increased for 2027 and 2028.</li>
<li><strong>Labor market policy:</strong> Employers must continue to pay their share of unemployment insurance contributions for older employees who are no longer personally subject to unemployment insurance, until they reach pension eligibility.</li>
<li><strong>Unemployment benefits:</strong> Stricter measures are introduced for individuals caught working while receiving unemployment benefits without prior notification to the AMS, including a mandatory six-week benefit reclamation.</li>
</ul>
<p><span style="text-decoration: underline">3.<strong>Family and education</strong></span></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Family allowance fund: </strong>Effective 1 January 2028, the Family Allowance Fund will receive an annual allocation of EUR 1.3 billion from income tax revenue. The contribution rate for employers to this fund is set at 2.7% starting in 2028.</li>
<li><strong>University funding:</strong> The Ministry of Education and the Ministry of Finance are tasked with re-evaluating and re-setting the total funding and budget pillars for universities for the 2025–2027 performance agreement period.</li>
</ul>
<p><span style="text-decoration: underline">4.<strong>Environment, climate, and agriculture</strong></span></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Forest and water resilience Act (Wald-Wasser-Resilienzgesetz):</strong> A new law is established to accelerate adaptation to climate change, improve the resilience of forest ecosystems, and enhance the ecological state of water bodies.</li>
<li><strong>Forest resilience fund:</strong> The existing Forest Fund is renamed the “Forest Resilience Fund” (Waldresilienzfonds), with EUR 54 million in federal funds pledged for 2027 and 2028.</li>
<li><strong>Environmental support:</strong> Funding frameworks for environmental measures, including thermal renovation, switching to climate-friendly heating, and industrial transformation, are extended and increased for the period 2027–2031 [168–174].</li>
</ul>
<p><span style="text-decoration: underline">5. <strong>Justice and media</strong></span></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Civil law reform: </strong>The bill abolishes “judicial wills” and the judicial recording of last wills, shifting these functions more exclusively to private or notarial processes.</li>
<li>Court fees: Various court fees are adjusted, and a new fee is introduced for cases where an appeal is announced but then not actually filed.</li>
<li><strong>ORF reform:</strong> The Austrian Broadcasting Corporation (ORF) is required to implement “structural measures” to substantially reduce its cost base in personnel, material costs, and production efficiency to ensure a balanced budget.</li>
</ul>
<p>6.<strong>Infrastructure and mobility</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>SCHIG renaming:</strong> The Railway Infrastructure Financing Company  is expanded and renamed to “Schieneninfrastruktur-Dienstleistungsgesellschaft mbH”. Its tasks will include the procurement and management of regional bus lines and “Rolling Road” (Rollende Landstraße) freight services.</li>
</ul>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Romania’s tax authority, the National Agency for Fiscal Administration (ANAF) has amended Order No. 1699/2021 to allow electronic issuance of both VAT Registration Certificates and Tax Registration Certificates, alongside the existing paper versions.</p>
<p>The original order, published in the Official Gazette of Romania Part I on 4 November 2021, set out the forms and procedures for tax registration. <p><strong>Paper certificates continue unchanged</strong></p>
<p>Tax authorities will still print paper certificates on A4 sheets (two per sheet), prepare them in duplicate, and retain one copy while giving the other to the taxpayer. Paper certificates are signed by the head of the issuing tax authority. Existing paper stocks already ordered from Imprimeria Națională (the National Printing House) can be used until exhausted.</p>
<p><strong>Digital certificates now the standard path forward</strong></p>
<p>New electronic certificates are signed with the Ministry of Finance&#8217;s advanced electronic signature using a qualified certificate. These are issued and circulated entirely in digital format, distributed through the Virtual Private Space (SPV) via secure remote transmission. This removes the need for physical printing and courier delivery.</p>

<p>The proposals would replace the current flat-rate excise tax on non-alcoholic beverages with a tiered sugar-based tax and introduce a separate sugar tax on food products by 2030 as part of the Cabinet&#8217;s broader strategy to reduce sugar consumption.</p>
<p>The proposal outlines various implementation scenarios, such as exempting essential items like mineral water and plain dairy while potentially using product labels as the primary basis for taxation. These exemptions are objectively justified by health guidelines, as dairy and soy provide essential nutrients like protein, calcium, and vitamins B2 and B12. Other unsweetened natural drinks, like pure fruit juices, will still be taxed because they lack the satiating fibers of whole fruit and can lead to high, unnoticed calorie intake.</p>
<p>Under the primary 6% sugar threshold variant, products that fit into a healthy dietary pattern (such as frozen fruit) would be exempt to align with overall public health goals. Additionally, non-prepackaged foods—such as fresh cake from a bakery or scooped ice cream from a vendor—would be exempt.</p>
<p>The consultation ends on 10 September 2026.</p>

These regulations apply to local exporters who must register their international sales agreements electronically before shipping, particularly when dealing with foreign...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Argentina’s tax authority (ARCA) has <a href="https://www.boletinoficial.gob.ar/detalleAviso/primera/343996/20260703" target="_blank" rel="noopener">published</a> General Resolution 5872/2026 in the Official Gazette of 3 July 2026, which consolidates and updates the mandatory registration process for export contracts involving goods with transparent market prices.</p>
<p>These regulations apply to local exporters who must register their international sales agreements electronically before shipping, particularly when dealing with foreign intermediaries or entities in low-tax jurisdictions.</p>
<p>Other key provisions are:</p>
<p><strong>The unification and abrogation of previous resolutions</strong></p>
<p>ARCA unified the rules governing the registration of export contracts for goods with public quotation by introducing General Resolution 5872/2026. This unification was driven by the need to streamline procedures based on past experiences, simplify compliance for obligated parties, and simultaneously strengthen ARCA&#8217;s monitoring and auditing capabilities. While General Resolutions 4653 and 4837 have been explicitly abrogated by this new framework, the specific tax forms associated with them (Forms F. 2669, F. 2670, and F. 2671) remain in effect for ongoing use.</p>
<p><strong>Strict pre-loading registration deadlines</strong></p>
<p>Exporters must register export contracts before shipment loading. For agricultural goods covered under Law No. 21.453, the Ministry of Agriculture, Livestock and Fisheries&#8217; timelines in Resolution 128/2019 also apply.</p>
<p><strong>Digital registration process via ARCA’s website </strong></p>
<p>All documentation must be submitted digitally, but the exact procedure depends on the type of goods being exported:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>For goods under Law No. 21.453 (agricultural products):</strong> Registration is satisfied by filing a Foreign Sales Affidavit  (DJVE). This declaration must be valid and in an approved &#8220;SALIDA&#8221; status in the system. Any modifications or cancellations to these contracts must follow the specific rules outlined for the DJVE.</li>
<li><strong>For goods NOT under Law No. 21.453: </strong>Exporters must file an electronic affidavit using Form F. 2669. This is done through the &#8220;Presentación de DDJJ y Pagos&#8221; portal on the ARCA website, which requires a Level 3 security Clave Fiscal (Tax Password). Upon successful submission, the system issues a receipt with a unique identifier linked to the affidavit.</li>
</ul>
<p>All forms for a single export operation must be linked by one &#8220;Contract Number,&#8221; with the exporter responsible for ensuring correct system correlation.</p>
<p><strong>Additional compliance and comparability rules </strong></p>
<p>Exporters must disclose comparability differences on contracts using Form F. 2670 within 15 days of initial registration; ARCA will presume no discrepancies exist if the form isn&#8217;t filed by the deadline. Non-agricultural contracts can be corrected before final shipment with supporting documentation in place, while contract annulments require Form F. 2671 notification.</p>
<p><strong>Effective Date and Penalties</strong></p>
<p>As noted, this new framework comes into full effect on 1 August 2026, applying to all operations registered from that date onward. ARCA will impose penalties under Law No. 11.683 for incomplete, inaccurate, or unsupported submissions and will deem mandatory registration obligations unfulfilled in cases of non-compliance.</p>

Oil and gas taxation — Oil and Gas Revenue Levy This measure...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The UK HMRC has published policy papers, draft legislation, and explanatory notes covering two proposed tax measures: the introduction of a new <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/oil-and-gas-taxation-oil-and-gas-revenue-levy" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Oil and Gas Revenue Levy</a> to replace the existing Energy Profits Levy, and <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/oil-and-gas-taxation-oil-and-gas-revenue-levy" target="_blank" rel="noopener">reforms to the foreign permanent establishment exemption regime</a>.</p>
<p><strong>Oil and gas taxation — Oil and Gas Revenue Levy</strong></p>
<p>This measure is about a new tax on oil and gas companies that will apply in times of high prices.</p>
<p><strong>Documents</strong></p>
<p><a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/oil-and-gas-taxation-oil-and-gas-revenue-levy/oil-and-gas-revenue-levy-ogrl" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Oil and Gas Revenue Levy (OGRL)</a></p>
<p><a href="https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6a4fc7e91228eb26a4cab726/Oil_and_Gas_Revenue_Levy_-_draft_legislation.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Draft legislation</a></p>
<p><a href="https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6a50e5ab9e9c95844ae64cc2/L-Day_2026_EN_-_Oil_and_Gas_Levy.odt" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Explanatory note</a></p>
<p><strong>Oil and gas on exceptional revenues</strong></p>
<p>This draft legislation for a new Oil and Gas Revenue Levy was published by HM Revenue &amp; Customs on 13 July 2026. The legislation imposes a 35% tax charge on the &#8220;exceptional&#8221; oil and gas revenues of companies engaged in a ring-fence trade. While this levy is administered similarly to corporation tax, it is strictly non-deductible. Companies are not permitted to deduct the cost of the levy when calculating their profits or losses for corporation tax, income tax, or petroleum revenue tax purposes.</p>
<p><strong>Calculating exceptional revenues</strong></p>
<p>To determine what qualifies as &#8220;exceptional&#8221; revenue, companies must apply a multi-step formula for each levy period:</p>
<ul>
<li>First, calculate total revenues from oil or gas disposals and adjust this figure for any hedging arrangements the company uses to mitigate price fluctuations.</li>
<li>Next, calculate a baseline of non-exceptional revenue by multiplying the volume of oil or gas disposed of by a set annual reference price. For the financial year ending in 2027, these baseline prices are fixed at USD 90 per barrel for oil and GBP 0.90 per therm for gas. In subsequent years, these prices will be adjusted for inflation using the consumer prices index.</li>
<li>Finally, subtract the baseline non-exceptional revenue from the total adjusted revenue. Any positive remainder is the &#8220;exceptional&#8221; revenue subject to the 35% tax.</li>
</ul>
<p>This new levy is designed to replace the Energy (Oil and Gas) Profits Levy Act 2022, which will be officially repealed. The new rules will come into effect for accounting periods beginning the day after the 2022 Act&#8217;s cessation date, which is slated to occur no later than 31 March 2030.</p>
<p><strong>Reform of the foreign permanent establishment exemption</strong></p>
<p>This measure reforms the taxation of foreign permanent establishments, making the elective exemption regime that applies to their profits and losses mandatory for Corporation Tax.</p>
<p><strong>Documents</strong></p>
<p><a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/reform-of-the-foreign-permanent-establishment-exemption/corporation-tax-reform-of-the-foreign-permanent-establishment-exemption" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Corporation Tax — reform of the foreign permanent establishment exemption</a></p>
<p><a href="https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6a50bbbcc3d64d94cacab753/foreign_branch_exemption_draft_legislation.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Draft legislation</a></p>
<p><a href="https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6a50f9021228eb26a4cab79c/L-Day_EN-Foreign_PE_Exemption.odt" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Explanatory note</a></p>
<p>The central reform involves transitioning the foreign permanent establishment exemption from a voluntary election to a mandatory requirement for companies.  By making this change, the government aims to standardise how profits and losses from overseas branches are handled for tax purposes.</p>
<p>The UK government opened a public consultation on draft legislation for the Finance Bill 2026-27, making the foreign permanent establishment exemption mandatory for Corporation Tax (previously elective). Interested parties can submit feedback via email to foreignpepolicy@hmrc.gov.uk by 13 September 2026.</p>
<p><a href="https://regfollower.com/uk-hmrc-proposes-to-make-foreign-permanent-establishment-tax-exemption-mandatory-from-2027/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Earlier</a>, the UK HMRC proposed reforms to the foreign permanent establishment (PE) exemption regime that would make the exemption for foreign PE profits and losses mandatory for most UK companies from accounting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2027. For UK-resident companies engaged in overseas oil and gas exploration and extraction, the changes would take effect from 1 September 2026.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>California introduced a cap on film and television tax credits that threatens to reverse one of the state&#8217;s rare recent industrial wins.</p>
<p>SB 122, part of the <a href="https://sbud.senate.ca.gov/system/files/2026-06/budget-act-of-2026-summary-final.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">2025-2026 budget</a> deal, limits annual claims to USD 5 million through 2029. Starting in 2030, the ceiling tightens further: companies can claim either USD 5 million or 70% of their state tax liability in a given year, whichever is higher.</p>
<p>The problem is timing.</p>
<p>Productions earned credits under AB 1138&#8217;s expanded Film &amp; Television Jobs Program based on a different set of rules, and now many of those credits won&#8217;t be worth what they were promised.</p>
<p>The implications are immediate. Productions don&#8217;t remain in a state that retroactively reduces the value of incentives.</p>
<p>On 10 July 2026, thirty-nine state legislators sent a <a href="https://drive.google.com/file/d/1FI0OXWD9j_jHvg87M0JN-O26A-HbvahW/view?usp=drive_link" target="_blank" rel="noopener">letter </a>to Governor Newsom warning that SB 122 would &#8220;significantly kneecap&#8221; the programme and risk &#8220;significant job loss.&#8221; Assemblyman Rick Chavez Zbur was blunt: &#8220;I don&#8217;t think that anyone understood what this cap was.&#8221;</p>
<p><strong>The success that needed protecting</strong></p>
<p>Between August 2025 and April 2026, the expanded programme retained 133 productions on location, generated USD 5.5 billion in economic activity, and created 38,050 cast and crew positions plus 247,934 background actor work days. This happened after California had haemorrhaged roughly 42,000 industry jobs over five years. The expanded programme reversed that slide in nine months. Then the budget landed, and the rules changed.</p>
<p><strong>How retroactivity breaks the deal</strong></p>
<p>A production company invests millions to shoot in California, backed by a tax credit commitment. They hire crews, rent equipment, and build sets. If the state then reduces what that credit is worth, the economics flip. What looked viable becomes cheaper to make in Atlanta or Vancouver.</p>
<p>California lawmakers warned that the state&#8217;s century-long leadership in film and television production is at risk without urgent action. While Governor Gavin Newsom&#8217;s office says it is confident in the tax credit programme and is working with industry and lawmakers to improve it, any delay in passing reforms before the legislative session ends could prompt productions planned for 2026 and beyond to relocate elsewhere.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

		<title>UAE: FTA clarifies downward transfer pricing adjustment rules under corporate tax law</title>
		<link>https://regfollower.com/uae-fta-clarifies-downward-transfer-pricing-adjustment-rules-under-corporate-tax-law/?utm_source=rss&#038;utm_medium=rss&#038;utm_campaign=uae-fta-clarifies-downward-transfer-pricing-adjustment-rules-under-corporate-tax-law</link>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Mohammed Al Mamun]]></dc:creator>

				<category><![CDATA[Transfer Pricing Rules]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Africa & Middle East]]></category>

					<description><![CDATA[The UAE Federal Tax Authority (FTA) has issued Public Clarification CTP011 on 15 July 2026, clarifying the requirements for transfer pricing adjustments under the Corporate Tax Law. It mandates that all transactions between Related Parties must adhere to the arm’s length standard, requiring a Taxable Person to adjust their Taxable Income if financial records do...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The UAE Federal Tax Authority (FTA) has issued <a href="https://drive.google.com/file/d/1T5gqIisMXH62LhGxhxbAAx1rKkmG_IHh/view?usp=drive_link" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Public Clarification CTP011</a> on 15 July 2026, clarifying the requirements for transfer pricing adjustments under the Corporate Tax Law.</p>
<p>It mandates that all transactions between Related Parties must adhere to the arm’s length standard, requiring a Taxable Person to adjust their Taxable Income if financial records do not reflect market-value pricing. While upward adjustments increase taxable income, downward adjustments decrease it and require rigorous disclosure in tax returns regardless of the transaction&#8217;s size.</p>
<p>Under Article 34(1) of the Corporate Tax Law (CTL), all transactions and arrangements between related parties must meet the arm’s length standard. When a taxable person&#8217;s financial statements do not reflect this standard, they must make a transfer pricing (TP) adjustment in their Tax Return. If this adjustment results in a decrease in the Taxable Income, it is classified as a downward adjustment.</p>
<p>The Federal Tax Authority (FTA) has outlined specific requirements and considerations for these downward adjustments to ensure strict compliance and transparency. These include:</p>
<p><strong>Self-assessment basis and audit risk </strong></p>
<p>Because the UAE Corporate Tax regime operates on a self-assessment basis, a taxable person is empowered to evaluate their own need for a TP adjustment. You do not need to obtain prior approval from the FTA to execute a downward adjustment in your Tax Return. However, this autonomy is balanced by regulatory oversight, meaning that any adjustment you make is fully subject to a potential Tax Audit by the FTA.</p>
<p><strong>Mandatory disclosure without thresholds </strong></p>
<p>The FTA imposes stringent disclosure rules specifically for downward adjustments. While upward adjustments (which increase taxable income) only require disclosure if the transactions exceed applicable prescribed thresholds, the rule for downward adjustments is absolute. All transactions and arrangements for which a downward adjustment is made must be disclosed in the Tax Return, irrespective of their value or nature. This ensures the FTA maintains total visibility over any self-directed reductions in a taxpayer&#8217;s taxable income.</p>
<p><strong>Rigorous documentation requirements </strong></p>
<p>To substantiate the downward adjustment and defend it during a potential tax audit, a taxable person must maintain sufficient and comprehensive documentation. The FTA mandates four key pillars of documentation:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>The rationale:</strong> You must clearly explain why the original pricing recorded in your Financial Statements failed to reflect the arm’s length principle, and demonstrate exactly how your revised outcome aligns with the arm&#8217;s length standard.</li>
<li><strong>Arm’s length analysis:</strong> You must provide a formal analysis, which includes a benchmarking study, to serve as evidence that your TP adjustment is consistent with applicable TP methodologies and regulations.</li>
<li><strong>Reconciliation: </strong>You must provide a clear mathematical mapping that reconciles the initial values recorded in your Financial Statements with the adjusted arm’s length values you are disclosing in the Tax Return.</li>
<li><strong>Symmetrical corresponding adjustments: </strong>You must provide evidence that the relevant related parties involved in the transactions or arrangements have made symmetrical corresponding adjustments on their end.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Scope limitation </strong></p>
<p>It is critical to note that the FTA&#8217;s clarification on this matter has a strict scope. It applies solely to initial adjustments required under Article 34(1) of the CTL to ensure transactions meet the arm&#8217;s length standard. The guidance does not extend to corresponding adjustments under Articles 34(10) and 34(11) of the CTL. To distinguish these:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Article 34(10):</strong> It applies when the FTA (or the taxable person) adjusts the taxable income of one party, and the FTA must make a corresponding adjustment to the taxable income of the related party.</li>
<li><strong>Article 34(11): </strong>It applies to international scenarios where a foreign competent authority adjusts a transaction, allowing the UAE taxable person to submit an application to the FTA for a corresponding adjustment to their own income.</li>
</ul>
]]></content:encoded>

The updated guidance explains who can apply for a Private Clarification, the types of issues that qualify, the...]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The UAE Federal Tax Authority (FTA) has published an updated <a href="https://tax.gov.ae//Datafolder/Files/Pdf/2026/Guide/Private%20Clarifications%20-%20EN%20-%2014%2007%202026.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Tax Procedures Guide on Private Clarifications (TPGPC1)</a>, dated 14 July 2026, setting out the process for taxpayers seeking the authority&#8217;s official view on uncertain tax technical matters.</p>
<p>The updated guidance explains who can apply for a Private Clarification, the types of issues that qualify, the application process, applicable fees, and the circumstances under which requests may be rejected or refunded.</p>
<p><strong>Private Clarifications provide binding administrative guidance</strong></p>
<p>According to the guide, a Private Clarification is an official document issued and signed by the FTA that sets out the tax treatment of a specific transaction based on the facts presented by an applicant.</p>
<p>The FTA states that it is administratively bound by the position contained in a clarification, provided the actual facts and circumstances are consistent with those submitted in the application.</p>
<p>However, the clarification applies only to the applicant that requested it and cannot be relied upon by other taxpayers. It also becomes invalid where there has been fraud, misrepresentation, or where the transaction ultimately differs from the facts provided.</p>
<p>The guide further notes that it is not legally binding legislation and does not amend existing tax laws. In addition, a Private Clarification is not considered an official decision and therefore cannot be challenged through the FTA&#8217;s reconsideration or dispute resolution procedures.</p>
<p><strong>Eligibility rules clarified</strong></p>
<p>The updated guidance confirms that any natural or juridical person facing genuine tax uncertainty may apply for a Private Clarification.</p>
<p>For VAT and Corporate Tax groups, only the representative member or parent company may submit an application using the group&#8217;s EmaraTax account and Tax Registration Number (TRN).</p>
<p>For Pillar Two Top-up Tax matters, applications may only be submitted by the Domestic Designated Filing Entity (DDFE) on behalf of the multinational enterprise group.</p>
<p>Registered tax agents may also apply on behalf of clients, provided they are authorised and registered with the FTA for the relevant tax type.</p>
<p>Applications must relate to federal taxes, including VAT, Excise Tax, Corporate Tax or Top-up Tax, and must address genuine technical uncertainty rather than seek confirmation of provisions that are already clear in the legislation.</p>
<p><strong>Application process and fees</strong></p>
<p>All applications must be submitted through the EmaraTax portal in either Arabic or English.</p>
<p>Applicants are required to provide a cover letter explaining the background to the request, the relevant legislative provisions and a detailed technical analysis. Supporting documents, such as contracts, invoices and any third-party tax advice, must also be included.</p>
<p>The application fee is AED 1,500 for requests covering a single tax type and AED 2,250 where more than one tax is involved.</p>
<p>Once a complete application has been received, the FTA aims to issue a Private Clarification within 60 business days.</p>
<p><strong>Circumstances where requests may be rejected</strong></p>
<p>The guide identifies several situations where the FTA will reject an application, including where the applicant is ineligible, lacks appropriate authorisation, or where the request falls outside the scope of the Private Clarification process.</p>
<p>Examples include applications relating to administrative penalty waivers, information technology issues or reviews of tax assessments.</p>
<p>Requests will also be rejected if the applicant fails to provide additional information requested by the FTA within 40 business days.</p>
<p>The authority may additionally reject applications that are incomplete, lack sufficient technical analysis, concern matters already addressed in existing public guidance, involve hypothetical scenarios, or are considered to relate to tax planning, avoidance or evasion.</p>
<p><strong>Refunds available in limited circumstances</strong></p>
<p>The FTA confirms that application fees are generally non-refundable.</p>
<p>However, refunds may be issued automatically if an applicant withdraws the request within two business days of submission or where the FTA decides not to issue a clarification because the applicant was already subject to a tax audit covering the same matter at the time the application was made.</p>
